articles.title: One outfit becomes a blueprint for six autumn remixes
articles.standfirst: A navy chore jacket, grey hoodie and wide dark trousers have set a practical new direction for six autumn outfit variations.

blocks.alt: One outfit becomes a blueprint for six autumn remixes

runs.text: A single outfit reference has become the basis for a six-look autumn wardrobe exercise, extending a wider attempt to define a recognisable personal style without reducing it to one uniform.

The source image combines a washed navy chore jacket with a grey hoodie, very loose dark corduroy trousers, black shoes and a tan backpack. None of the pieces is especially formal or attention-seeking on its own. The character comes from the proportions: short practical layers on top, substantial volume through the trousers and a narrow finish at the feet.
Remixing the rules, not copying the outfit
The new brief asks for six outfits that feel similar while remixing the underlying style. That makes the reference more useful as a system than as a shopping list.

Its first rule is layering. The hoodie softens the workwear jacket and gives the upper half depth without adding a complicated colour story. Navy, grey, charcoal and tan also sit comfortably together, making the outfit feel considered while remaining easy to repeat.

The second rule is contrast in shape. The jacket is comparatively neat and structured, while the trousers are deliberately oversized and heavily cuffed. That imbalance prevents the look from becoming a generic workwear combination. It feels relaxed, youthful and slightly off-centre, but still practical enough for everyday use.

A third rule is texture. Washed cotton, jersey and corduroy create variation even though the palette is muted. Autumn dressing often relies on exactly that kind of material contrast: interest comes from surface and weight rather than bright graphics or obvious branding.

The backpack matters too. Its warm colour breaks up the blues and greys, while its utilitarian shape supports the rest of the outfit. Accessories are therefore part of the structure rather than an afterthought.
A broader autumn direction

The exercise follows earlier explorations of six autumn and winter outfits, then a further set focused on jumpers in different colours, including a more traditional “grandpa jumper” direction. Together, they suggest a wardrobe built around adaptable layers rather than isolated statement pieces.

That approach suits Glasgow’s changeable weather. A hoodie, overshirt or jacket can be added or removed without collapsing the whole outfit, while looser trousers allow heavier fabrics and warmer base layers. The same silhouette can move between chore jackets, knitted cardigans, wool overshirts and compact outerwear.

The aim is not to reproduce the reference image six times. A successful remix should retain its balance of practical clothing, soft layers, roomy proportions and restrained colour while changing at least one major variable: fabric, outer layer, knitwear, footwear or accent colour.

Within the Government for SwS framework, the work sits clearly in the Identity strand. Clothing becomes a repeatable visual language—distinctive enough to feel personal, flexible enough to function in ordinary life and broad enough to evolve through winter.

The result is a useful shift from asking whether one outfit works to identifying why it works. Once those rules are visible, six variations become more than alternatives: they become the beginnings of a coherent wardrobe.

articles.title: Headline spending totals hide where the squeeze lands
articles.standfirst: Real-terms public spending is higher than a decade ago, but welfare and debt interest absorb much of the rise while several services still face cuts.

blocks.alt: Headline spending totals hide where the squeeze lands

runs.text: A claim that total UK public spending is higher in real terms than it was a decade ago is broadly correct. But it does not settle the argument over austerity, because the total says little about which parts of the state received the money — or what those budgets can now buy.
The distinction matters as the country approaches another difficult Budget. Spending can rise overall while individual services face cuts, if faster-growing commitments absorb the increase.
The total is not the whole story
The
Office for Budget Responsibility
expects total managed expenditure to reach 45 per cent of GDP in 2025–26, above its pre-pandemic share. The
House of Commons Library
likewise records social protection and health as the two largest spending areas, together accounting for almost half of the 2025–26 total.

Those figures make it misleading to describe every year since 2010 as a uniform reduction in government spending. The pandemic produced an exceptional surge, health spending has grown, an ageing population raises pension and care costs, and higher prices require larger cash budgets simply to maintain the same purchasing power.

Yet none of that disproves the experience of cuts elsewhere. Between 2010–11 and 2019–20, the OBR says spending fell by 6.4 percentage points as a share of GDP, driven partly by a 3.8-point reduction in day-to-day departmental spending. Local government, justice, transport and other unprotected services did not move in step with pensions or the NHS.

That is why a rising national total can coexist with fewer staff, reduced opening hours, deteriorating assets and councils withdrawing services. “More spending” and “cuts” are not always competing descriptions of the same budget; they can describe different lines within it.
Welfare and interest change the composition

Two pressures now loom especially large. Social protection is expected to account for £407 billion in 2025–26, around 30 per cent of all public spending. That includes the state pension as well as working-age benefits, so treating the entire category as discretionary welfare obscures its scale and structure.
Debt interest is also consuming far more than before the pandemic. The
Commons Library

says the government spent about £109 billion servicing debt in 2025–26 — roughly eight per cent of total spending and one of the highest shares in 50 years. Higher inflation and interest rates have made that bill much more expensive without producing an extra nurse, teacher, bus or repaired road.
The squeeze is likely to remain uneven. Recent
Institute for Fiscal Studies analysis

found that planned growth in health and defence takes up most of the real-terms increase available through 2028–29, leaving several other departments facing reductions. Higher pay and inflation could erode those settlements further.

The useful question, then, is not simply whether the state spends more pounds than it did ten years ago. It is how much remains for everyday services after pensions, benefits, health, defence and debt interest are met — and whether those services can still deliver the same standard. Headline totals can answer the first question while concealing the second.

articles.title: Upright & Vertical identity channels Carnaby Street energy
articles.standfirst: A bold green-and-pink wordmark sets a deliberately handmade direction for a new culture, music and arts Substack inspired by 1960s Carnaby Street publishing.

blocks.alt: Upright & Vertical identity channels Carnaby Street energy

runs.text: A new visual identity concept for a culture, music and arts Substack has taken shape around a deliberately handmade wordmark, using bright colour and uneven lettering to evoke the independent publications associated with 1960s Carnaby Street.
The design presents the name
Upright & Vertical

across two stacked lines. “Upright” appears in green, while “Vertical” is picked out in pink, with a small green ampersand joining the two. The letterforms vary in width, angle and baseline, giving the mark the appearance of paper shapes assembled by hand rather than text placed from a conventional digital font.
A wordmark that behaves like print

The strongest feature is its physical quality. Individual letters look as though they have been cut, shifted and pressed into position, producing a rhythm that feels lively without becoming unreadable. That roughness separates the identity from the polished minimalism common to newsletter platforms and gives it a clearer editorial personality.

The two-colour palette reinforces the effect. Green and pink are vivid enough to suggest shop signage, posters and youth magazines, while the large block shapes keep the name legible at a glance. The wordmark can therefore behave as both a publication title and a graphic object.

The design was shown as work in progress inside Figma, with further variations visible below the main lock-up. Music clippings and printed ephemera around the screen add context to the reference point: a period when record culture, fashion, illustration and editorial design frequently overlapped.
Carnaby Street as a direction

The intention is not to reproduce one historic masthead exactly. Instead, the concept draws on a broader visual language associated with London’s 1960s counterculture: irregular typography, assertive colour and the feeling that a publication has been assembled by people rather than generated from a neutral template.

That suits a Substack covering culture, music and the arts. The identity promises something selective and authored, with enough looseness to accommodate different subjects while retaining a recognisable point of view.

The name adds another layer. “Upright” can imply confidence or principle, while “Vertical” describes both the stacked composition and the shape of contemporary screen-based publishing. Placed together, the words feel slightly formal and slightly absurd, a tension matched by the playful treatment of the letters.

The concept is still presented as a design direction rather than a finished publication system. Questions remain around how the wordmark will scale, how accompanying typography will work and whether the same character can carry through article pages, email headers and social graphics.

Even at this stage, however, the central idea is clear: Upright & Vertical is being positioned as a publication with the energy of a small independent magazine, translated for a modern scrolling format.

articles.title: Mystery cat spotted arriving at Homlea Road
articles.standfirst: Photographs show an unidentified woman carrying a ginger-and-white cat into a Glasgow residential building, with the reason for the visit unknown.

blocks.alt: Mystery cat spotted arriving at Homlea Road

runs.text: A woman has been photographed carrying a cat into a residential building at 37 Homlea Road in Glasgow, in an unexplained arrival captured on Monday 26 October.

Two photographs taken from above show the woman walking across the wet approach to the property with a grey plastic pet carrier in one hand and a drink in the other. In a closer view, a ginger-and-white cat is visible behind the carrier’s metal grille, sitting on bedding inside.

Neither the woman nor the cat has been identified. There is also no confirmed explanation for the visit, how long the animal might remain at the address, or whether the woman was arriving as a resident, visitor or in some other capacity.
Arrival captured on camera

The wider photograph shows the woman dressed in a bright blue hoodie, dark trousers and white trainers as she makes her way towards the building. The road and pavement are visibly wet, placing the arrival amid damp conditions.

The second photograph gives a much closer view of the carrier. The animal is positioned towards the front of the container and appears to be looking through the grille, with light-coloured bedding arranged beneath it.

blocks.alt: Mystery cat spotted arriving at Homlea Road

runs.text: Together, the images establish that a person carrying a cat approached the building. They do not establish where the pair had come from, which flat they were visiting, who owns the animal or whether this was the beginning of a longer stay.

The carrier appears to be a rigid, ventilated model with a secured metal door. Nothing in either photograph suggests that the animal was loose or being transported without restraint. Beyond those visible details, however, the pictures offer few clues about the circumstances of the journey.
Questions remain unanswered
The sighting raises several straightforward questions: who is the woman, who owns the cat, and what brings the animal to Homlea Road?

For now, none can be answered from the available evidence. No name, destination within the building or purpose of the visit has been independently established. It is therefore not possible to say whether the cat is a new resident, a temporary guest, being looked after by someone in the building or simply passing through.

There is no indication from the photographs of an emergency or anything untoward. Carrying a cat in a secure travel container is an ordinary way of transporting an animal, although the context of this particular journey remains unknown.
For Sam, whose building was the scene of the arrival, the photographs record a small but intriguing development on an otherwise ordinary Monday.
Until more information emerges, the identity of the ginger-and-white passenger — and the reason for its arrival — remain a mystery.

articles.title: Sam joins urgent BBC government presentation project
articles.standfirst: A rapid-turnaround Backstage assignment will demonstrate how one BBC programme could power an entire universe of digital content.

blocks.alt: Sam joins urgent BBC government presentation project

runs.text: A new assignment in the BBC's Backstage Content Production team has placed UX designer Sam Smith on a rapid-turnaround creative project supporting a forthcoming presentation to the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS).

The brief, delivered by creative director Gruff on Monday 26 October, concerns a keynote presentation outlining how the BBC could transform its media supply chain. The talk is expected to make the case for investment in the technology and skills needed to support the broadcaster's future. Gruff said he had heard a figure of £850 million associated with the occasion, although he was unable to confirm precisely what that sum represented.

The presentation's narrative had reportedly received sign-off from the BBC director-general over the weekend. Its third act, the focus of the Backstage assignment, explores the capabilities required to turn traditional broadcast programmes into a much wider range of digital experiences.
From one programme to a content universe
At the centre of the demonstration is
Evolution

, a BBC natural history series selected both for its strong visual material and its thematic relevance. The concept is to show how a single episode could be repurposed into news-style articles, short-form social videos, audio experiences and other editorial formats.

Rather than treating every new format as a separate production exercise, the imagined supply chain would ingest media into a unified system and enrich it with detailed, time-based metadata. Editorial teams could then discover relevant sequences, identify stories within programmes and create versions tailored to different audiences and platforms.

The ambition extends beyond faster editing. Structured information could enable systems to suggest new content packages proactively, connecting a programme's scenes and subjects to potential editorial or marketing opportunities.

The finished demonstration will take the form of a continuously looping, widescreen video behind the keynote speaker. Its purpose is to communicate the scale of the idea visually, without requiring the audience to follow a conventional slide-by-slide explanation.
An urgent first assignment

Smith has been asked to help develop the individual content assets that will populate the sequence. These include a realistic BBC-style article drawing on the programme's subject matter, vertical videos adapted from broadcast footage and representations of content within recognisable device and platform interfaces.

The work involves retrieving programme material and transcripts from BBC Library, then adapting it into convincing examples of future audience experiences. During the briefing, Smith successfully regained access to the archive service after an initial permissions issue.

Gruff will build the overall motion framework and assemble the finished 16:9 composition, while coordinating the visual direction with Hannah, who is working on the presentation. A shared planning document is intended to divide the asset work between them.
The deadline is unusually tight. The team expects to undertake most of the production on Monday, with the possibility of additional work on Tuesday before the presentation.
More than a design exercise

The assignment marks an early opportunity for Smith to contribute to the Backstage team's work beyond conventional product interface design. It combines archival research, editorial storytelling, motion design and speculative UX into a single communication challenge.

The broader argument is that the BBC's future will depend not simply on producing programmes, but on building the infrastructure that allows its creativity, knowledge and culture to reach audiences in more flexible ways.
For now, the challenge is immediate: turn one television series into a credible glimpse of what an entire connected content ecosystem might look like.

articles.title: Body tab takes shape as a native health dashboard
articles.standfirst: A new landing-page brief gives Body a stretchable blue header, modular health summaries and reusable native interactions.

blocks.alt: Body tab takes shape as a native health dashboard

runs.text: The Body section of the
SWS.GOV

iOS app has moved from a broad ambition to a defined native landing-page brief. The proposed screen brings health information, quick routes and recent activity into one place, while giving the tab a visual identity distinct from News, Food and the rest of the app.

Its most deliberate feature is a blue header fixed to the top edge of the display. When the page is already at the top and the user pulls down, the interface will keep showing blue rather than revealing a white layer behind it. The familiar iOS rubber-band movement remains, but the colour field stretches with the gesture so the screen continues to feel like one coherent surface.

Content inside the header will move down as the pull extends. The date will also respond through variable typography, becoming progressively heavier with the gesture before settling back when released. The effect is intended to reward a natural interaction rather than introduce a separate animation for its own sake. It should remain restrained, responsive and compatible with reduced-motion preferences.

blocks.alt: Body tab takes shape as a native health dashboard

runs.text: Below the header, the landing page will organise Body material through native carousels, shortcuts and modular sections. These can provide routes into the fuller parts of the service without turning the first screen into a dense control panel. The information hierarchy should make the most useful items immediately visible while allowing additional detail to sit one step deeper.

Health metrics will initially use clearly designed placeholders where live data or final integrations are not yet available. That keeps layout work moving without pretending that sample figures are real. Placeholder states must be visually credible, easy to replace and explicit inside the development build, so the final components can accept genuine data without a redesign.

The brief continues the wider rule for the native app: use SwiftUI controls and established project components before creating new patterns. Navigation, cards, typography, spacing and loading states should draw from the existing design system. The aim is not to reproduce a web page inside a native shell, but to make Body behave like a first-class iOS destination while remaining recognisably part of
SWS.GOV

blocks.alt: Body tab takes shape as a native health dashboard

runs.text: Accessibility is part of the structure rather than a finishing pass. The stretched header needs reliable contrast at every size, the changing date weight must remain legible with Dynamic Type, and the pull interaction cannot be the only way to understand or reach information. VoiceOver order should follow the visual hierarchy, while any decorative motion should disappear cleanly when reduced motion is enabled.

The resulting direction is calm but tactile. Most of the page stays familiar: a header, useful summaries and routes to deeper content. The character comes from how those pieces respond at the top of the scroll view and how consistently the blue field holds together during movement.

Body is therefore becoming more than another tab label. The new brief establishes a recognisable home for personal health information and a reusable model for expressive native behaviour elsewhere in the app. With the layout, motion principle and component strategy now stated, implementation can concentrate on polish and data integration instead of deciding what the screen is meant to be.

articles.title: The internet became a global majority only in 2018
articles.standfirst: The halfway point arrived later than popular memory suggests, with 51.2% of the world online by the end of 2018.

blocks.alt: The internet became a global majority only in 2018

runs.text: A simple question about when the internet became normal has produced a surprisingly recent answer. On the broadest global measure, the first year in which most people were online was 2018. That was when the International Telecommunication Union estimated that internet use had crossed the halfway point, reaching 51.2 per cent of the world’s population.

The threshold represented about 3.9 billion people. It arrived later than the popular story of the web might suggest, partly because memories of adoption are often shaped by countries, workplaces and social groups that connected earlier. Broadband, smartphones and social media could feel universal while billions of people still had no regular access.

The definition matters. The World Bank’s version of the ITU indicator counts an internet user as someone who has used the internet from any location during the previous three months. That access can happen through a computer, mobile phone, games machine, digital television or another connected device. The measure is therefore about actual recent use, not simply whether a household has a cable or a country has network coverage.

blocks.alt: The internet became a global majority only in 2018

runs.text: Growth before the halfway point was rapid. ITU’s 2018 report estimated that one billion people, or 15.8 per cent of the global population, were online in 2005. Thirteen years later, the total had nearly quadrupled. Yet the headline concealed a steep divide: four in five people in developed countries were online, compared with 45 per cent in developing countries. In the 47 least-developed countries, four in five people remained offline.

That inequality also explains why there is no single answer for every place. Individual countries passed the 50 per cent mark in different years, and some groups within them connected much earlier than others. Asking when “most people” used the internet therefore needs a population and a definition. For the world as a whole, using the standard international indicator, 2018 is the defensible answer.

The network has expanded substantially since then. ITU estimates for 2025 put the number of users at about six billion, equal to 74 per cent of the global population. Around 1.3 billion people came online between 2020 and 2025. Even so, an estimated 2.2 billion people remained offline, a reminder that a global majority is not the same thing as universal access.

blocks.alt: The internet became a global majority only in 2018

runs.text: The timing changes how the internet age looks in retrospect. The web was invented in 1989, commercial and domestic use spread through the 1990s, and smartphones accelerated access after 2007. But the point at which an average human being was more likely than not to be an internet user came almost three decades after the web began.

The answer is therefore both 2018 and a warning against treating technological history as a single shared experience. The internet could already dominate culture, commerce and politics before it reached most people. Its majority moment was not the beginning of the digital world; it was the moment global participation finally caught up with a transformation that had long appeared complete from inside its most connected parts.

articles.title: Reader redesign brings type and colour controls to SwS iOS
articles.standfirst: A new appearance menu will add themes, type choices and persistent reading preferences to the native SWS.GOV article view.

blocks.alt: Reader redesign brings type and colour controls to SwS iOS

runs.text: SwS.GOV

’s native iOS article reader is set for a more personal second pass, with a new design brief introducing colour themes, typeface choices and remembered reading preferences. The work builds on the existing reader rather than replacing it, concentrating on controls that make longer articles more comfortable without turning the interface into a settings screen.

The current Open in Safari button will be removed from the toolbar. In its place, a compact appearance menu will bring the most useful reading controls into the article itself. Readers will be able to change the visual treatment while keeping their place, see the result immediately and return to the story without navigating away.

The theme selector will offer System, Light, Dark and a warmer beige treatment. System will continue to follow the iPhone’s appearance automatically, while the three fixed choices will let people keep a particular reading environment regardless of the device setting. The beige option is intended as a softer, paper-like alternative for longer sessions rather than a decorative novelty.

blocks.alt: Reader redesign brings type and colour controls to SwS iOS

runs.text: Typography will remain rooted in the identity of
SWS.GOV

. BBC Reith will be the default combination, using Reith Serif for headlines and Reith Sans for body copy, supporting information and interface details. Alternative choices are expected to include Apple’s San Francisco and New York families, alongside a restrained monospaced option. Each choice will be applied as a coherent reading system instead of mixing unrelated headline and body styles.

Font size and line spacing controls will sit alongside those typeface choices. Adjustments should be visible in the open article and should not disturb the reading position. The selected appearance will persist between articles and launches, making the reader feel like a considered part of the app rather than a temporary web-style view.

The brief also protects the simplicity of the existing interface. The appearance menu belongs in the native toolbar, uses standard SwiftUI controls and should reuse components already present in the project. It must work with Dynamic Type, VoiceOver, increased contrast and reduced motion. Theme colours need sufficient contrast across headlines, body text, links, captions and controls, while images should remain unaffected by cosmetic filters.

blocks.alt: Reader redesign brings type and colour controls to SwS iOS

runs.text: A small preview inside the menu may help people compare choices, but the article itself remains the primary preview. Defaults should stay sensible: System theme, BBC Reith typography and the standard text scale. A reset action will return every preference to that baseline.
This is a focused refinement rather than a new destination. The reader already provides the structure; the next step is to make it feel more native, more adaptable and more recognisably part of
SWS.GOV
. Removing an outward-facing Safari shortcut in favour of useful reading controls keeps attention on the article while giving the reader meaningful control over how it is presented.

articles.title: A dark joke leads to a Seinfeld reckoning
articles.standfirst: A conversation moves from Michael Jackson and an old gentile joke to Tim Whatley, Jewish humour and Jerry Seinfeld's politics.

blocks.alt: A dark joke leads to a Seinfeld reckoning

runs.text: A conversation about comedy has taken an unlikely route from Michael Jackson to Jewish anti-humour, through an episode of
Seinfeld
, and finally into the politics of Israel and Palestine.

What began as the unveiling of a deliberately offensive joke became an impromptu discussion about what makes dark humour work, how much an audience must already know, and whether a comedian's public convictions change the way their older material is received.
Hello, Michael

The opening contribution was a brutal variation on the familiar three-people-walk-into-a-bar format. A Black man, a white man and a man described as a paedophile walk into a bar. The barman looks up and says simply: “Hello, Michael.”

The intended subject was Michael Jackson. The gag compresses three apparently separate characters into one famous figure, drawing on Jackson's changing appearance and the allegations made against him. Jackson publicly discussed sharing his bed with children, but allegations of sexual abuse should not be mistaken for convictions: he denied wrongdoing and was never convicted.

The joke's mechanism is almost mathematical. Set up three people, remove two, and deliver a completely mundane greeting. Its creator defended the darkness on the grounds that the controversy concerned the celebrity himself, rather than the telling of the joke. Whether that defence convinces an audience is another matter.
No complaints
A second, older joke seemed almost absurdly mild by comparison. Two gentile businessmen meet. One asks how business is going. The reply: “No complaints.”
Initially interpreted as a joke about
genteel
businessmen and British understatement, the crucial word turned out to be
gentile
, meaning non-Jewish. The joke relies on the familiar stereotype of Jewish complaining, a recurring device within traditions of Jewish self-deprecating humour.
It illustrates a different kind of efficiency. Nothing explicitly funny happens. The listener has to supply the implied contrast, and the ordinary response becomes the punchline.
Converted for the jokes
That led directly to Tim Whatley, the dentist played by Bryan Cranston in
Seinfeld

. Whatley's conversion to Judaism prompts Jerry to suspect he has converted solely for access to Jewish jokes. The sitcom escalates the dispute until Jerry faces accusations of being an “anti-Dentite”.

The exchange prompted a joke about claiming a distant connection to Jewish ancestry largely for the comedy. Once again, the underlying question was who is entitled to tell a particular joke, and whether offence depends on identity, intention or context.
A different Jerry

The final turn was political. Jerry Seinfeld's public support for Israel, and particularly his comments about pro-Palestinian activism, were raised as a jarring contrast with the playful satire of his sitcom.

At Duke University in September 2025, Seinfeld compared the Free Palestine movement with the Ku Klux Klan, arguing that the movement concealed antisemitism. His remarks attracted criticism, including from a Jewish state senator who shared the event stage.
The Guardian reported the remarks

There is no neat equivalence between fictional Jerry and the real comedian. But the contrast offers a fitting closing question: when a performer famous for mocking moral certainty takes a firm public position on a contentious political conflict, does it alter the audience's relationship with the jokes?
The conversation began with a barman greeting Michael Jackson. It ended with comedy itself on trial.

articles.title: Windows XP sample rekindles a taste for Beethoven
articles.standfirst: A half-remembered Windows sample has been identified as the Scherzo from Beethoven’s Ninth, prompting a search to hear it live.

blocks.alt: Windows XP sample rekindles a taste for Beethoven

runs.text: A piece of music remembered from Windows XP has been identified as the Scherzo from Ludwig van Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 in D minor, turning a fragment of computer nostalgia into a new interest in hearing the work live.

The track appeared in Windows XP’s sample-music collection under the title “Beethoven’s Symphony No. 9 (Scherzo)”. Music catalogues and surviving references to the operating system’s media folder consistently connect it with the Ninth Symphony’s second movement, marked Molto vivace.

That identification explains why the music feels so immediately energetic. The movement is driven by forceful rhythms, sudden contrasts and prominent timpani, giving it a physical momentum that can sound surprisingly modern. It is not the famous choral “Ode to Joy” finale most readily associated with the Ninth, but the restless orchestral movement that comes before the slower Adagio.

blocks.alt: Windows XP sample rekindles a taste for Beethoven

runs.text: For anyone who first encountered it through a PC, the route into Beethoven is unusually domestic. Windows XP placed sample audio inside the same environment as desktop backgrounds, startup sounds and Windows Media Player visualisations. A short demonstration file could become part of the atmosphere of using a family computer, remembered years later even when its name had been forgotten.

The rediscovery has now produced a more practical question: where to hear the Scherzo performed by a full orchestra. The answer is to look for concerts programming Beethoven’s complete Symphony No. 9 rather than searching only for the word “Scherzo”. Orchestra listings normally advertise the symphony as a whole, with the second movement included automatically.

blocks.alt: Windows XP sample rekindles a taste for Beethoven

runs.text: A live performance would make the qualities compressed into the old sample much clearer. The timpani can answer the orchestra across the hall, string entries pass through the ensemble, and changes in weight and speed become visible as well as audible. The urge to move or conduct along with it is understandable, although large gestures from a seat would risk distracting nearby listeners. Quiet movement is a safer compromise.

There is also a pleasing reversal in the story. The Windows file existed to demonstrate a computer’s multimedia capabilities; decades later, the computer has become the clue leading back to a work first performed in 1824. The technology is obsolete, but the music has escaped the folder that introduced it.

No concert has yet been selected. The next step is to watch Scottish orchestra and concert-hall programmes for Beethoven’s Ninth, while distinguishing full performances from events that feature only the final movement or an arrangement.

The discovery shows how software can leave cultural memories beyond its interface. Windows XP is usually recalled through its green hill, blue taskbar and startup sound. For Sam, its more durable legacy may be a furious Beethoven rhythm and the realisation that the familiar sample belongs in a concert hall rather than an old media folder.

articles.title: Old iMac server plan reaches bootable USB stage
articles.standfirst: The recovered 32GB drive is being prepared for Debian as the old iMac media-server project gains a printable installation guide.

blocks.alt: Old iMac server plan reaches bootable USB stage

runs.text: The plan to turn an older Intel iMac into a lightweight Linux media machine has moved from recovery to preparation, with the 32GB USB stick now becoming the route into Debian.

The drive was found in a wallet after being missing long enough to stall the project. Its return removed the most mundane blocker, but the next stage immediately became more technical: preparing the flash drive on a modern Apple silicon Mac and making sure the whole physical device, rather than only one partition, was visible.

That distinction matters when creating bootable media. A partition is only one volume on the stick; the installer image needs to be written to the device correctly so the Intel iMac can recognise it at startup. Disk Utility can hide physical drives unless its view is changed to show all devices, which made the preparation look more confusing than it was.

blocks.alt: Old iMac server plan reaches bootable USB stage

runs.text: The intended setup remains deliberately modest. Debian will provide a lightweight base for an old machine that no longer needs to behave like a conventional desktop. Plex is being considered for low-quality local streaming, while DVD playback would give the built-in optical drive a practical role. The emphasis is on using the hardware within its limits rather than expecting modern server performance.

The project has also acquired something it lacked when it was first discussed: a proper installation manual. A detailed guide has been requested from the point at which the USB drive is flashed, covering the iMac’s boot process, Debian installation, storage and networking choices, media software, remote access and the checks needed before the machine can be left running independently.

That approach turns a collection of chat instructions into something closer to documentation supplied with a product. It reduces the risk of reaching a critical screen during installation and having to guess which disk, partition or network option is safe. It should also make the process easier to resume after a pause.

Printing is part of the design. The guide is intended to work on paper beside the iMac, where switching between installation screens and online instructions would be awkward. The discovery of a dedicated “print as booklet” option simplifies that further, allowing the document to be folded into a compact reference rather than handled as a loose stack of pages.

blocks.alt: Old iMac server plan reaches bootable USB stage

runs.text: None of this means the server is finished. The USB still needs to boot successfully on the Intel iMac, Debian must recognise the machine’s networking and graphics hardware, and Plex performance will need to be tested against realistic files. DVD playback may also require additional packages after the base installation.

Even so, the project now has a clear sequence. The recovered stick provides the installer, the modern Mac prepares it, the old iMac becomes the target, and the printed guide carries the process through each decision. What began as an idea for reusing ageing hardware is finally becoming an installation plan that can be followed from start to finish.

articles.title: Returning to GCU exposes a familiar live-chat trap
articles.standfirst: A fourth or fifth visit to review student projects revealed how quickly live streams, polls and chat can become substitutes for a distinctive design idea.

blocks.alt: Returning to GCU exposes a familiar live-chat trap

runs.text: A return to Glasgow Caledonian University has highlighted a familiar pattern in student design work: the live-event app built around polls, chat and a large broadcast stream.

This was at least the fourth time, and possibly the fifth, that Sam had gone back to GCU to review student projects since leaving the course for the BBC. The repeat visit brought an odd sense of recognition. A pitch for another live experience sounded strikingly similar to concepts seen in previous years, often attached to Eurovision, Glastonbury or a major football tournament.

The format is easy to understand. A live video sits at the centre, with audience comments moving beside it and a poll inviting people to vote. Each feature is plausible. Broadcasters already use participation, conversation and voting, while students naturally reach for ideas they recognise from services they use.

blocks.alt: Returning to GCU exposes a familiar live-chat trap

runs.text: The problem is not that live chat or polls can never work. It is that they often appear as the first and most literal interpretation of a brief, before a distinctive audience need, editorial purpose or behaviour has been established. Swapping one festival or tournament for another does not necessarily create a new product idea.

That creates a challenge for anyone giving feedback. A critic needs to recognise the effort behind an early concept without pretending that familiarity is originality. The useful question is not simply whether the interface can be built, but why it should exist, what it changes for the user and what makes this version meaningfully different from the many similar proposals before it.

The strongest student work tends to reveal something specific. It may identify an overlooked moment in a journey, a tension in how people experience an event or a group whose needs are poorly served. Once that insight exists, a chat, poll or notification can become an appropriate response rather than a decorative bundle of expected features.

Returning as an alumnus makes the pattern especially visible. Sam once completed the same kind of student work before leaving during the final year to join the BBC as a UX trainee. Since then, professional experience has changed the standard by which an idea is judged. A polished screen matters less than the quality of the thinking that led to it.

The session was not entirely severe. There were lighter exchanges too, including a joke about modern concert prices after one project cited annual ticket spending. Those moments helped keep the review conversational, even when the underlying feedback was demanding.

blocks.alt: Returning to GCU exposes a familiar live-chat trap

runs.text: The lesson from the latest visit is not that students must invent something nobody has ever imagined. It is that familiar ingredients need a sharper reason for being there. Originality can come from the problem chosen, the evidence gathered, the trade-offs made and the clarity with which a designer refuses the obvious answer.

After four or five rounds of reviewing projects, the recurring live-chat pitch has become a useful warning. If the first concept arrives too quickly, it may be a sign that the real design work has not started yet.

articles.title: SwS iOS roadmap adds native Food and News
articles.standfirst: Two native SwiftUI sections will bring the web recipes and edition-led News experiences into the SwS iOS app without duplicating its design system.

blocks.alt: SwS iOS roadmap adds native Food and News

runs.text: A pair of new development briefs has put Food and News next on the roadmap for the native SwS iOS app. The two sections will translate existing
SWS.GOV
web experiences into SwiftUI while keeping the app’s current visual language and shared components intact.

The first brief turns the website’s recipes area into a native section called Food. The name is deliberately broader and more direct than Recipes, but the immediate job is clear: make the existing recipe experience feel at home on iPhone rather than presenting a web page inside the app.

That means treating the website as the source for content structure and behaviour, then rebuilding the interface with native controls already available in the project. Recipe imagery, cards, lists and detail views should sit comfortably beside the rest of the app. Navigation, loading states and typography should also inherit the established system instead of creating a second design language.

blocks.alt: SwS iOS roadmap adds native Food and News

runs.text: A native build also creates room for the small interactions people expect on iOS. Scrolling, swiping between collections, opening a recipe and moving back through the app should all feel immediate and familiar. The important point is restraint: those interactions should support the content, not become a showcase of effects that makes a simple task harder.

News follows the same principle, with one extra requirement: its editorial character must survive the move. The website’s “The Early Edition” and “The Late Edition” headings are part of that identity, including their distinctive type treatment. They should remain recognisable in the native experience rather than being flattened into a generic feed.

The News brief also calls for native carousels and the varied display patterns used on the web. A lead story can carry more visual weight, while supporting items can move through horizontal collections or tighter card groups. The aim is not to reproduce every pixel. It is to preserve the rhythm and hierarchy that make an edition feel curated.

blocks.alt: SwS iOS roadmap adds native Food and News

runs.text: Both briefs set useful limits. They ask for native SwiftUI, reuse of components already in the repository and a straightforward implementation. That should reduce duplication, make future maintenance easier and keep Food and News consistent with the homepage and other native areas as the app grows.

Consistency matters beyond appearance. Shared components give accessibility behaviour, spacing and dynamic type a common foundation. They also make it less likely that a future change to navigation or card styling will need to be repeated separately across several sections.
This is still a development direction, not a completed release. The next step is to audit the existing project, map reusable components and connect each screen to the same content sources that power
SWS.GOV
. Once that groundwork is done, Food and News can become focused native destinations without turning the app into a collection of unrelated experiments.

Together, the two additions make the iOS roadmap clearer. SwS is not abandoning the web or copying it blindly. It is using the website as an editorial and structural reference, then choosing the native patterns that work best on a phone.

articles.title: Lost USB stick turns up in wallet
articles.standfirst: A missing 32 GB memory stick has resurfaced in an unlikely place, clearing the way for a 2006 iMac Linux and Kodi project.

blocks.alt: Lost USB stick turns up in wallet

runs.text: A missing 32 GB USB memory stick has been recovered from an unexpected location: a wallet. The discovery clears an obstacle to plans to give a 2006 iMac a new lease of life as a dedicated media player.

The stick had been missing for some time. There was a lingering recollection of having seen it somewhere, but not enough information to establish where it had gone. The answer turned out to be much closer at hand than expected. On checking the wallet, the missing drive was found inside.

It is an unremarkable discovery in practical terms, but a satisfying one. A device which had been mentally filed as lost was not lost at all. It had simply been put somewhere memorable enough to feel safe at the time, then forgotten.
A small discovery unlocks a bigger project

The memory stick is intended for use in a project to repurpose an ageing 20-inch Intel iMac. The machine, identified as an iMac5,1, dates from 2006 and still runs Mac OS X Snow Leopard. It has a 2.16 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo processor, 2 GB of memory and an ATI Radeon X1600 graphics card.

The proposed upgrade would introduce a lightweight Debian Linux installation and Kodi, turning the computer into a straightforward media player. The plan is to preserve the existing Mac OS X installation on a separate partition rather than erase it, allowing the machine to retain its original character while gaining a more useful contemporary role.

A bootable USB installer is the first practical step. The recovered 32 GB drive has more than enough capacity for the installation media, which can be prepared on a newer Apple Silicon Mac before being tested on the older machine.

There are still technical uncertainties. The iMac's early Intel firmware and ageing graphics hardware mean that Linux booting, display acceleration and video playback must be tested before any changes are made to the internal hard drive. The intention is to try the installer first, not immediately repartition the machine.
The mystery of the familiar hiding place

The wallet discovery also closes a minor but persistent loop: the sense of having seen an object recently without being able to place the memory. It is precisely the sort of everyday mystery that can linger without ever becoming important enough to prompt a proper search.
In this case, the resolution arrived before the installation project had properly begun. No replacement stick is needed, and there is now a clear route to the next experiment.

For the Government's digital and hardware interests, the immediate outcome is modest but welcome: one recovered memory stick, one avoided purchase, and a nearly 20-year-old iMac a step closer to becoming a Kodi player.
The Linux installation itself remains a future task. The first milestone will be seeing whether the old machine can boot from the newly recovered USB drive at all.

articles.title: Pitch correction can polish singing, not replace it
articles.standfirst: A Logic Pro workflow using Stem Splitter and Flex Pitch can make a rough vocal sound convincing, but it cannot manufacture the whole performance.

blocks.alt: Pitch correction can polish singing, not replace it

runs.text: A proposed Logic Pro experiment could make a rough vocal sound dramatically more tuneful, but it would not manufacture the full impression of being a confident singer. Separating a song into stems, recording a new vocal against the isolated original and then correcting the new take is a sensible production workflow. Its limits lie in what pitch correction does not change.

Apple’s Stem Splitter can isolate vocals, drums, bass, guitar, piano and other instrumental material from a mixed recording. That makes the original singer easier to hear as a guide and creates a cleaner backing track for a replacement performance. It does not, by itself, transfer the singer’s delivery into another voice.

blocks.alt: Pitch correction can polish singing, not replace it

runs.text: Flex Pitch can then analyse the new recording as notes. Logic allows those notes to be moved vertically for pitch, horizontally for timing, resized, split and joined. Vibrato and the gain of individual notes can also be adjusted. The separate Pitch Correction effect can pull an incoming vocal towards notes in a chosen scale, with Apple noting that moderate corrections can introduce very few audible artefacts.

Used carefully, those tools can fix notes that land sharp or flat, tighten entrances and make a hesitant melody feel more deliberate. If the recording already follows roughly the right notes and rhythm, the finished version may sound convincingly in tune. Comping the strongest phrases from several takes can improve the result further before any correction is applied.

The missing ingredients are the reason the process cannot simply create singing ability. Tone, breath control, vowel shape, consonants, dynamics, phrasing and emotional emphasis remain part of the recorded performance. Pitch software can move a note to the right frequency, but it cannot fully replace a clean attack, a controlled breath or a phrase that builds naturally. Large corrections can also expose themselves through warped transitions, unstable formants or a recognisably processed sound.

blocks.alt: Pitch correction can polish singing, not replace it

runs.text: The strongest version of the experiment would therefore use the extracted vocal as a rehearsal and timing reference, not as a template to be copied mechanically. The song should first be moved into a comfortable key if necessary. Several complete takes can then be recorded, followed by a comp of the best sections. Flex Pitch should correct the most distracting notes rather than flatten every variation, with timing changes kept small enough to preserve natural phrasing.

Compression, equalisation, de-essing, reverb and perhaps a quiet double can then help the vocal sit inside the instrumental. Those production choices can make an ordinary home recording feel finished, but they work best when the source performance is already intelligible and reasonably controlled.

The realistic outcome is a polished demo that may sound far better than the untreated take. It could create the impression of a capable, stylised studio vocal. It would not prove that the same performance could be reproduced live, but it could provide a useful bridge between mimicking a melody and learning how to sing it with increasing control.

articles.title: Rail data plan targets rare Cathcart Circle trains
articles.standfirst: A monitoring plan will use detailed timetables and open railway data to flag measurement, engineering and freight movements near the Cathcart Circle.

blocks.alt: Rail data plan targets rare Cathcart Circle trains

runs.text: A plan is taking shape to turn a view of the Cathcart Circle into a more deliberate watchpoint for rare railway movements. The aim is to spot the New Measurement Train, plain-line pattern-recognition sets, engineering workings and any freight paths before they pass the home-office window, rather than recognising them only after they have gone.

There is no single public calendar devoted to unusual trains, but the raw ingredients already exist. Realtime Trains offers detailed searches by railway location and says its timetable can be searched up to 180 days ahead, although information more than 84 days into the future may be less reliable. Its detailed view includes trains that do not stop, making it more useful than an ordinary passenger departure board.

For the Cathcart area, the practical approach is to save searches for the nearest stations and relevant junctions, then inspect the full daily list rather than looking only at ScotRail departures. An unusual path may appear as a passing movement, an empty coaching-stock service or a departmental working. Checking neighbouring timing points can also reveal a train routed close to the Circle even when the most familiar station name is absent from its schedule.

blocks.alt: Rail data plan targets rare Cathcart Circle trains

runs.text: Network Rail’s open-data service creates a route towards automation. It provides operational feeds covering schedules and train movements, meaning a small personal monitor could compare each day’s workings with a baseline of normal passenger services. Anything outside that baseline could be flagged for review and, where live movement data is available, followed as it approaches Glasgow.

The most recognisable target is Network Rail’s New Measurement Train, widely known as the Flying Banana. Network Rail says the converted High Speed Train records track condition at speeds of up to 125mph, using measurement systems, scanners and high-resolution cameras to identify faults before they become a safety or performance problem. Other infrastructure-monitoring vehicles can be less visually obvious, so timing data and service detail are as important as livery.

blocks.alt: Rail data plan targets rare Cathcart Circle trains

runs.text: The system would need to handle uncertainty honestly. Departmental and freight schedules can be altered, cancelled or activated at short notice, while a booked path does not guarantee that a particular locomotive or unit will appear. Live running information is therefore best treated as a warning, not a promise. A useful alert would show the planned passing time, the latest reported movement and how confident the identification is.

A first version does not need custom software. Bookmarked detailed searches, checked each morning and again shortly before a candidate movement, would cover much of the need. The next step could be a lightweight script using the official feeds, with notifications reserved for services that differ meaningfully from the normal pattern.
That would turn a passing interest into a small piece of personal railway infrastructure: part timetable, part anomaly detector and part prompt to look out of the window at the right moment.

articles.title: Hidden iOS gallery takes shape behind weather card
articles.standfirst: A private gallery planned for the SwS iOS app will use an Apple Photos-style interface and a concealed animated route from the homepage.

blocks.alt: Hidden iOS gallery takes shape behind weather card

runs.text: A concealed gallery is taking shape as one of the most distinctive ideas for the SwS iOS app. The proposal places a private clothing-image archive behind the weather card on the homepage, reached by a deliberate double-tap rather than an ordinary navigation item.

The gesture would trigger a full-screen card flip. The whole interface would turn as if it were a hidden bookcase door, revealing the gallery on the other side. It is a playful transition, but it also gives the feature a clear sense of place: the public-facing app remains calm and familiar, while the personal archive feels like a separate room.

Inside, the design brief borrows the clarity of Apple Photos. People and collections would appear in horizontally scrolling carousels, with a broader image grid below. Search and filters would make the archive useful at scale, allowing images to be narrowed by person, type of sag, underwear colour and other available metadata. The aim is not to reproduce Apple’s app exactly, but to use familiar patterns so a potentially large collection remains quick to browse.

blocks.alt: Hidden iOS gallery takes shape behind weather card

runs.text: That interaction is now defined well enough for detailed interface work. The technical route into the media library is not. A review of the available web checkout found a local-only Cloudflare media Worker build, but no confirmed production media address and no Google OAuth configuration that could safely be reused by an iOS client.

Those gaps matter. A hidden gesture is a delightful entrance, not a security boundary. The production app still needs an authenticated service that can decide who may see each image, issue appropriate media responses and protect the underlying archive. Guessing a Worker address or inventing OAuth credentials would create a convincing prototype with an unreliable foundation.

blocks.alt: Hidden iOS gallery takes shape behind weather card

runs.text: Two concrete decisions are therefore needed before the gallery can move from design into a connected build. The first is the authoritative SwS Media source or deployed Worker URL. The second is whether an iOS Google OAuth client has already been registered, including the correct bundle identifier and redirect arrangement. If either does not yet exist, it should be created deliberately as part of the implementation rather than patched in later.

Once those details are settled, the build can proceed in layers: connect the authenticated feed, map the returned metadata into people and collections, add search and filters, and then polish loading, empty and error states. The card-flip transition can be added around that reliable core, with reduced-motion behaviour for people who prefer less animation.

The result would be more than an easter egg. Done properly, it would turn the homepage into a memorable doorway while giving a growing personal archive the structure, speed and privacy controls it needs. The visual idea is ready; the next milestone is establishing the media and identity foundations that make it real.

articles.title: Homer archive plan sets PNG and 8MB standards
articles.standfirst: A maintenance plan will convert mixed-format photographs in a personal archive to PNG while limiting each file to 8MB.

blocks.alt: Homer archive plan sets PNG and 8MB standards

runs.text: A new maintenance plan for the Homer archive will standardise a collection of personal photographs as PNG files while introducing an 8MB maximum for each image. The work is focused initially on the Lewis Leonard folder within the external drive’s Archive/System32 directory, where mixed formats and large files have made the collection less consistent to manage.

The immediate requirement is straightforward: convert every non-PNG image in the folder to PNG, replace the original-format copy only after a successful conversion, and reduce any oversized result until it falls below the agreed ceiling. The plan emerged alongside restoration work on an older photograph, including efforts to brighten, sharpen and add controlled grain without losing the character of the source.

Standardising the format should make the folder easier to preview, process and reuse. PNG is widely supported and avoids the generational loss associated with repeatedly saving JPEG files. A single format also simplifies later automation because scripts do not need separate branches for every extension before beginning an edit, resize or gallery import.

blocks.alt: Homer archive plan sets PNG and 8MB standards

runs.text: The size limit introduces the harder part of the job. PNG compression is lossless, so an image with lots of photographic detail may remain larger than 8MB even after optimisation. Meeting the ceiling reliably can therefore require a staged approach: first remove inefficient encoding, then reduce colour complexity where acceptable, and finally resize dimensions if the file is still too large.

That process needs to protect the archive rather than tidy it destructively. A robust command should create a temporary converted file, check that it opens correctly, confirm its final size and only then remove the original. If any step fails, the source should remain untouched. Existing PNG files also need to pass through the size check rather than being skipped simply because their format is already correct.

Metadata deserves separate attention. Conversion tools can discard capture dates, orientation and location information unless explicitly told to preserve them. Those details may be valuable in a personal collection, particularly when filenames are generic or the visual context is unclear. The clean-up should therefore treat image pixels and historical metadata as equally important parts of the asset.

blocks.alt: Homer archive plan sets PNG and 8MB standards

runs.text: The Lewis Leonard folder will act as a contained test for a wider archive workflow. If the commands handle uppercase extensions, spaces in paths, existing PNGs and unusually large photographs safely, the same method could later be used elsewhere on Homer without turning the whole drive into one high-risk batch operation.

The goal is not simply to save space. Consistent, validated files are easier to browse, back up and feed into future gallery or restoration tools. For the current collection, the PNG standard and 8MB ceiling create a practical baseline: high enough to retain useful detail, but controlled enough to stop individual images becoming awkward to move, upload or process.

articles.title: Repository check confirms SWS.GOV runs without PHP
articles.standfirst: A review of the site’s project configuration confirms its application is built around Next.js, React and TypeScript rather than a PHP backend.

blocks.alt: Repository check confirms SWS.GOV runs without PHP

runs.text: SWS.GOV

’s current application runs on a modern JavaScript stack rather than PHP, a review of the project’s main configuration has confirmed. The repository’s package manifest identifies Next.js, React and TypeScript as the core technologies used to build and operate the site, with no PHP runtime or package manager declared.

The finding settles a straightforward but useful technical question about what sits behind the public service. A .GOV-style identity and a publishing system can easily suggest a traditional server-rendered content platform, particularly WordPress, but the current codebase follows a different model. Its development, build and start commands all call Next.js or Node.js tooling.

That distinction matters because it explains how the site combines a familiar editorial front end with newer application behaviour. The same project can serve published articles, interactive features and administration routes while sharing a common React component system. TypeScript is used for testing and operational scripts, giving the site one main language family across interface work and publishing infrastructure.

blocks.alt: Repository check confirms SWS.GOV runs without PHP

runs.text: The evidence comes from operational files rather than from the site’s visual appearance. The main package manifest defines how developers run, test and build the application, while the repository guide identifies the project as Next.js and points contributors to TypeScript React files. Together, those records establish the technology required by the current application. They are more reliable for this question than guessing from page markup, URLs or the choice of content management system.

The repository also shows that content operations are handled through JavaScript-based scripts. Notion is the canonical content management system for News and Press Office material, and the package configuration includes dedicated TypeScript commands for migration, synchronisation and verification. The site’s own documentation describes validated article snapshots and automated checks that keep published material moving from Notion to the public site.

This does not mean the project is a single, simple front-end bundle. Its dependencies cover data visualisation, Google services, image conversion, schema validation and AI features, while its build commands include paths for Vercel and Cloudflare tooling. The architecture is therefore broader than “a React website”, even though PHP is not part of the application’s declared runtime.

The clarification is also a reminder that a content source and a web runtime are separate choices. Notion stores and structures articles; Next.js turns that material into pages, routes and components; deployment services handle the public build. None of those decisions requires a PHP application server.

blocks.alt: Repository check confirms SWS.GOV runs without PHP

runs.text: For
SWS.GOV

, the practical outcome is consistency. Article syncing, migration checks, front-end components and tests can all live in the same repository and use closely related tooling. That reduces the need to maintain a second server-side language merely to support publishing.
Future changes could, of course, alter the stack. The conclusion applies to the current main configuration inspected on 22 October 2026. For now, however, the evidence is clear:
SWS.GOV
is built and operated through Next.js, React, TypeScript and Node.js tooling, not a PHP backend.

articles.title: Kassiopi holiday photos reveal a recurring waistband
articles.standfirst: Three photographs from a Corfu holiday show visible boxer waistbands becoming an unmistakable feature of the trip.

runs.text: The Government for SwS has reviewed photographic evidence from a holiday in Kassiopi, Corfu, and confirmed a recurring feature of the trip: the waistband of Sam Smith’s boxer shorts was visible above his outer clothing on more than one occasion.

The three photographs document otherwise unremarkable moments of holiday life. There is a book, a balcony, a striking sunset and a respectable amount of relaxation. Yet across these different settings, the exposed underwear provides an unexpectedly consistent visual detail.
An appearance in three acts

blocks.alt: Kassiopi holiday photos reveal a recurring waistband

runs.text: The clearest example comes from an evening photograph taken on a balcony. Wearing a grey Boston Classic Marathon T-shirt and bright blue Adidas-style shorts, Sam leans against the railing as the sky turns vivid orange. Between the hem of the T-shirt and the waistband of the shorts sits a noticeable strip of red fabric and a white Calvin Klein waistband.

It is a photograph ostensibly about a sunset, but the clothing arrangement supplies its own supporting storyline. The shorts sit low enough for the boxers to become an unmistakable part of the outfit, rather than an occasional glimpse.
A second image moves indoors. Sam is reclining on a bed, reading Jon Sopel’s
Strangeland

, wearing green sports shorts and dark Calvin Klein underwear. The book occupies much of the foreground, but the boxer waistband is plainly visible above the shorts. Warm bedside lighting adds a distinctly leisurely atmosphere to the scene.

blocks.alt: Kassiopi holiday photos reveal a recurring waistband

runs.text: The third photograph returns to the balcony in daylight, this time viewed through a window. Sam is seated outside, apparently absorbed in the same book. A red Supreme waistband is visible above dark underwear, making this the most direct continuation of the holiday’s established styling theme.

blocks.alt: Kassiopi holiday photos reveal a recurring waistband

runs.text: Deliberate styling or holiday indifference?

The photographs cannot establish precisely how consciously the clothing was arranged at each moment. What they do show is a repeated preference for wearing shorts below the waistband of the underwear, across multiple outfits and settings.

That is the central feature of sagging: the position of the outer garment makes the underwear visible and, in some instances, a deliberate component of the overall look. In these photographs, the contrast between brightly coloured sportswear and branded waistbands makes the effect particularly noticeable.

It is also worth recognising what the pictures are not. They do not document a wardrobe malfunction, a public complaint or an intervention by anyone else. Nothing in the supplied images suggests that a problem arose. They simply capture a holiday wardrobe being worn in a recognisable, relaxed way.
The wider holiday picture

Beyond the waistbands, the series captures three familiar pleasures of time away: reading without urgency, sitting outside in the sun and enjoying a dramatic Mediterranean evening. Kassiopi provides the backdrop, while the clothes give the pictures a consistent personal signature.

The Government’s assessment is therefore straightforward. The boxer shorts were showing, repeatedly and quite visibly. But rather than detracting from the holiday photographs, the detail has become part of what makes the collection distinctive.

For an administration concerned with Body and Identity, the Kassiopi photographs offer an unusually clear case study in everyday personal style. The sun set, the book was read, and the boxers remained firmly in view.

articles.title: Seven-language goal turns AI into a coding tutor
articles.standfirst: A lifetime ambition spanning PHP, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, Swift, Objective-C and C will use real projects and AI-supported learning rather than seven parallel courses.

blocks.alt: Seven-language goal turns AI into a coding tutor

runs.text: Sam has set a deliberately broad coding goal: by the end of his life, he wants to be able to write PHP, Python, Ruby, JavaScript, Swift, Objective-C and C. It is not a promise to become equally expert in seven languages, and there is no artificial deadline. It is a statement about the kind of technical literacy he wants to build over time.

The starting point is stronger than “complete beginner” suggests. Functions, loops, classes and common data structures already make sense as concepts. The challenge is turning that conceptual understanding into fluency: reading unfamiliar code, choosing the right structure, debugging failures and writing something useful without every decision being supplied in advance.

blocks.alt: Seven-language goal turns AI into a coding tutor

runs.text: The seven languages are not a random collection. JavaScript connects directly to the existing
SWS.GOV

web project. Swift is central to the planned native iOS app. Python offers a practical route into automation, data work and AI tooling. PHP and Ruby provide two different ways into mature web development, while Objective-C explains more of the Apple platforms that came before Swift. C sits underneath the list as the language most likely to make memory, pointers and the machine itself feel less abstract.

That last part is the biggest shift. Sam understands what memory management is for, but has mostly worked in environments where the language or framework handles it. Learning C means confronting allocation, addresses, lifetimes and failure directly. It will probably be the least immediately comfortable language on the list, which is precisely why it matters.

AI is now a significant part of the learning process. It can compare the same idea across languages, generate small exercises, explain compiler errors and keep a project moving when documentation becomes opaque. That makes learning faster and more connected than working through seven isolated textbooks.

blocks.alt: Seven-language goal turns AI into a coding tutor

runs.text: There is an obvious risk, though. AI can produce working code before the learner understands why it works. The safeguard is not to reject the tool, but to use it actively: predict what code will do before running it, ask for explanations instead of replacements, change generated examples, and occasionally rebuild a small feature without assistance. If the code cannot be explained, maintained or debugged, it has not really been learned.
The sensible route is project-led and sequential. Swift and JavaScript can deepen first because they serve live
SWS.GOV

work. Python can support automation around those projects. PHP and Ruby can follow as contrasting web languages, with C and Objective-C introduced when there is enough confidence to explore systems and Apple history properly.

The goal is feasible because mastery is not binary. A person can be productive in several languages while remaining strongest in two or three. What matters is the ability to recognise shared ideas beneath different syntax. AI does not make that ambition less legitimate. Used properly, it becomes the patient tutor that helps turn scattered understanding into a durable mental model.

articles.title: America knew who Trump was. It voted for him again.
articles.standfirst: An angry reflection on Donald Trump’s return, voters’ responsibility and why Europe should stop waiting for America to fix itself.

blocks.alt: America knew who Trump was. It voted for him again.

runs.text: I am angry with America. Not just Donald Trump, not just the Republican Party, but the country that watched him for decades and then returned him to the White House. I'm aware that this is a sweeping, emotionally driven judgement. I'm not pretending it's perfectly fair. But I'm exhausted by being expected to treat America's political dysfunction as an unfortunate domestic problem when its consequences reach the rest of us.

In 2024, more than 77 million Americans voted for Trump. He won all seven major swing states. He received 49.8% of the popular vote, a plurality rather than a majority, but a vast number of votes nevertheless. And nobody could honestly argue that he was an unknown quantity.
America knew
We'd seen his remarks about Mexican immigrants at his 2015 campaign launch. We'd heard the
Access Hollywood

recording. We'd watched him promote false claims about Barack Obama's birthplace. During the 2024 debate he repeated the baseless allegation that Haitian immigrants in Springfield, Ohio, were eating people's pets.

Most significantly, we'd watched him lose the 2020 election, refuse to accept the result, pressure Georgia officials to find enough votes to reverse it, and attempt to obstruct the peaceful transfer of power. We saw the attack on the Capitol on 6 January 2021 and heard rioters calling for Mike Pence to be hanged.
Then Americans elected him again.

Of course, voters had different reasons. Some believed misinformation. Some prioritised inflation or immigration. Some understood his conduct but judged other issues more important. My argument is that explaining those decisions does not absolve people of responsibility for making them.
I'm tired of American exceptionalism

I hear American progressives campaigning for universal healthcare and paid maternity leave, things which many other countries treat as ordinary features of a functioning society. I recognise that Americans born into difficult circumstances cannot simply emigrate. I don't expect them to abandon their fight. I just no longer want America's domestic struggle to dominate the world's agenda.

I care more urgently about Palestinian and Ukrainian children facing bombardment than about the disappointment of Americans who dislike their president. The US supplies military assistance to Israel, while its choices over Russia, Ukraine, sanctions and diplomacy have consequences far beyond its borders. People elsewhere cannot vote in an American election, yet they live with its outcomes.

And I am frustrated with Democratic leaders, too. Opposition cannot consist solely of condemnations, social media posts and rallies. It must involve organising, winning power and creating durable alternatives. That is a criticism of political effectiveness, not a claim that every American Democrat has the power to change the result.
Europe cannot keep waiting

I know there are millions of Americans who oppose Trump, including people who dedicate their lives to doing so. They are not morally interchangeable with those who support or implement his policies. My anger doesn't always make that distinction, but my considered position does.
What I reject is the idea that a future Democratic president can simply arrive on the world stage, announce that America is back, and expect everybody to forget what happened.

Europe needs the capacity to defend its own interests, make its own decisions and reduce its dependence on American electoral cycles. That means a stronger, more coordinated Europe, not a literal wall around the United States.

I can acknowledge the complexity of an electorate while still judging its collective decision harshly. I can understand why somebody voted for Trump without excusing that vote. And I can accept that my anger isn't always fair without pretending it came from nowhere.
America knew who Donald Trump was. Enough voters chose him again. The rest of the world is entitled to remember that.

articles.title: Bowls clubs need openness, not nostalgia, to survive
articles.standfirst: Ageing membership will not be reversed by rhetoric alone; clubs must make entry easier, share facilities and plan honestly for consolidation.

blocks.alt: Bowls clubs need openness, not nostalgia, to survive

runs.text: The future of small bowls clubs cannot rest on waiting for a mass youth revival that may never arrive. A discussion today produced a blunt but useful position: protecting every individual club is not the job of a prime minister, and public policy should not pretend that ageing membership can always be reversed.

That does not mean bowls has no future. It means the future will probably be smaller, more flexible and less attached to the assumption that every existing club must survive unchanged. Where membership has fallen to a handful of regulars, amalgamation, shared facilities and broader community hubs may be more credible than permanent rescue.

blocks.alt: Bowls clubs need openness, not nostalgia, to survive

runs.text: Evidence from
Bowls England’s Fit for the Future research

supports the scale of the challenge. Its club survey found that 77 per cent of memberships were stagnant or declining, while a quarter of clubs said they were not sustainable at their current size.
