More than 97 per cent offered only one adult membership option, and fewer than 30 per cent provided pay-and-play access.

Those figures also show why blaming younger people is too easy. Among people considering bowls, 69 per cent said an open day or free trial would encourage them to try it. Yet the traditional full-membership model asks newcomers to commit before they know whether the club feels welcoming. Long matches, rigid dress expectations, weak digital communication and closed social circles can all raise the threshold further.

The discussion was sharpened by anecdotal reports of cliquish behaviour: clubs complaining about a lack of new members while making unfamiliar people feel like intruders. Those reports are not a census of the sport, but they identify a basic contradiction. A club cannot demand public concern about its decline while treating accessibility as someone else’s problem.

blocks.alt: Bowls clubs need openness, not nostalgia, to survive

runs.text: A credible public response should therefore focus on access and community value, not sentimentality about every institution. Councils can help clubs share maintenance, open greens to casual players, combine ageing memberships and repurpose clubhouses as multi-use local spaces. Any financial support should come with clear expectations around open sessions, flexible payment, inclusive governance and visible routes for newcomers.
This is not an argument against older bowlers, or against the companionship that clubs provide. Bowls remains sociable, skilful and unusually adaptable across ages. A
recent sportscotland feature

profiled a thriving Scottish club with more than 160 adult and junior members, showing that decline is not universal. The lesson is that survival depends on behaviour and structure, not simply enthusiasm for tradition.

Some clubs will change and grow. Others will merge, broaden their purpose or close. The honest policy is to help communities manage that transition without promising an impossible return to the sport’s former scale. Bowls does not need false reassurance; it needs open gates, lower barriers and a willingness to share space before the membership disappears.

articles.title: BBC UX team holds final meeting ahead of Backstage move
articles.standfirst: Photos, party snacks and a farewell to familiar rituals marked the final gathering as colleagues prepared for new teams.

blocks.alt: BBC UX team holds final meeting ahead of Backstage move

runs.text: The BBC UX team's final regular gathering on Wednesday 21 October marked the end of a familiar weekly ritual as colleagues prepared to move into different teams. Rather than a formal retrospective, the roughly 22-minute meeting centred on camera-roll photographs, favourite party food, games and the sort of running jokes that accumulate when people work together.

The session offered a small but revealing portrait of a team culture at the moment it was dispersing. Members shared pictures of pets, family outings, a sculpture park, a Halloween trail and homemade knitting. One colleague showed how much their dachshund Basil had grown in eight weeks; another recounted buying a cat toothbrush seen on Dragons' Den, only for the cat to chew it apart. “It didn't kill my cat. That's also a plus,” they said.
A final round of familiar rituals

The party-food discussion travelled from chocolate cake and sausage rolls to a distinctly retro cheese-and-pineapple hedgehog: cocktail sticks arranged in a foil-covered grapefruit or potato. “It's like a 3D Hawaiian, isn't it?” one colleague suggested. Favourite games ranged from Scrabble and Jackbox to Cranium, charades and the Christmas challenge of moving an After Eight from forehead to mouth without using hands.

None of this amounted to a project handover, and it was not presented as one. The purpose was social. That became clearer when one colleague said: “Oh, I'm going to miss seeing everyone's photos though. Like this is the best meeting of the week.” Another recalled how the Monday photo-sharing tradition had previously disappeared and wondered whether it could be introduced in their next team.

Dan's response was dry: “I can't imagine you won't try.” He later encouraged colleagues to carry the format into their new groups: “We can all disperse that amongst you as we go to our new places. We can take what we've learned.” The joke continued with a comparison to “virus carriers”, albeit carriers of “a bit of a good virus”.
A changing team, a familiar sense of humour

The impending reshuffle surfaced explicitly when colleagues asked whether Bernie and Sam were both heading to Backstage. Other destinations mentioned included Account and Identity and User Engagement. For Sam, the transition comes as work with the new Backstage design group begins to take shape.

The group also teased Dan about the silences that sometimes punctuated meetings. “I don't make the silences. I just don't break the silences,” he replied, prompting the observation that, as the boss, others naturally looked to him to speak first.

The final minutes became increasingly surreal. Dan's unsettling dolls made a farewell appearance, including Babsie and her unnamed daughter, while other participants showed Halloween props and objects to their cameras. The closing exchanges included “Well, that was a nice meeting”, “Good farewell party” and a joking “Forever!” as colleagues signed off.

There was no grand speech or catalogue of achievements. Instead, the team's last gathering preserved the informal things that had made its working week recognisable: photographs, gentle mockery, shared references and room for people to be people. As the team splits into new assignments, those small rituals may prove among the easiest parts of its culture to carry forward.

articles.title: Monzo balances planned for SwS iOS and web
articles.standfirst: A proposed Monzo connection will bring account balances into the new SwS iOS app, with equivalent functionality planned for the web.

blocks.alt: Monzo balances planned for SwS iOS and web

runs.text: A new integration with Monzo is being planned for the forthcoming native SwS iOS app, bringing personal banking information into the Government for SwS Money pillar. The proposed feature would show an up-to-date account balance alongside selected spending and savings information, without requiring a separate visit to the banking app.
The same capability is expected to reach
SWS.GOV
on the web.
Feature parity between iOS and web is the goal
, rather than treating the mobile application as an isolated product with features that never reach other platforms.
Banking information in context

The initial ambition is deliberately focused: a clear, glanceable view of available funds, today's spending and, where permitted by the API, money held in savings pots. These figures could eventually sit alongside existing financial goals and personal planning tools, giving the Money pillar a more immediate connection to actual finances.
This would be a read-only experience. It is not intended to replace Monzo for transfers, card controls or day-to-day banking. Instead, the integration would answer a more useful question for
SWS.GOV
: how does the current financial position relate to the Government's own plans?
Any balance figures shown in design concepts are illustrative.
No live Monzo connection has yet been implemented or launched.
Native first, but not native only

The new SwS iOS project is being developed as a gradual transition towards a native SwiftUI experience. Its homepage and shared interface foundations are expected to be built natively, while other areas may initially rely on web views until they can be progressively rebuilt.

Monzo integration offers a practical early example of what the native app could add: an unobtrusive personal finance card, designed for quick reading and integrated into the wider experience rather than presented as another dashboard to manage.

However, the web remains a first-class destination. The intention is to provide a consistent financial picture on both platforms, with equivalent information and user controls even where the interfaces differ to suit their environments.
One secure source of truth

The technical direction centres on Monzo's developer API. Following the account holder's authorisation, a protected server-side service would retrieve permitted account information and provide a limited response to the authenticated
SWS.GOV
interface.

Banking credentials and API tokens must not be exposed in the iOS application or browser. The implementation will also need to address token renewal, access revocation, private authentication and the freshness of displayed figures. Shared backend logic would reduce the risk of the two platforms reporting inconsistent values.

The first release is expected to remain intentionally modest. More ambitious tools, such as spending trends, pot-based progress indicators or links to wider Money objectives, are possibilities for later development rather than confirmed launch features.
Parity as a product principle
The broader significance extends beyond Monzo. As
SWS.GOV
evolves from a personal website into a family of interfaces, its core services should remain recognisable and useful wherever they are accessed.

For the Government for SwS, feature parity does not mean that every screen must look identical. It means that the underlying information, functions and outcomes should be available across platforms, without one version becoming a permanent second-class experience.
No launch date has been announced

for the Monzo feature or its planned web counterpart. The current direction establishes the ambition: start with a useful native iOS implementation, share its secure foundations, and bring the web into line.

articles.title: Hidden bolt unlocks acrylic shelf mounting kit
articles.standfirst: A confusing wall-mounting kit became straightforward once its removable end bolt was separated from the metal spacer and used to clamp the acrylic shelf.

blocks.alt: Hidden bolt unlocks acrylic shelf mounting kit

runs.text: The last obstacle in fitting a set of bright orange acrylic shelves was not the adhesive pads, the wall or the shelves themselves. It was a metal spacer that looked as though it ought to attach in one piece.

The kit arrived with clear adhesive mounting plates, cylindrical silver spacers and the acrylic shelves, each protected by film. At first glance, the parts suggested a simple sequence: stick the plate to the wall, screw on the cylinder and fit the shelf. The problem was that the apparently plain opening in the spacer did not seem to meet the protruding fixing in any convincing way. With no useful exploded diagram, the hardware looked incompatible.

blocks.alt: Hidden bolt unlocks acrylic shelf mounting kit

runs.text: The breakthrough came from treating the cylinder as an assembly, not a single component. The small end bolt could be unscrewed from the spacer. Once removed, it revealed the internal thread and made the mounting order legible: attach the spacer to the wall fixing, place the shelf against it, then pass the bolt through the acrylic and tighten it back into the cylinder. The bolt does the clamping; the spacer holds the shelf away from the surface.

That sounds obvious after the fact. Before it, every visible cue pushed in the wrong direction. The neat cylindrical body looked sealed, the dark central hole looked passive, and the removable bolt appeared to be a finished end cap. The successful installation depended on discovering that the cap was also the fastener.

blocks.alt: Hidden bolt unlocks acrylic shelf mounting kit

runs.text: The photographs preserve that small piece of problem-solving. One shows the full kit, including the orange acrylic, clear wall plates and two spacers. A second brings the plate and spacer together, making the apparent mismatch visible. The third lays out the separate bolt and threaded cylinder — the exploded view that the instructions should have supplied.

With the mechanism understood, the shelves could be fitted without forcing the acrylic or improvising a different fixing. The sensible sequence is to dry-fit the parts first, keep the protective film on while aligning the holes, and tighten only until the shelf is secure. Acrylic can crack if a fastener is over-tightened, while adhesive mounts need a clean surface and the cure time specified by their manufacturer. The finished shelves should also be treated as light-duty storage unless the product states otherwise.

The episode is a useful reminder that installation problems are often information problems. A single diagram showing the removable bolt, shelf hole and spacer in order would have prevented most of the confusion. Instead, the hardware required reverse-engineering. The result is now secure, but the real fix was conceptual: stop asking how the cylinder screws onto the shelf, and notice that the bolt comes out.

For a tiny domestic fitting, it is a surprisingly complete design lesson. Good hardware can still feel broken when its moving parts are disguised, while a clear sequence can make an unfamiliar mechanism immediately understandable. Here, the shelf was installed only after the user supplied the missing explanation for the product.

articles.title: Viral live-TV catchphrase began as a staged hoax
articles.standfirst: The notorious clip was not a genuine broadcast accident: its creator performed the reporter and built follow-up videos that later inspired real harassment.

blocks.alt: Viral live-TV catchphrase began as a staged hoax

runs.text: The viral clip remembered as a reporter accidentally delivering the obscene “fuck her right in the pussy” line on live television was not a genuine broadcast failure. It was a scripted performance designed to look like one.

Cincinnati-area filmmaker John Cain uploaded the original video in January 2014. Cain played the reporter, apparently unaware that he was on air, while the presentation borrowed the visual language of local television news. The shock came from the gap between a familiar broadcast format and a line no real newsroom would expect to transmit.
That apparent authenticity helped the clip travel before many viewers knew who had made it.
The follow-ups were staged too

Cain followed the first video with more elaborate clips featuring a hooded character often identified as “Fred”. They appeared to show the man interrupting reporters during local stories and delivering the same phrase into a television microphone.

blocks.alt: Viral live-TV catchphrase began as a staged hoax

runs.text: Contemporary media coverage found that these were also fabrications.
Mediaite reported in May 2014

that the station supposedly responsible for one broadcast confirmed the woman shown had no connection to it. The article also identified mismatched presenters, subdued studio reactions and location details that did not fit the claimed reports.

The construction was convincing enough for viewers encountering a short, reposted version without context. News graphics, microphone branding and edited reaction shots supplied the cues of a real live broadcast, while the crude interruption supplied the shareable surprise.
Cain’s own promotion made the commercial logic clearer. Merchandise carrying the phrase followed, turning attention generated by the fake clips into sales.
A fake origin produced real harassment
The important qualification is that the hoax did not remain fictional. Once the phrase became a recognisable meme, copycats began shouting it during genuine live reports and sports coverage.

blocks.alt: Viral live-TV catchphrase began as a staged hoax

runs.text: Radio Canada International described

the original videos as fakes that inspired real incidents across the United States and Canada. Many of those interruptions targeted women doing their jobs in public and were experienced as sexualised humiliation rather than a harmless reference.
The consequences became especially visible in May 2015, when CityNews reporter Shauna Hunt confronted men outside a Toronto FC match after the phrase was shouted during her work.
CityNews reported
that the confrontation drew international attention and intensified discussion about the routine harassment of television reporters.
The verdict
The original “hot mic” moment was a setup. Cain was acting, the broadcast was simulated and the later Cincinnati-style interruptions were produced as part of the same viral project.

But it would be wrong to conclude that every later clip was staged. The fake videos established a script that real people then copied, often against reporters who had not consented to becoming part of the joke.

The episode is a useful warning about viral authenticity. A clip can imitate the production details of news, lose its context through reposting and become culturally real even when the event at its centre never happened. In this case, the hoax was fake; the behaviour it normalised was not.

articles.title: BBC recommendations session puts editorial judgement beside AI
articles.standfirst: An internal BBC skills session has focused on how recommendation models are developed and tested while balancing relevance, discovery and public-service editorial priorities.

blocks.alt: BBC recommendations session puts editorial judgement beside AI

runs.text: A BBC internal skills session scheduled for Tuesday 20 October has put recommendation systems under the spotlight, focusing on how artificial intelligence is balanced with audience needs and editorial judgement.

The 30-minute AI Unpacked Insights session was billed as a general introduction to the technology behind content recommendations across BBC products. Its agenda covered what an AI-powered recommender does, how models are developed and tested, the relationship between personalisation and discovery, and lessons from current work.

The session was led by Alessandro Piscopo, Lead Data Scientist for Recommendations in BBC Media Technology. It formed part of an autumn series intended to make practical AI work more understandable beyond specialist teams.
Recommendations are not simply generated content

A recommendation system does not necessarily create programmes, articles or clips. Instead, it helps decide which existing items to surface, order or suggest. That distinction matters because the current debate around generative AI can obscure the quieter machine-learning systems that have shaped digital discovery for years.

blocks.alt: BBC recommendations session puts editorial judgement beside AI

runs.text: For a public-service organisation, success cannot be reduced to maximising clicks or watch time. A useful recommendation may help somebody find something relevant, but it should also preserve the breadth of the BBC’s output and avoid trapping people inside an increasingly narrow pattern of familiar choices.
The BBC’s published
Machine Learning Engine Principles

say machine-learning systems should reflect organisational values, explain clearly how audience data is used, comply with editorial standards and broaden rather than narrow people’s horizons. The document also places algorithms alongside human editorial curation, rather than presenting automation as a replacement for it.
Testing is both technical and editorial

Developing a recommender involves more than choosing a model. Teams must define what a good outcome looks like, decide which signals are appropriate, examine data quality and check whether different groups are treated fairly. Technical performance can show whether a model predicts behaviour accurately, but it cannot decide on its own whether the resulting experience serves the public.

blocks.alt: BBC recommendations session puts editorial judgement beside AI

runs.text: The principles call for multidisciplinary work, documented sign-off and continued monitoring after launch. They also ask teams to consider alternatives to machine learning, the impact on protected groups and the risk of bias or harm.

That makes recommendation design a product and editorial problem as much as a data-science problem. The visible interface—rows, rails, labels and explanations—shapes whether a suggestion feels useful, repetitive or intrusive. The underlying system meanwhile needs clear accountability when its results are unexpected.
Discovery remains the real test

The most important tension is between relevance and surprise. Personalisation should reduce the effort needed to find worthwhile content without turning the BBC into a mirror of somebody’s previous behaviour.

Tuesday’s session did not announce a new audience-facing feature. Its significance was educational: it made the development, testing and editorial constraints behind recommendations a subject for a broader BBC audience.

That is a healthy framing for AI work. Recommendation systems are already part of everyday digital products, but their public value depends on choices about data, success measures, transparency and human oversight. The algorithm matters; so do the people deciding what it should optimise for.

articles.title: Climate warning is urgent without a 125-year countdown
articles.standfirst: A viral-style climate claim captures the need for action but overstates the science with a fixed deadline, a historical ranking and near-certainty.

blocks.alt: Climate warning is urgent without a 125-year countdown

runs.text: A dramatic claim that the world is “125 years away” from the worst humanitarian catastrophe in history contains a real warning about climate change, but presents uncertain outcomes with a precision the science does not support.
The strongest part of the claim is the urgency. Climate damage is not confined to a distant future. The
World Meteorological Organization
reported that extreme weather in 2024 drove the highest number of new annual displacements since 2008, while homes, infrastructure, farmland and ecosystems were damaged across the world.
What does not follow is a single countdown to disaster.
There is no fixed catastrophe date

Climate science does not identify 2151 as the year when one defined humanitarian catastrophe will begin. Risks build as greenhouse gases accumulate, temperatures rise and hazards interact with poverty, conflict, infrastructure and the ability of communities to adapt.

blocks.alt: Climate warning is urgent without a 125-year countdown

runs.text: The
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change

describes a gradient rather than a cliff edge: every additional increment of warming intensifies multiple hazards. Some consequences are already visible, while others become more likely or more severe at higher levels of warming.

That makes “125 years away” sound more exact than the evidence allows. It can also accidentally suggest that the next century is safe, when choices made during the 2020s and 2030s will shape conditions long before 2151.

Calling the outcome “almost certain” is similarly misleading. Severe impacts are expected to increase without deep emissions cuts, but the scale, location and human cost are not predetermined. Emissions policy, adaptation, finance, technology and political stability all change the result.
‘Worst ever’ cannot be measured cleanly

“The worst humanitarian catastrophe in history” is not a standard scientific category. Comparing a future global climate crisis with wars, pandemics, famines and other historical disasters would require assumptions about deaths, displacement, duration, inequality and geographic reach.
Climate change could amplify several of those harms at once. That makes the risk potentially enormous, but not something that can be ranked confidently today as a single event with one starting date.
The technology point is broadly right
The claim is strongest when it says that much of the technology needed to act already exists. The
United Nations Environment Programme
says the low-carbon technologies required for major emissions reductions are available, with wind and solar deployment expanding and costs falling.

blocks.alt: Climate warning is urgent without a 125-year countdown

runs.text: Technology alone is not enough. UNEP also identifies policy, governance, finance and institutional barriers, particularly the need for greater support to developing countries. Cutting emissions must be accompanied by adaptation, resilient infrastructure and protection for people already exposed to climate risks.

A more accurate warning would be: climate change is already causing humanitarian harm; every additional increment of warming increases the danger; and proven technologies can reduce future damage if governments deploy them quickly and fairly.

That wording loses the memorable countdown, but keeps the part that matters. The future is dangerous without being fixed, and the absence of certainty is not a reason to wait. It is the reason action can still change the outcome.

articles.title: Backstage onboarding guide puts Jupiter at the centre
articles.standfirst: Meeting transcripts and product documents are being assembled into a durable Backstage reference, with a dedicated Jupiter section at its core.

blocks.alt: Backstage onboarding guide puts Jupiter at the centre

runs.text: A dedicated BBC Backstage onboarding guide is being prepared to turn a growing collection of meeting transcripts, product documents and system notes into one dependable reference for Sam’s new assignment.

The source pack now includes transcripts from the introductory meeting with creative director Gruff and the first meeting involving the wider team, alongside Jupiter guidance, a classic Windows screen layout, material on recordings and live clipping, and an explainer covering Silver.

The aim is not to produce another pile of notes. It is to build a guide that can answer practical questions quickly while Sam begins working with senior designer Matilda, fellow midweight designer Andrew and Gruff across a broad content-production space.
Jupiter at the centre
Jupiter will have its own dedicated section because it appears repeatedly in the onboarding material and is likely to be one of the most important systems to understand.

blocks.alt: Backstage onboarding guide puts Jupiter at the centre

runs.text: That section needs to connect several kinds of evidence. The screen-layout document can show the shape and density of the classic interface. The Gateway guidance can explain the system in operational terms. The recordings and live-clipping material can reveal how particular tasks fit into the wider production workflow.

Bringing those sources together should make it easier to understand not only what Jupiter contains, but why people depend on it, where complexity has accumulated and which parts of the experience may be open to change.

The guide should resist pretending that every term or relationship is already settled. Clear labels can distinguish confirmed facts from interpretations, assumptions and questions that still need to be taken back to the team.
A map for unfamiliar territory

Beyond Jupiter, the guide can provide a simple map of the Backstage space: the people involved, the systems and products being discussed, the users of those tools, the kinds of work entering the team and the decisions designers are expected to influence.

A glossary will help with unfamiliar BBC language, while a timeline of relevant meetings can preserve how the assignment has developed. Short “why this matters” summaries can keep the document useful when a technical description is accurate but does not yet explain its design significance.

blocks.alt: Backstage onboarding guide puts Jupiter at the centre

runs.text: The best version should also remain easy to update. New evidence can be added without rewriting the entire guide, and unanswered questions can become prompts for future conversations rather than disappearing inside transcripts.
Ready for the first working sessions

The timing is useful. The BBC calendar includes a Backstage UX stand-up today and a wider weekly Backstage meeting tomorrow. Those sessions create an immediate opportunity to test the guide against the language and priorities used by the team.

Sam does not need to memorise every part of the production landscape before contributing. A well-structured reference can reduce the pressure to hold everything at once, leaving more attention for listening, spotting patterns and asking better questions.

The materials are now assembled; the next task is careful synthesis. If the guide keeps Jupiter central while showing how the wider Backstage system connects around it, it can become both an onboarding aid and a durable working companion for the assignment.

articles.title: Repeated AirPods Max failures trigger repair-or-replace review
articles.standfirst: Intermittent first-generation AirPods Max failures now need a documented diagnosis, as factory resets restore the headphones without preventing the fault from returning.

blocks.alt: Repeated AirPods Max failures trigger repair-or-replace review

runs.text: A recurring fault with Sam’s first-generation AirPods Max has moved from an occasional nuisance to a repair-or-replace question.

The headphones can sometimes stop working entirely: they do not connect, appear unresponsive when plugged in and offer no obvious route back into normal use. A factory reset has brought them back on previous occasions, but the fault later returns. That makes the reset a useful recovery step rather than evidence that the problem has been solved.
What Apple recommends

Apple’s current support guidance separates a restart from a full reset. A restart requires the Digital Crown and listening-mode button to be held until the status light flashes amber, which normally takes about ten seconds. Continuing to hold both buttons for roughly fifteen seconds, until the light flashes amber and then white, resets the headphones to factory settings.

blocks.alt: Repeated AirPods Max failures trigger repair-or-replace review

runs.text: For AirPods Max that do not appear to charge, Apple recommends connecting them for at least five minutes before reassessing the fault. If charging and a restart do not resolve the issue, the full reset is the next documented step.
Those instructions closely match the process that has revived Sam’s headphones. They do not, however, identify why the same failure keeps returning.
A fault needs evidence

Several causes could produce similar symptoms, including a charging problem, an ageing battery, an intermittent internal connection or a software failure. There is not yet enough evidence to select one, and repeatedly resetting the headphones can hide the pattern by restoring them before useful details are recorded.

The next failure should therefore be documented before another reset. The useful evidence is simple: whether any status light appears, whether a known-good cable and power adapter change the response, how long the headphones were charged, which devices can see them over Bluetooth, and whether a restart behaves differently from a factory reset.

It would also help to record how long the recovery lasts. A fault that returns after hours suggests something different from one that returns after weeks, even if the user-facing symptom looks identical.

blocks.alt: Repeated AirPods Max failures trigger repair-or-replace review

runs.text: Repair before replacement

If the fault recurs after a controlled charging test and reset, Apple’s service route is the sensible next step. The headphones should ideally be presented while unresponsive, accompanied by the short incident record, rather than reset immediately before inspection.
Apple says service costs depend on the issue and whether warranty, AppleCare or consumer law applies. That means a repair quote should come before any replacement decision.

The value question is wider than the price of a new pair. These headphones remain useful when they work, and replacing expensive hardware without establishing whether the failure is repairable would be wasteful. Equally, a high out-of-warranty quote for an intermittent fault may make replacement the more reliable long-term choice.

For now, the decision is not “buy new headphones”. It is to stop treating the reset as a permanent fix. One documented recurrence, followed by a formal service assessment, should provide enough information to choose between repair, continued use and replacement without guessing.

articles.title: Backstage working model points towards greater design autonomy
articles.standfirst: Early signs from the new BBC Backstage assignment suggest a design-led team with more control over triage, priorities and the shape of its work.

blocks.alt: Backstage working model points towards greater design autonomy

runs.text: Early signs from Sam’s new BBC Backstage assignment point towards a working model with more design autonomy and less dependence on the routines of a single product squad.

The expectation is still taking shape, but the role appears likely to sit within a UX group that can assess incoming work, decide what matters and organise its own priorities. That would be a meaningful change from being embedded in one delivery team, where design time can become tied to engineering stand-ups, sprint rituals and a narrowly defined backlog.
A better fit for the work
The appeal is not simply fewer meetings. It is the chance to approach Backstage as a connected design problem.

Internal content-production tools can produce requests from several directions at once. A design-led team could compare those needs, identify recurring patterns and decide when one shared solution is better than a series of local fixes. Designers would be closer to the decisions about what to investigate, prototype and test.

That model also looks well suited to Sam’s experience. Work on the BBC Account design system involved bringing consistency across products rather than polishing one isolated screen. Backstage offers another systems problem, but with the possibility of more tangible interfaces and visual design than the recent experimentation assignment provided.

blocks.alt: Backstage working model points towards greater design autonomy

runs.text: Autonomy needs structure

A team with control over its own priorities still needs a clear way to use that freedom. Without one, autonomy can turn into an intake queue in which every request arrives as urgent and designers become a helpdesk.

A lightweight triage process could separate immediate usability problems from longer-term opportunities. Requests could be judged against audience or staff impact, frequency, technical feasibility and whether the same issue appears elsewhere. A visible decision log would make it easier to explain why work has moved up, down or out of the queue.

Regular design critique could then provide the useful rhythm that ceremonies often promise without recreating a full product-team calendar. Engineers, editorial colleagues and users of the internal tools would still need to be involved at the right moments, but not necessarily in every daily ritual.

blocks.alt: Backstage working model points towards greater design autonomy

runs.text: The first week of the new rhythm

The BBC calendar now includes a Backstage UX stand-up on Tuesday and the weekly Backstage team meeting on Wednesday. Those sessions offer an early opportunity to understand how requests enter the team, who owns prioritisation and how design work moves towards delivery.
The most useful first step may be to observe before proposing a new process: map the existing flow, note where decisions stall and look for repeated problems across the content-production landscape.

Optimism about the move is therefore grounded in more than a change of subject. The emerging structure appears to offer the kind of work Sam has been asking for: visual and interface-led, connected to a wider system, and shaped by designers who can exercise judgement.

The details remain open, but that openness is part of the opportunity. If the team protects its autonomy while keeping strong links to engineering and editorial colleagues, Backstage could provide a much better fit for the next phase of Sam’s BBC career.

articles.title: Transparent texture sheets could make poster design physical again
articles.standfirst: A proposed analogue workflow would print digital artwork, introduce real grain and blur through physical layers, then photograph the result back into the design process.

blocks.alt: Transparent texture sheets could make poster design physical again

runs.text: A new creative experiment could move poster-making away from the screen and into a small, repeatable physical process.

The proposal is simple: make a clean digital composition, print it, place a transparent or translucent texture sheet over the top, then photograph or scan the layered result. The captured image would return to the computer carrying real grain, softened edges, reflections and tiny registration errors that did not come from a plug-in.
Texture as material
The aim is not to manufacture an instant “vintage” look. It is to let light and material take part in the design.

blocks.alt: Transparent texture sheets could make poster design physical again

runs.text: Clear film printed with grain or halftone patterns could create one kind of surface. Frosted plastic, tracing paper or textured acrylic could create others. Changing the gap between the artwork and the sheet would alter the softness of the image, while side-lighting could reveal scratches, dust and shadows.
Those variables would make each capture slightly different. That is the appeal: the system could be repeated without producing a perfectly identical result every time.
A practical workflow

The digital artwork would remain the master, so the experiment would not put the original composition at risk. A first trial could use a modest set of black-and-white posters and three texture sheets: fine grain, coarse noise and a diffused blur.

Each poster could then be photographed several times with small changes to distance, focus and lighting. The strongest capture could be used as the finished artwork, or brought back into the design file as a mask or texture layer.

A camera fixed square to the print would help prevent distortion. Soft, even light would reduce unwanted glare, while a high-resolution capture would leave enough room for cropping and print reproduction. Reflections, moiré, printer banding and colour shifts are all possible, but they are useful constraints to test rather than reasons to keep the work entirely digital.

blocks.alt: Transparent texture sheets could make poster design physical again

runs.text: Building a reusable texture book

The same idea could grow into a physical library. Instead of buying a conventional book of texture images, a ring-bound collection could hold numbered transparent sheets, translucent papers and printed patterns ready to place over future work.

A small reference photograph beside each material could record what it does under different lighting. Notes on distance, lens, paper and exposure would make promising effects easier to repeat without turning the process into a rigid recipe.
The result would be part sample book, part tool kit and part archive of experiments.

This approach fits a wider interest in designs that show evidence of how they were made. The imperfections would not be decoration added at the end. They would come from an actual encounter between ink, light, plastic, paper and camera.

A short test would establish whether that material character survives digitisation. If it does, transparent texture sheets could become a compact analogue stage inside an otherwise digital poster workflow.

articles.title: Proposal links Glasgow housebuilding to better public services
articles.standfirst: A proposed Glasgow standard would connect private development with clearer expectations for infrastructure, walkability, greenspace and complete neighbourhoods.

blocks.alt: Proposal links Glasgow housebuilding to better public services

runs.text: A proposal for a “Glasgow standard” has set out how private housebuilding could be tied more clearly to better public services, greener streets and neighbourhoods designed around everyday life.

The idea is not an existing Glasgow City Council policy. It is a policy concept developed through a Government for SwS discussion about whether councils could offer developers clearer incentives in return for meeting a published set of social, environmental and design requirements.
Rather than treating each new housing scheme as a collection of individual homes, the standard would ask what it adds to the city around it.
From new homes to complete neighbourhoods

A Glasgow standard could assess developments against practical outcomes: access to public transport, safe walking and wheeling routes, useful greenspace, play, affordable homes, community facilities and the capacity of nearby schools, health services and local shops.

That direction already has roots in Scottish planning policy. National Planning Framework 4 promotes “local living”, where people can meet most daily needs within a reasonable distance of home. Its Policy 15 says new and existing communities should be planned alongside infrastructure including schools, community centres, greenspace, health and social care, digital connections and sustainable transport.
Glasgow’s own Liveable Neighbourhoods programme also combines the 20-minute-neighbourhood idea with Scotland’s Place Principle.

blocks.alt: Proposal links Glasgow housebuilding to better public services

runs.text: The proposed standard would make those ambitions easier to see and measure. It could give residents, planners and builders one public checklist rather than leaving good placemaking as a broad promise attached to individual applications.
It should not impose one architectural style across Glasgow. The value would come from consistent outcomes while allowing different neighbourhoods to retain their character.
What developers could contribute

Scottish councils can already use planning obligations under Section 75 of the Town and Country Planning (Scotland) Act 1997. Updated Scottish Government guidance published in December 2025 says these obligations can remove obstacles to planning permission and help deliver necessary infrastructure alongside development.

That provides a mechanism, but not a blank cheque. Any obligation has to meet legal and policy tests, including a clear relationship to the development. A council could not simply exchange planning permission for unrelated spending elsewhere.

Within those limits, a transparent standard could establish what larger schemes may need to provide or fund. Contributions might support a crossing, active-travel connection, school capacity, public space or other infrastructure made necessary by the development. Stronger proposals could receive clearer guidance, earlier coordination or other lawful forms of support, rather than an automatic guarantee of approval.

blocks.alt: Proposal links Glasgow housebuilding to better public services

runs.text: The risks need designed out

A workable model would need to avoid vague deals and token gestures. Developers could otherwise add a small landscaped area while leaving residents dependent on cars, or argue that meaningful contributions make a project unviable.

The answer would be published criteria, evidence on local need, consistent viability rules, community involvement and monitoring after homes are occupied. Requirements would also need to reflect the size and impact of each scheme; a small infill project cannot carry the same burden as a major new neighbourhood.

The proposal’s central principle is nevertheless strong. Private development changes demand on public systems and creates value from the city around it. A Glasgow standard could make the exchange more explicit: permission to build should come with a responsibility to help create a place that works.

articles.title: Sam’s taste gets an interactive deep dive
articles.standfirst: A new interactive feature maps the precise logic connecting Beatles deep cuts, Glasgow infrastructure, modernist interiors and a dislike of manufactured spontaneity.

blocks.alt: Sam’s taste gets an interactive deep dive

runs.text: A new interactive
SWS.GOV
feature has attempted to answer a deceptively difficult question: what, exactly, connects Sam Smith’s most specific tastes?

The result ranges from Beatles deep cuts and Jane McDonald to Glasgow transport, glass-block lamps, old Apple interfaces and a lasting affection for software that looks as though somebody actually designed it. It is not a conventional list of favourites. It is a map of the principles underneath them.
Sincerity matters more than coolness
The starting point is a recent family memory about television. Sam’s gran watched an apparently spontaneous
Britain’s Got Talent

interruption with complete enthusiasm: a man in the audience claimed he had tried to audition for 15 years, was invited on stage by Simon Cowell and turned out to be brilliant. Sam and his dad immediately suspected the whole thing had been arranged.

That reaction captures an important dividing line. Sam can enjoy enormous quantities of camp, sentiment and showbusiness, but becomes intensely resistant when television pretends its construction is reality. The objection is not to popularity or theatricality. It is to concealed machinery.
That is why Jane McDonald, Barry Manilow,
Cats

and Paul McCartney can sit together perfectly happily. None requires the defence of being obscure or fashionable. Their appeal comes from commitment, melody and the sense that the performer means it. A visibly constructed spectacle can feel honest; a supposedly candid moment can feel false.

blocks.alt: Sam’s taste gets an interactive deep dive

runs.text: The interactive feature turns this into an “authenticity dial”, moving from something entirely manufactured to something sincere, odd and unmistakably itself.
Detail is where affection begins

The same rule explains interests that appear unrelated. A train is more interesting when it has a unit number, route history and particular window view. Glasgow becomes richer through traffic lights, wayfinding, demolished buildings and the systems that organise everyday movement.

Design works similarly. Sam’s ideal home is clean and modernist, but never anonymous: ribbed glass, heavy cutlery, acrylic magazine holders, vintage frames and a reclaimed glass-block lamp all have enough character to reward attention.

Digital taste follows the same pattern. The glossy surfaces of iOS 6, the extravagant Office-inspired styling of DotNetBar and the physicality of old skeuomorphic controls feel authored. Flat corporate neutrality may be tidier, but it often removes the evidence that a person made a choice.

blocks.alt: Sam’s taste gets an interactive deep dive

runs.text: The joy of committing to the bit

Personal style completes the picture. Turning up to a Halloween party as Sgt Pepper-era Paul McCartney works because the commitment is precise, even when the costume’s blue is not. The real 1967-style moustache carries much of the reference before the jacket does.

The interactive’s music room uses “If I Needed Someone”, “Maybe I’m Amazed” and Talking Heads’ “This Must Be the Place” as three routes into the same taste. One is a respectable Beatles deep cut, one is emotionally direct without embarrassment, and one makes awkwardness look like freedom.

The conclusion is that Sam’s taste is broad but not random. It favours specificity over generic polish, visible craft over fake spontaneity and wholehearted commitment over defensive irony. The best things do not collapse under examination. They become more themselves.

articles.title: A deep dive into Sam’s taste
articles.standfirst: From golden buzzers and Coleen Nolan to pandemic parodies and supermarket heroism: mapping Sam’s fascination with the earnest, naff and spectacularly British.

blocks.alt: A deep dive into Sam’s taste

runs.text: SPECIAL FEATURE | CULTURE & IDENTITY | 18 October 2026

What connects an elderly contestant being swept into a golden-buzzer standing ovation, a family earnestly rewriting pop hits about COVID, Coleen Nolan singing on daytime television, and a woman declaring that adverts are the best thing on television? For Sam Smith, these are not random examples of rubbish telly. They form a coherent and surprisingly rich niche fascination: the aesthetics of British manufactured sincerity.

This is a study of taste rather than a claim that every participant is deluded or every emotion is false. Its central proposition is that Sam enjoys the exact point at which entirely conventional entertainment begins to feel spectacularly excessive.
Explore the interactive taste laboratory

Use the embedded interactive dossier to examine five cultural specimens, turn up the emotional volume on an imaginary television segment, compare three audience reactions and grade your own examples. The video archive includes a verified Coleen Nolan performance and links to search for the Marsh family's lockdown songs.
The central theory: earnestness camp
The useful terms are
camp
kitsch
cringe
and
cultural observation

, but none on its own captures Sam's interest. Camp describes the pleasure of artifice and theatrical excess; kitsch the familiar sentimental imagery and emotional shortcuts; cringe the mismatch between intended effect and received effect. The fourth layer is sociological: watching what entertainment reveals about Britain's tastes, aspirations and emotional rituals.
Susan Sontag's 1964
Notes on “Camp”

discusses the artifice of camp and the experience of failed seriousness. That helps illuminate this interest, although the formula need not literally fail for the intended audience. A talent-show sequence can be genuinely moving to one viewer and wonderfully absurd to another. Both responses coexist.
What matters in Sam's version is
sincerity

. He can appreciate an SNL UK parody of an X Factor ensemble number as a competent joke, but the original broadcast often offers something the parody cannot: the breathtaking assurance that what is happening deserves every inch of its own enthusiasm.
Exhibit A: the golden-buzzer emotional machine
Consider a story relayed by Sam's gran. On
Britain's Got Talent

, a man supposedly calls out to Simon Cowell from the audience and asks for a chance to audition after years of trying. Simon relents, the man sings brilliantly, and he gets through. His gran was enchanted; his dad immediately suspected an elaborate setup. The incident has not been independently identified or verified here, and it would be wrong to assert that it was staged.

The divergence in their reactions is the point. His gran accepted the emotional terms of the programme and enjoyed its promise of belated recognition. His dad interrogated the production machinery. Sam enjoys the collision: the careful construction of spontaneous wonder and the earnest delight with which it can be received.
The elderly gentleman singing
My Way

, swelling strings, close-ups of a crying judge and the patriotic proclamation are recurring ingredients in the broader imagined genre. The actual singer need not be untalented; the comedy is the inflated ceremonial treatment of an ordinary television moment.
Exhibit B: the Marsh family's pandemic songbook
The Marsh family represents a different sort of earnestness. Rather than ITV spectacle, this is the domestic stage: a family arranging and performing topical parodies of familiar songs. Sam remembers
Goodbye Pandemic Road
with particular affection, while finding much of their gently satirical, broadly mainstream political outlook bland. Yet he keeps returning.

The pleasure sits in the paradox. There is genuine commitment, family talent and effort, but also a wholesome housebound presentation and a political register that Sam finds comically unadventurous. He is appreciating the work and the cultural world from which it emerges, not simply demanding that it be 'bad'.
Why the original beats a parody of the parody

A sketch already announces the joke and tells the viewer where to laugh. The sincerely performed source leaves the second reading to Sam. The less it asks to be laughed at, the more rewarding his own interpretation can become.
Exhibit C: ordinary people, extraordinary supermarket advertising
Then there is the inspirational advertising manifesto:
for the early risers, the grafters, the mums, the dads, the dreamers

. A George Ezra-adjacent acoustic anthem plays; someone makes breakfast; somebody else goes to work. By the end, the nation has apparently achieved something magnificent and a supermarket logo appears.

These are invented examples of a real advertising idiom, not quotations from a named campaign. What appeals to Sam is the gulf between mundane behaviour and the moral or emotional grandeur assigned to it. Corporate sentimentality turns shopping into belonging, routine into courage, and brand preference into a national story.

As a UX designer with an eye for communication systems, Sam is well placed to recognise the formula. Music, narrative pacing, predictable emotional cues and carefully chosen images are orchestrated towards a remarkably precise response. His pleasure lies partly in reversing that intended response.
Exhibit D: Coleen Nolan and the joy of recognition
A particular jewel in the collection is Coleen Nolan performing
I'm in the Mood for Dancing
on
Loose Women

. The appeal here is not an elaborate narrative twist, but the tiny scale of the occasion beside the sheer positivity surrounding it. A familiar celebrity sings the familiar song; the audience enjoys the fact that it is happening.

There is also a legitimate, affectionate history behind songs and performers like these. Recognising that history need not extinguish Sam's amusement. The object of fascination is an entertainment ecosystem in which familiarity itself is treated as sufficient occasion for delight. Other names in its constellation include Michael Ball, Alfie Boe, Aled Jones and Anton Du Beke.
Exhibit E: British national wholesomeness

Captain Tom, NHS applause, charity singalongs, optimistic pandemic television and a certain memory of London 2012 occupy a related aesthetic territory. They are not equivalent events or equally sincere projects. What links them in Sam's taste is the public language used to package togetherness: inspirational music, wholesome heroes, national affirmation and a suspicion that positivity is itself being made into the product.

It would be reductive to conclude that everyone moved by this material is naive. Viewers can know the formula perfectly well and still enjoy it, just as audiences willingly suspend disbelief for fiction. What Sam notices is that different viewers grant very different permissions to that formula.
The adverts woman: a crucial turning point

Perhaps the purest illustration comes from a story his mum told him. When Sky+ or TiVo-style recording made it possible to skip advertising breaks, a colleague reportedly asked why anyone would want to do that: the adverts were the best thing on telly.

To Sam, that statement was astonishing. Not because there is no pleasure in advertising, which can be witty, beautiful or musically memorable, but because it revealed a radically different hierarchy of culture. The material he might skip, analyse or watch ironically was another person's favourite part.
This suggests the real object of fascination is twofold:
the artefact and the audience that sincerely loves it
The surprising contrast in Sam's wider taste

Outside this niche, Sam gravitates towards the Beatles, Talking Heads, film, visual design, modernist aesthetics and the deliberate construction of cultural objects. He notices packaging, systems, editing and presentation. He enjoys creating his own posters and films, and is particular about how objects and interfaces look.
That doesn't make him incapable of sentimentality. His fondness for the Beatles, for instance, is quite sincere. The distinction seems less about emotion versus irony than about the
way emotion is made public and performed
: he can be profoundly affected by art while being amused by a programme insisting that a perfectly serviceable audition is a defining moment in Britain's national story.

It is also a specifically British, often English-coded, cultural landscape in his imagination: the daytime sofa, ITV applause, suburban living-room singalong, mild topical satire and compulsory uplifting chorus. This is a recognisable mainstream style, not a claim that English people all share one sensibility.
Is it camp, then?
Partly, yes.
But the strongest label may be
British feel-good kitsch, viewed through camp appreciation
. 'Earnestness camp' is a useful personal shorthand, not a recognised academic category.

The distinction matters: calling something camp is not the same as arguing that it is objectively bad. Nor does delighting in the naffness of a production have to mean contempt for its performers or viewers.

The article's working conclusion is that Sam has developed a connoisseur's taste for the rituals of reassuring British entertainment: the tropes, the celebrities, the songs, the staged crescendos and, perhaps most of all, the extraordinary fact that the emotional contract still works for so many people.
He doesn't want this stuff to disappear. He wants another specimen.
Watch and read further
Watch Coleen Nolan singing on Loose Women
Search YouTube for Marsh Family: Goodbye Pandemic Road
Search YouTube for Marsh Family lockdown parodies
Read Susan Sontag's original Notes on “Camp” (1964)

This is an interpretive profile based on Sam's own examples and recollections. Its taxonomy is an editorial framework, not a psychological diagnosis. Original quoted conversations have been paraphrased where necessary.

articles.title: The dream of a harmless cigarette meets the reality of smoke
articles.standfirst: A reflection on cannabis, cigarettes and why removing tobacco does not make inhaled smoke harmless.

blocks.alt: The dream of a harmless cigarette meets the reality of smoke

runs.text: A wish for “cancer-free cigarettes” has crystallised a difficult distinction between wanting smoke and wanting everything that surrounds it.

The phrase emerged while looking back at five years of smoking pure cannabis joints, without tobacco or nicotine, and wondering whether that period might have caused harm comparable with five years of cigarette smoking. It is an understandable question, but not one that can be answered with a neat one-for-one calculation.
What it does reveal is a clearer tension: the ritual still has an appeal, while the health consequences do not.
The smoke is the problem

Leaving tobacco out of a joint removes tobacco and nicotine, but it does not remove combustion. Burning plant material still produces smoke, particles and toxic chemicals that are taken into the lungs.

The NHS warns that smoking cannabis can increase the risk of lung cancer and cause other health problems. Public-health guidance on cigarettes makes a related distinction: nicotine is the addictive substance, but most of the damage from smoking comes from the thousands of other chemicals released when tobacco burns.

blocks.alt: The dream of a harmless cigarette meets the reality of smoke

runs.text: That does not mean every cannabis joint can be treated as medically identical to every cigarette. Frequency, quantity, depth of inhalation, the product itself and a person’s wider health all matter. Without those details and a clinical assessment, it would be misleading to declare that one five-year period caused exactly the same damage as another.
The safer conclusion is simpler. Smoke is not made harmless merely by removing tobacco, and no combustible cigarette can currently be described as cancer-free.
What the dream is really asking for

The dream may be less about tobacco than about the object and the pause: holding something, lighting it, inhaling, exhaling and stepping outside ordinary time for a few minutes. That ritual can be calming and familiar even when the substance or smoke around it is not.

This also explains why the idea of a harmless cigarette is so persistent. It imagines keeping the sensory experience while deleting the risk. But combustion is not a cosmetic detail that can be engineered away while leaving the cigarette unchanged; it is the process that creates the smoke.

There are products that avoid burning tobacco and can reduce harm for people who would otherwise smoke. NHS guidance says nicotine replacement provides nicotine without the harmful chemicals in cigarette smoke, while vaping exposes users to fewer toxins than smoking. Neither point turns those products into a recommendation for someone who does not already use nicotine, and vaping is not risk-free.

blocks.alt: The dream of a harmless cigarette meets the reality of smoke

runs.text: For the Government of SwS, the useful insight is not a retrospective verdict expressed in imaginary cigarette equivalents. It is recognition that the attraction has several parts: cannabis, smoking, routine, escape and the physical performance of taking a break.

Those parts do not all need the same answer. Past exposure cannot be recalculated with precision from memory alone, but future exposure can be reduced by not returning to smoked products. Any persistent cough, breathlessness, chest pain or other concern belongs in a conversation with a clinician, not in improvised arithmetic.
The “cancer-free cigarette” remains a compelling dream. The practical challenge is finding ways to preserve the pause without preserving the smoke.

articles.title: Tesco age check becomes an unexpected moment of warmth
articles.standfirst: A routine self-scan check became briefly funny and affectionate when a stranger decided that 28 was entirely believable.

blocks.alt: Tesco age check becomes an unexpected moment of warmth

runs.text: A routine self-scan age check at Tesco has produced one of the day’s most unexpectedly charming encounters.
The exchange began when a Spanish man assisting at the check put an arm around Sam and said: “Just tell me how old you are.” Sam answered, “28,” and received the immediate reply: “I believe you!”

It was brief, funny and unusually warm for an interaction built around a till requesting approval. The response turned what could have been a mechanical interruption into a tiny moment of recognition. Sam’s verdict afterwards was simple: thank you.

The story is not that a supermarket process changed or that physical familiarity should become part of every age check. As Sam quickly added, it was “not exactly policy”. Its appeal came from the fact that it was particular to those few seconds: spontaneous, good-natured and apparently judged well.
A human break in the interface

Self-service checkouts are designed to reduce conversation. Instructions arrive through buttons, lights and repeated recorded phrases, while assistance is usually summoned only when the machine cannot continue alone. An age restriction makes the hidden human layer visible again.

In this case, that intervention did more than clear the screen. The man’s relaxed question removed the slightly absurd tension of a 28-year-old waiting to prove adulthood, while “I believe you” landed as both permission and a joke.

blocks.alt: Tesco age check becomes an unexpected moment of warmth

runs.text: The arm around Sam mattered because it changed the tone immediately. It was familiar without requiring a longer conversation and confident enough to make the exchange feel affectionate rather than administrative. That judgement is personal: the same gesture from someone else, or in different circumstances, could feel unwelcome. Here, it was appreciated.

There is a useful design lesson hidden inside the anecdote. Efficient systems still depend on people who can read tone, context and the individual in front of them. The checkout handled the transaction; the human being made it memorable.
Not exactly policy

It would be a mistake to turn the moment into a recommended script. Warmth cannot be standardised by instructing every member of staff to repeat the same words or gesture. The encounter worked precisely because it did not feel rehearsed.

blocks.alt: Tesco age check becomes an unexpected moment of warmth

runs.text: Nor does the story need to become larger than it was. No friendship was formed, no grand lesson was delivered and nothing material changed. A stranger simply offered a few seconds of easy confidence in the middle of an ordinary shopping trip.

For the Mind pillar of Government for SwS, that smallness is part of the value. Good days are not built only from planned milestones or major successes. They can also be punctuated by an interaction that is impossible to schedule and pleasant enough to retell later.
The final judgement therefore remains deliberately modest. It was probably not Tesco policy. It was, however, very nice.

articles.title: Paperback-first rule ends hardback release pressure
articles.standfirst: A newly explicit reading rule rejects launch-day pressure and makes the preferred paperback edition worth waiting for.

blocks.alt: Paperback-first rule ends hardback release pressure

runs.text: A firm paperback-first reading rule has taken shape after a new hardback release prompted a simple response: waiting for the later edition is entirely acceptable.

The position is unambiguous. “I ain’t reading no hardback, motherfuckers,” Sam said while considering a book he wants to read. The language is comic, but the preference behind it is real. A desirable book does not become urgent merely because publishers have chosen to release it first in a heavier and usually more expensive format.

That removes a familiar pressure from the reading cycle. A hardback launch can create the impression that a book must be bought immediately to remain part of the conversation. The new rule rejects that timetable. Interest can survive the gap between editions, and choosing to wait does not make the eventual reading experience less serious.
Format is part of the experience

Hardbacks and paperbacks deliver the same core text, but they are not interchangeable objects. Hardbacks are built to feel substantial and permanent. For some readers that is part of their appeal; for others, the weight, rigid covers and size make them less comfortable to hold, carry or read in bed.

A paperback is usually easier to treat as an everyday object. It can move between a bag, a sofa and a bedside table without feeling precious. The pages and cover flex with use, and the format asks less ceremony of the person reading it.

blocks.alt: Paperback-first rule ends hardback release pressure

runs.text: The choice is therefore not a judgement on the book itself. It is a refusal to separate the content from the physical experience of reading it. Wanting the text does not create an obligation to accept whichever edition reaches the shops first.
Waiting becomes the default

Paperback publication dates vary, and the delay can stretch for months. The new approach treats that interval as a normal part of deciding what to read, rather than a problem requiring an immediate hardback purchase.

That also creates space for a calmer reading list. A book can remain wanted without becoming an instant task. By the time the paperback arrives, early publicity has settled, reviews are easier to assess and the decision can be based on lasting interest rather than launch-week momentum.

blocks.alt: Paperback-first rule ends hardback release pressure

runs.text: The policy sits naturally between the Mind and Money pillars of Government for SwS. It protects the pleasure of reading while avoiding a purchase made in the wrong format simply to satisfy impatience. Any saving is useful, but the more important point is that the preferred object is worth waiting for.

There is no need to turn the preference into a universal argument against hardbacks. Plenty of people collect them, value their durability or enjoy their design. The new position is personal and deliberately blunt: a publishing schedule does not get to overrule the way someone actually likes to read.
The outcome is a small but freeing decision. When an interesting book appears in hardback, the answer can simply be: not yet.

articles.title: The case for judging AI one use at a time
articles.standfirst: A new personal position rejects the pro-or-anti binary while drawing a firm distinction between technical achievement and creative value.

blocks.alt: The case for judging AI one use at a time

runs.text: A clearer personal position on artificial intelligence has emerged: the technology is too broad, varied and consequential to be reduced to a choice between being “pro-AI” or “anti-AI”.

The starting point is a frustration with the label itself. “AI” is routinely used as if it describes one product, one capability or one political programme. In practice, it can mean anything from language models and recommendation systems to image generators, automation tools and features embedded inside familiar software. Supporting one use does not require enthusiasm for every other use, just as objecting to one output does not amount to rejecting the entire field.
That makes case-by-case judgement more useful than allegiance to a camp. The important questions become what a system is doing, who benefits, what is lost and whether the result is actually good.
Use is not endorsement
The distinction is already visible in practice. Recent work has involved AI-assisted planning for the new
SWS.GOV

Planner, connected Notion workflows, coding prompts and tightly constrained image enhancement. These are practical tasks with specific intended outcomes, not declarations that every application of the technology is desirable.

That selective use matters. It allows technical capability to be recognised without turning novelty into a moral or aesthetic instruction. A system can be useful in one context, unhelpful in another and actively unpleasant somewhere else.

blocks.alt: The case for judging AI one use at a time

runs.text: The position therefore resists two easy stories. The first says that rapid technical progress should be welcomed as a single package. The second treats any use of AI as proof of support for everything associated with it. Neither leaves much room for people who use particular tools while remaining critical of their effects or outputs.
Imagery draws the clearest line

AI-generated imagery produces the strongest objection. Its technical achievement is acknowledged: producing coherent pictures from text is impressive and, at a systems level, undeniably clever. That does not make the results appealing.

The stated reaction is much harsher. AI imagery can feel “completely devoid of charm” and “quite repulsive to look at”. This is not a claim that the software is incapable of making recognisable or polished pictures. It is a judgement that polish and visual plausibility are not the same as character, intention or taste.

blocks.alt: The case for judging AI one use at a time

runs.text: For a design-led approach, that distinction is fundamental. Technical success answers whether something can be generated. Creative judgement asks whether it should exist in that form, whether it communicates anything worthwhile and whether a person would genuinely want to spend time with it.

The result is not a settled manifesto for or against AI. It is a demand for more precise language and more discriminating choices. Tools can be judged by their actual use; outputs can be judged on their merits; and admiration for engineering does not require affection for what it produces.

articles.title: Ravenscraig was a European powerhouse, not the world’s
articles.standfirst: The Motherwell steelworks was vast enough to shape Scotland and lead Western Europe, but its real history is stronger without global exaggeration.

blocks.alt: Ravenscraig was a European powerhouse, not the world’s

runs.text: Ravenscraig deserves to be remembered as an industrial powerhouse, but calling the Motherwell steelworks a “powerhouse of the world” stretches the evidence too far.

The distinction matters because the reality is impressive without inflation. At its peak, Ravenscraig employed around 7,000 people and was described by Historic Environment Scotland as the largest steel-maker in Western Europe, producing roughly two million tonnes a year. Its scale made it central to Scotland’s industrial economy and inseparable from the modern identity of Motherwell and surrounding Lanarkshire communities.

A stronger and more precise description would be that Ravenscraig was one of Western Europe’s great steelmaking centres, operating within a Scottish industry whose products, skills and reputation reached far beyond the country.
A vast integrated works

Construction began in the 1950s, turning open land between Motherwell and Wishaw into a fully integrated steelworks. Ironmaking, steelmaking and rolling could all take place on the site, allowing raw materials to move through successive stages into finished or semi-finished steel.

The hot-strip mill known as the Big Mill captured the scale of the operation. North Lanarkshire’s museum service records that its building was about 300 metres long, while the mill could roll more than two million tonnes of steel annually. It was the longest such mill in Europe.

blocks.alt: Ravenscraig was a European powerhouse, not the world’s

runs.text: Those figures justify the language of European industrial power. They do not quite support the idea that Ravenscraig alone powered the world. It was a major plant within a much larger international steel industry that included still greater centres of production in the United States, Soviet Union, Japan and elsewhere.

The phrase nevertheless captures something true about how the works felt locally. Ravenscraig dominated employment, landscape and civic identity on a scale that is difficult to reproduce in a service economy. Its towers, furnaces, rail movements and shift patterns organised daily life well beyond the site boundary.
Closure changed more than the skyline

Ravenscraig closed in 1992, ending large-scale steelmaking in Scotland. The final shutdown directly removed 770 jobs, but contemporary parliamentary estimates put the combined impact across Lanarkshire at more than 2,400 jobs, with wider Scottish losses potentially exceeding 3,000. The shock was therefore social and regional as well as industrial.

blocks.alt: Ravenscraig was a European powerhouse, not the world’s

runs.text: The cleared site later became one of Europe’s largest brownfield regeneration projects. Homes, New College Lanarkshire, the regional sports facility and The Craig park now occupy parts of land once defined by heavy industry, while major areas remain subject to long-term redevelopment.

That afterlife reinforces the fairest verdict. Ravenscraig was not a world powerhouse in the literal sense of rivalling the greatest industrial complexes on Earth. It was, however, a genuinely enormous European steelworks, a pillar of Scotland’s post-war economy and a place whose closure reshaped an entire part of the country. “Western European powerhouse” is not a consolation prize; it is the historically stronger claim.

articles.title: Computer room refurbishment puts storage first
articles.standfirst: Two extra BILLY shelves and a set of storage boxes form a practical plan for a calmer, more useful computer room.

blocks.alt: Computer room refurbishment puts storage first

runs.text: The computer room is set for a modest refurbishment focused on storage, calm and making better use of furniture already in place.

The proposal centres on two additional oak-effect shelves for the room’s existing IKEA BILLY bookcase, alongside a pack of three 30-litre storage boxes. Rather than replacing the bookcase or beginning a larger redecoration, the plan would add capacity where it is already needed and give loose equipment, cables and project materials more reliable homes.

It follows this week’s wider organisation drive, which saw drawers in the computer room and bedroom cleared and the room’s filing cabinet brought back under control. That work exposed a familiar problem: tidying is easier to maintain when the things being kept have a sensible place to go. The refurbishment is therefore less about buying more furniture than making the existing room work harder.
More room in the BILLY

The selected BILLY shelves measure 76 by 26 centimetres and cost £15 each, giving the shelving element of the proposal a confirmed subtotal of £30 before delivery. IKEA says each shelf is designed for an 80-centimetre-wide, 28-centimetre-deep BILLY frame and supports up to 30 kilograms.

A compatibility check will be needed before purchase. IKEA states that the current shelf does not fit bookcases bought in spring 2014 or earlier. Once that point is settled, the two additions should allow the spacing inside the unit to be tightened, reducing tall gaps and creating more usable levels for books, technology and smaller stored items.

blocks.alt: Computer room refurbishment puts storage first

runs.text: The second part of the package is a set of three transparent 30-litre storage boxes. Their price has not yet been verified, so the full refurbishment cost remains open. Used inside the room’s enclosed or lower storage, the boxes would keep groups of less frequently used items together while making their contents easy to identify.

That matters in a room which has to support several different activities. It is a home office, a place for computing and creative work, and a store for hardware and materials that are useful but not required every day. Better-defined storage should reduce the amount of visual noise competing with the main desk and make it easier to switch between those uses.
A small intervention with a wider purpose

The project is deliberately incremental. No completion date or full budget has been fixed, and the storage boxes remain the main uncosted item. The confirmed elements nevertheless give the refurbishment a practical starting point that can be delivered without committing to a wholesale room redesign.

blocks.alt: Computer room refurbishment puts storage first

runs.text: The intended result is not an immaculate showroom but a calmer working room in which everyday technology stays accessible and the rest can be put away without disappearing into an unsorted drawer. It continues the Government for SwS emphasis on small improvements that make the home easier to live and work in.
If approved after the compatibility and cost checks, the extra shelving and boxes will turn the recent clear-out from a one-off burst of organisation into a more durable system.

articles.title: Multiroom audio plan reaches every room
articles.standfirst: Existing Apple TV and HomePod coverage could expand into the hall, computer room and kitchen through a mix of new and refurbished hardware.

blocks.alt: Multiroom audio plan reaches every room

runs.text: A proposed multiroom audio network would extend music and spoken audio into every main room of Sam’s flat, combining equipment already in place with a small number of carefully chosen additions.

The living room is already served by Apple TV, while the bedroom has a HomePod. The new plan focuses on the remaining gaps: a HomePod mini in the hall, a refurbished AirPort Express in the computer room and one of two possible systems for the kitchen.

The hall option is the simplest.
