A compact HomePod mini would provide direct playback in the connecting space between rooms, making it possible to continue music, radio or podcasts while moving through the flat. It would also avoid the need to install conventional speakers in an area where space is limited and visual clutter would be especially noticeable.

In the computer room, the proposal is to use a refurbished AirPort Express to bring existing or future speakers into the same network. Apple added AirPlay 2 support to its 802.11n AirPort Express base stations through firmware version 7.8. That allows a compatible unit to appear alongside newer AirPlay devices and join synchronised playback across rooms.

blocks.alt: Multiroom audio plan reaches every room

runs.text: This is an example of older technology remaining useful after its original purpose has faded. The AirPort line is no longer current hardware, but the Express can still act as a small bridge between an Apple-based audio system and traditional speakers. A refurbished unit would need to be checked for the correct model, updated firmware and dependable network performance before purchase.

The kitchen decision remains open. One option uses another AirPort Express with a pair of bookshelf speakers, offering flexibility over sound quality and allowing the speakers to become part of the wider AirPlay system. The alternative, described in the proposal as Apple HomeView, remains a single-device option under consideration rather than an approved purchase.

Those choices involve different priorities. Separate speakers would offer more control over the sound and could be replaced independently. A single-device route would use less space and reduce the number of components, but would represent a larger commitment to one product.

blocks.alt: Multiroom audio plan reaches every room

runs.text: The purpose is not simply to make every room louder. AirPlay 2 allows multiple compatible devices on the same Wi-Fi network to play together or be selected individually. The result would be a continuous system in which the living room, bedroom, hall, computer room and kitchen can operate as one group or as separate zones.

No purchases have yet been approved. The hall and computer-room components are the clearest parts of the proposal, while the kitchen requires a decision between the speaker-based route and HomeView. Costs, refurbished-device condition and the wider Autumn/Winter 2026–27 budget will determine the order of work.

If completed, the plan would turn a collection of separate devices into a coherent household service. The emphasis is on using what already exists, giving older hardware a practical role and filling the remaining rooms without creating unnecessary duplication.

articles.title: Government unveils proposals for hallway refurbishment by end of 2026
articles.standfirst: AW26 Budget savings to fund a proposed hallway transformation with a new console, glass-block lamp and acrylic magazine displays.

runs.text: GOVERNMENT FOR SwS | PRESS RELEASE | 15 October 2026

blocks.alt: Government unveils proposals for hallway refurbishment by end of 2026

runs.text: New investment under the Autumn/Winter 2026 Budget will transform the entrance hall into a warmer, more functional and carefully designed space, with improvements funded through monthly household savings.
The Government for SwS has today announced proposals for a modest but significant refurbishment of the entrance hallway, with the ambition of completing all works before the end of December 2026.
The proposals form part of the forthcoming Autumn/Winter 2026 (AW26) Budget, which will identify opportunities to reinvest savings from routine household expenditure into improvements to the home.

The scheme represents a continuation of the Government's wider programme of domestic improvement, following recent efforts to organise drawers, rationalise household storage and create a calmer living environment.

The hallway proposals are the latest in a series of announcements ahead of the AW26 Budget. They follow the completion of a long-overdue decluttering exercise across bedroom and computer-room drawers and household paperwork; consideration of selling the underused bicycle to reduce ongoing costs and release funds; and the emerging two-year ambition to be financially and professionally ready for a possible move to London by the Government's 30th birthday. Together, these measures signal a budget concerned both with improving daily life now and creating greater freedom for the future.
Proposed improvements

At the centre of the proposals is the installation of a narrow, industrial-style console table featuring a dark wood-effect surface and black metal frame. Positioned against the left-hand wall, the new furniture will replace the existing open shelving arrangement while maintaining adequate circulation through the hallway.

The console will provide a dedicated location for keys, everyday essentials and decorative objects. Proposed additions include a shallow organiser tray, carefully selected greenery, ceramic vessels and a small number of books.

A distinctive illuminated glass-block lamp, producing a warm amber glow, will serve as the centrepiece of the refurbishment. The lamp will introduce a secondary lighting source, allowing the hallway to be illuminated without relying on the existing overhead fitting.
On the opposite wall, the Government proposes removing the current collection of framed prints and assorted magazine displays, replacing them with two wall-mounted amber acrylic magazine holders.
These will display a rotating selection of design, architecture and culture publications, creating a more deliberate visual arrangement that reflects the interests and identity of the household.
The existing large black-framed mirror, framed railway artwork, flooring and hallway runner will be retained, avoiding unnecessary expenditure and reducing waste.

blocks.alt: Government unveils proposals for hallway refurbishment by end of 2026

runs.text: Funding through the AW26 Budget
Rather than financing the refurbishment through borrowing or a substantial one-off purchase, the Government intends to allocate funds progressively from monthly household savings.
The AW26 Budget will establish the financial framework for the programme, with purchases prioritised according to affordability, practical benefit and visual impact.

No final spending allocation has yet been approved. The programme will remain subject to wider financial commitments, including the Government's ongoing efforts to reduce debt and strengthen household savings.
A considered approach to domestic improvement
The proposals reflect a broader shift towards incremental, carefully targeted investment in the quality of everyday life.

Rather than pursuing an extensive or costly renovation, the Government intends to make better use of existing space, retain serviceable fixtures and introduce a limited number of objects that combine utility with considered design.
The refurbishment will also establish a more welcoming entrance to the property, improving the experience of arriving home and providing a consistent visual identity across the hallway.
Next steps
The Government will now proceed with finalising the AW26 Budget allocation, confirming furniture dimensions and assessing procurement options.
Subject to funding and delivery, the programme is expected to be completed by
31 December 2026
ENDS
Government for SwS | Press Office
This release announces proposals. No expenditure or installation is implied to have been authorised or completed.

articles.title: Drawers cleared as home organisation drive gathers pace
articles.standfirst: A long-overdue clear-out has brought order to the computer room, bedroom and filing cabinet, with larger storage spaces earmarked for a possible resale exercise.

blocks.alt: Drawers cleared as home organisation drive gathers pace

runs.text: A long-overdue clear-out has brought a little more order to the Battlefield flat, with drawers across the computer room and bedroom emptied, reviewed and reorganised as part of an ongoing effort to make the home feel nicer and calmer.

The work has included the filing cabinet drawer in the computer room, an area where paperwork and important documents can easily accumulate without much attention. Giving it a proper sort is a small but useful piece of household maintenance, and one that has been waiting to happen for some time.

There is no dramatic renovation to report, nor any grand reveal. Instead, the latest changes amount to the sort of practical tidying that makes an ordinary home easier to live in: knowing where things are, reducing unnecessary clutter and dealing with storage spaces that have quietly become jobs for another day.
Small changes, noticeable difference

The computer room and bedroom have both received attention, with several drawers tackled rather than a single isolated cupboard. Together, the improvements represent progress on a familiar domestic problem: belongings can be put away and out of sight without ever really being organised.

The filing cabinet is a particularly worthwhile part of the exercise. Although much of everyday life now takes place digitally, physical documents still have a place, especially where financial and administrative records are concerned. Keeping those papers in a sensible arrangement makes the drawer more useful than simply treating it as somewhere to deposit the next envelope.

More broadly, the clear-out is about making the flat feel less busy. A home does not need to be completely minimalist to feel orderly, and tidying the hidden corners can be just as satisfying as improving the spaces that are immediately visible.

The Government for SwS has placed increasing emphasis on manageable improvements to day-to-day life. This latest effort fits within that approach: not a complete transformation, but another practical step towards a more comfortable, calmer environment.
Bigger storage spaces still to come

Two substantial jobs remain on the domestic agenda. The main cupboard in the hallway and the bedroom wardrobe have both been identified as needing attention, but neither forms part of the completed work being reported today.
Those areas could instead be tackled during a more extensive review of possessions in the near future. One possibility is a broader effort to
liquidate unused assets
, selling items no longer needed through Vinted and other resale platforms.

Such an exercise could serve two purposes at once: freeing up space and recovering some money from belongings that otherwise sit unused. The prospect remains under consideration, however, with no timetable or resale target yet confirmed.

For now, the achievement is more modest and immediate. Several neglected drawers have finally been dealt with, the filing cabinet is in better order, and the flat is a little closer to the sort of peaceful, pleasant place it ought to be.
There are still cupboards to confront. They can wait for the next round.

articles.title: Mac mini plan would combine desktop and home server
articles.standfirst: A proposed sub-£1,200 Mac mini would combine the main desktop with remote AI, agent, media and file-server duties.

blocks.alt: Mac mini plan would combine desktop and home server

runs.text: A single Mac mini could become both Sam’s main desktop computer and the centre of a new home server setup under an emerging technology plan being considered by Government for SwS.

The proposal would combine everyday desktop work with remote access to AI and agent tools, media services and personal files. Instead of buying one computer for the desk and another device to leave running in the background, the same Mac would do both jobs.

The spending limit is deliberately modest. Sam wants to keep the purchase at no more than about £1,200, with at least 1TB of internal storage. The machine does not need to carry Apple’s newest processor. The priority is that it remains fast, dependable and capable of handling several roles for years.

That creates a different buying test from a conventional desktop upgrade. Processor generation still matters, but memory, storage, networking and sustained performance become more important when the machine must also answer requests from elsewhere. A refurbished or carefully chosen used model could therefore be more useful than a lower-specification new one.

blocks.alt: Mac mini plan would combine desktop and home server

runs.text: The concept builds on several parts of Sam’s existing digital setup. A Mac mini could host shared files, run a personal media library and provide a stable place for automation. It could also support local or remotely accessed AI tools without requiring the main laptop or another computer to stay switched on.

There are practical compromises. A computer used interactively at a desk cannot behave exactly like an appliance hidden in a cupboard. System updates and restarts would interrupt remote services, while a demanding AI job or media conversion could compete with the applications being used on the desktop. Remote access would need to be secured, and important files would still require a separate backup rather than relying on the Mac’s internal drive alone.

Those issues do not make the plan unrealistic, but they do shape the specification. The strongest initial options are likely to put at least 24GB of memory, 1TB of storage and wired Ethernet ahead of having the latest chip. External storage could later hold a larger media library while the internal drive keeps applications, active projects and server software responsive.

blocks.alt: Mac mini plan would combine desktop and home server

runs.text: The Mac mini’s small footprint and low power use also suit an always-on role better than a large desktop tower. It could sit beneath a monitor during the day, then continue serving files and running selected tasks after the desk is no longer in use.

No purchase has been approved. The machine is one of several major items competing for space in the forthcoming Autumn/Winter 2026–27 budget and the wider two-year Plan for 30. Any decision will need to balance the usefulness of the server idea against debt repayment, saving and other planned technology purchases.
For now, the proposal establishes a clear principle: the next desktop should do more than replace the current one. If the numbers work, it should become a piece of personal infrastructure as well.

articles.title: Government considers ‘cutting losses’ and selling bike ahead of Plan for 30
articles.standfirst: After fewer than 15 rides in 14 months, an £849 electric bicycle faces a possible sale as the Government reviews the cost of keeping it.

blocks.alt: Government considers ‘cutting losses’ and selling bike ahead of Plan for 30

runs.text: The Government for SwS is considering selling its privately owned electric bicycle after a review found that the £849 purchase has seen fewer than 15 outings since August 2025.

The ELOPS city bike, bought from Decathlon just over a year ago, was intended to make travelling around Glasgow easier and encourage more regular cycling. Instead, it has spent much of its life in storage, while occasional journeys have increasingly been served by hired Voi bikes.

No final disposal decision has been taken. However, the Government is now weighing up whether continued ownership can be justified when the bicycle attracts recurring locker and insurance charges without seeing regular use.
An expensive resident of the bike locker

The figures are difficult to ignore. In roughly 14 months of ownership, the bike has been ridden fewer than 15 times, representing no more than around one journey a month. Insurance alone costs £6 monthly, with the storage locker adding a further recurring expense.
A Decathlon buyback estimate issued in July valued the bicycle at
up to £373
, subject to an in-store condition assessment. That estimate expired after 30 days and would have to be renewed before any sale.

Against its original £849 purchase price, the indicative return implies a loss of £476. Yet retaining the bicycle cannot reverse that depreciation, and would leave the Government continuing to pay for an asset it rarely uses.
The decision is therefore becoming less about recovering the initial investment and more about whether the bike has a meaningful role in everyday life.
A different model of cycle ownership
The review does not represent a retreat from cycling. Rather, it reflects a distinction between having access to a bicycle and bearing the costs of owning one.

Voi's hire bikes already provide an alternative for occasional journeys, particularly when the urge to cycle arises spontaneously. Hiring removes the need for dedicated storage, ongoing insurance and personal maintenance. Private ownership retains advantages, especially for longer rides or journeys beyond hire-bike coverage, but those advantages have so far seen limited practical use.
There is also an environmental and practical argument for resale: a lightly used bicycle could find a new owner willing to make fuller use of it instead of remaining idle in a locker.
If the Government proceeds, Decathlon's buyback scheme offers a relatively straightforward exit, although a private sale might command a higher price at the expense of more time and effort.
A small decision in a bigger financial review

The bicycle's future is being examined as wider financial priorities come under scrutiny. Reducing avoidable recurring costs and releasing money tied up in underused possessions are among the practical options under consideration.
The timing is notable. Work is developing around an
Autumn/Winter 2026/27 Budget
and a broader
two-year Plan for 30

, with further details expected to emerge in due course. The Government has not yet set out the full scale of those ambitions, and the potential bicycle sale should not be mistaken for an announcement of wider measures.
For now, the immediate question remains modest: whether an electric bike which has scarcely left its locker deserves to keep its place there.
A refreshed valuation is the likely next step.

articles.title: Strange train turns the home-office window into a railway lesson
articles.standfirst: A passing 3S92 MPV revealed the seasonal work behind leaf fall, high-pressure water jets and one of the best views in Mount Florida.

blocks.alt: Strange train turns the home-office window into a railway lesson

runs.text: The view from Sam’s home office offered a particularly unusual piece of railway theatre on Thursday when a strange-looking train passed on the southern approach to Mount Florida.

It was immediately clear that this was not one of ScotRail’s familiar electric passenger units. The working looked more industrial, prompting a quick search of the live timetable and a simple question: what exactly had just gone past the window?

The strongest match is 3S92, a departmental service running from Bridgeton Yard back to Bridgeton Yard. The published schedule carries the train reporting number 3S92 and timetable identifier P00800. It is booked to pass Mount Florida at about 9am after a long circuit through the west and south of the Glasgow rail network, including reversals that allow it to cover different lines.

blocks.alt: Strange train turns the home-office window into a railway lesson

runs.text: That unusual route is the point. This is not a train taking passengers from one place to another. It is railway equipment doing a job across the network, and the available timetable and seasonal allocations indicate that 3S92 is a rail-head treatment working, most likely formed by a Network Rail multi-purpose vehicle. The exact unit seen from the window has not been independently confirmed.

Rail-head treatment trains are one of autumn’s less visible but essential railway operations. Fallen leaves are compressed by passing wheels into a hard, slippery layer on the rail. Network Rail compares the effect to black ice: it can reduce grip for acceleration and braking, and it can interfere with the electrical track circuits used to detect trains.

The specialist fleet tackles that contamination with high-pressure water jets. Multi-purpose vehicles can also apply an adhesion modifier, a mixture designed to improve the contact between wheel and rail. Network Rail says its treatment equipment can deliver water at 1,500 bar, which explains why the machines look so different from the passenger trains that usually dominate the Cathcart Circle.

blocks.alt: Strange train turns the home-office window into a railway lesson

runs.text: The timetable labels 3S92 as a departmental train operated by GB Railfreight and scheduled to run on weekdays when required. A specialist path can show a generic diesel timing load, so that description alone does not prove the physical formation. Enthusiast reports from the current treatment season, however, identify the working as an MPV rather than a conventional locomotive-hauled train.

For Sam, the technical explanation arrived after the more immediate pleasure of the sighting. “Very interesting to witness this,” he said, describing the line-side view as one of the many perks of a home-office window looking directly onto the Cathcart Circle’s southern approach to Mount Florida.

Most home-office distractions are less useful. This one offered a brief live lesson in the hidden work that keeps Glasgow’s railway moving: an odd-looking train, an unusual route and a seasonal maintenance operation passing almost at arm’s length.

articles.title: An evening with Obama becomes a once-in-a-lifetime moment
articles.standfirst: Seeing Barack Obama speak with his mum gave Sam a meaningful encounter with a defining political voice, without erasing the complexity of his legacy.

blocks.alt: An evening with Obama becomes a once-in-a-lifetime moment

runs.text: Sam Smith attended an evening with Barack Obama on Wednesday with his mum, describing the experience afterwards as an honour and a once-in-a-lifetime moment. The significance came less from spectacle than from hearing one of the defining political speakers of his lifetime address the condition of democracy in person.

Smith described Obama’s manner as reserved. The former US president spoke about the importance of democracy and the negative consequences of social media, placing the evening within a wider argument about how public life is changing. For Smith, those themes felt substantial rather than simply nostalgic.

blocks.alt: An evening with Obama becomes a once-in-a-lifetime moment

runs.text: The event carried the unavoidable weight of comparison with the current US presidency. Smith said Obama was “a hell of a lot better than the current fool in office”, while making clear that this did not amount to an uncritical defence of everything Obama did in power. Admiration for the speaker and scrutiny of the record were able to coexist.

That distinction mattered. The evening was meaningful because Obama remains a major figure in Smith’s political memory, not because the years of his presidency have been flattened into a perfect alternative. Seeing him in person offered contact with the style of political communication that defined an era, while leaving room for disagreement about policy and legacy.

Smith called Obama “the most prolific speaker of my time”. The description captured the personal scale of the encounter: a voice previously experienced through television, campaigns, speeches and news coverage was suddenly present in the same room. That shift from mediated figure to physical presence made the night feel singular.

blocks.alt: An evening with Obama becomes a once-in-a-lifetime moment

runs.text: The discussion of social media gave the evening a contemporary edge. Platforms that once appeared to widen political participation have also intensified fragmentation, outrage and distrust. Smith did not report a detailed prescription from Obama, but the warning about negative consequences connected the event to questions he regularly considers about technology, politics and public institutions.

Attending with his mum added another layer. The night was not only a chance to hear a former president but a shared family experience, the kind that becomes a reference point long after the details of individual answers have faded. Smith’s first reaction was not to produce a full political assessment, but to register how fortunate he felt to have been there.

No attempt is needed to turn the event into an endorsement of Obama’s complete legacy. Its value lies in the encounter itself: hearing a historically significant public figure speak seriously about democracy at a moment when democratic norms and digital public life feel under strain.
For
SWS.GOV

, the evening belongs in the Mind and Identity record as both political reflection and personal memory. Smith left with his admiration qualified but intact, and with the sense that he had witnessed a speaker whose presence shaped his understanding of modern politics. The verdict was simple: reserved, interesting and profoundly meaningful.

articles.title: Adam’s old jacket begins a second life with Sam
articles.standfirst: A brown leather jacket passed between partners is finding a new identity as Sam makes it part of his own wardrobe.

blocks.alt: Adam’s old jacket begins a second life with Sam

runs.text: A brown leather jacket once worn by Adam has started a second life in Sam Smith’s wardrobe. Adam recently gave the jacket to Smith, who has begun wearing it as part of his own rotation rather than treating it as borrowed clothing or a sentimental piece kept safely at home.

When the pair met on Wednesday, Smith described the handover in deliberately presidential terms. He said that “a lot of people are saying” he had made the jacket his own and that it was “working very strongly” for him. The performance was a parody of Donald Trump’s speaking style, not a report of genuine public acclaim.

blocks.alt: Adam’s old jacket begins a second life with Sam

runs.text: Smith later acknowledged that nobody had actually said any of it. The joke worked because it inflated an ordinary exchange between partners into a claim of overwhelming consensus. In his version, Adam had worn the jacket, Smith inherited it, and the garment immediately became a major success with unnamed observers.

Beneath the routine, however, there is a real change. Clothes can look closely tied to the person who first owned them, particularly when they have a strong colour or material. Once the same piece is worn with a different wardrobe, posture and set of associations, it can stop reading as a hand-me-down and begin to feel personal.

The jacket’s brown leather gives it enough presence to shape an outfit without needing much around it. It suits Smith’s interest in distinctive but practical clothing and offers a warmer alternative to more minimal black outerwear. Its history with Adam also makes it different from a new purchase chosen only for appearance.

blocks.alt: Adam’s old jacket begins a second life with Sam

runs.text: The timing also places the jacket within the colder months, when outerwear becomes the most visible part of everyday clothing. Smith’s extended parody wandered through cold weather, climate change and the former language of global warming before returning, repeatedly, to the central message that the brown jacket was working very well.

No outfit decision has been confirmed for Wednesday evening’s Barack Obama event, which Smith is attending with his mother. Earlier styling advice favoured a structured jacket with a black T-shirt, dark trousers and clean trainers, but there is no evidence that the brown leather jacket was selected for the occasion.

For now, its significance is simpler. Adam passed on something he no longer needed, and Smith found a way to wear it that felt like his own. The transaction saved an existing garment from becoming dormant and added a small shared history to an otherwise ordinary part of getting dressed.

The new life of the jacket is therefore both sincere and knowingly over-announced. It does not need invented crowds to validate it. Smith is wearing it, enjoying it and treating it as part of his identity. In the language of the original joke, the performance may be exaggerated, but the jacket itself is doing very strongly.

articles.title: Loft CRT could give digital designs an analogue edge
articles.standfirst: A small television believed to be in a Cumbernauld loft could become a practical tool for giving digital artwork genuine CRT and VHS character.

blocks.alt: Loft CRT could give digital designs an analogue edge

runs.text: A small portable television believed to be sitting in Sam Smith’s parents’ loft could become the next piece of equipment in his creative workflow. The set is thought to be a cathode-ray tube television of roughly 12 inches, with a VHS player built into the unit. It has not yet been retrieved or tested.

The plan is to bring the television back into use as a physical display for digital artwork. Rather than applying a software filter that imitates an old screen, Smith wants to send finished designs through the real hardware, then photograph or film what appears on the glass. The result could carry genuine scan lines, colour bleed, glow and distortion from the display itself.

blocks.alt: Loft CRT could give digital designs an analogue edge

runs.text: Getting a modern signal into the set will depend on the connections available. The intended route is to convert HDMI from a computer or media device into the RCA or composite signal expected by older televisions. That remains a proposal until the exact model, sockets and working condition of the set have been checked.

The built-in VHS player creates another possible layer. Designs could be recorded to tape and played back before capture, introducing the movement, softness and instability associated with the format. That would be a more deliberate process than placing a texture over an image, and it would allow different results to emerge from the same digital source.

The experiment fits Smith’s wider effort to make existing design work feel more tangible. Recent plans have focused on publishing poster art, revisiting the IPP archive and building a recognisable creative identity. A CRT workflow could give selected pieces a physical finish while also producing behind-the-scenes material showing how the final image was made.

blocks.alt: Loft CRT could give digital designs an analogue edge

runs.text: Capturing the screen will be part of the test rather than a solved step. The camera will need to record the image without losing the television as an object, while shutter speed, frame rate and exposure may affect visible flicker and banding. Smith has asked what kind of camera would be suitable, but no equipment choice has yet been confirmed.

The first task is therefore practical: retrieve the television, identify its make and model, inspect the available inputs and confirm that both the screen and VHS mechanism still work. Only then will it be possible to choose the correct converter and decide whether the set is useful for still photography, moving images or both.

If the experiment works, the television will move from stored family technology to active studio equipment. Its value will not come from nostalgia alone, but from giving digital work an authentic analogue passage before it returns to a modern screen. For now, the CRT remains a promising idea in the loft rather than a completed production tool.

articles.title: DeBasement request puts the IPP archive back to work
articles.standfirst: A request for the original IPP material is turning a finished creative project into a practical, reusable handover.

blocks.alt: DeBasement request puts the IPP archive back to work

runs.text: DeBasement has asked Sam Smith to send over the original material from his IPP work, reopening a finished creative project as something that can be used again. The request is small in form but significant in what it says about keeping creative work organised beyond the final export.

The message asked what video program had been used and suggested sending the project file alongside the video exports. Smith’s work was built in Adobe After Effects, so the practical answer is a collected project rather than a loose selection of finished clips. That should give DeBasement the working composition as well as the files it depends on.

blocks.alt: DeBasement request puts the IPP archive back to work

runs.text: Smith is preparing a single ZIP containing the original After Effects project, its collected footage, images, audio and other linked assets, plus the most relevant exports and project material. The intention is to make the handover self-contained while avoiding a folder full of caches, abandoned experiments and unrelated working files.

That balance matters. A master folder can be comprehensive without becoming impossible to understand. The project file needs its dependencies beside it, the final exports provide a quick reference, and a short note can explain what is included. Smith has also left the door open for DeBasement to ask for anything more specific once they have inspected the package.

A collected project is useful because motion work rarely lives in one file. Fonts, footage, audio and linked artwork can all disappear from a composition when they are moved between computers. Checking the package before it leaves reduces that risk and makes the archive easier for somebody else to open without reconstructing the original setup.

There is no confirmed follow-up yet, and the material should not be described as delivered until the transfer has actually happened. For now, the news is the request itself and the decision to respond with editable source material rather than only flattened outputs. It gives the recipient more room to revisit, adapt or learn from the original work.

blocks.alt: DeBasement request puts the IPP archive back to work

runs.text: The development also connects with the new INSTAPLAN publishing programme. Five IPP archive posts are already planned, including DeBasement graphics scheduled for November. That programme is about presenting finished work to a public audience. This handover serves a different purpose: preserving the structure behind the work so it remains useful to a collaborator.
For
SWS.GOV

, it is another example of an archive becoming active infrastructure. Keeping source files, assets and exports together creates options that are easy to lose once a project is considered complete. A request arriving later can then be answered with something better than a search through old drives or a single compressed video.

The next step is straightforward: finish the collected package, check that the After Effects file opens with its assets intact, and send the ZIP with a concise explanation. Until DeBasement replies, the scope of any further use remains unknown. Even so, the request already shows that careful archiving can extend the life of creative work.

articles.title: A ‘naughty problem’ opens the BBC Backstage chapter
articles.standfirst: Gruff’s candid welcome turned the new Content Production assignment from a promising outline into a real team, real systems and a likely first problem.

blocks.alt: A ‘naughty problem’ opens the BBC Backstage chapter

runs.text: The next BBC chapter became real on Tuesday afternoon as Gruff welcomed Sam into the newly formed Backstage Content Production squad, replacing the abstract promise of “more tangible work” with named systems, a provisional start date and an unusually candid introduction.

The distinction matters: Sam was the incoming designer being welcomed, not the person introducing somebody else. The meeting, titled “What’s Backstage all about?”, gave the first proper view of a team still being assembled around internal content-production products and workflows.

Gruff’s tone made the uncertainty feel energising rather than evasive. “If you like a naughty problem, we have got plenty of them,” he said, while also admitting: “I don’t exactly know how the squad is going to work yet.” He punctured the density of the introduction with “I’ve just said a lot of words at you” and a reference to “how ridiculous this place is.”

Those comments did more than make the call entertaining. They suggested a lead willing to acknowledge complexity, laugh at institutional oddity and avoid pretending that a new squad already has every boundary settled. After months in which experimentation work often felt distant from a product surface, that honesty is a good starting condition.

blocks.alt: A ‘naughty problem’ opens the BBC Backstage chapter

runs.text: The emerging remit spans Graphics & Automation, Silver and Jupiter. Jupiter is the likely starting point, although the allocation remains provisional while the wider squad takes shape. That mix points towards internal tools with visible interfaces, real production constraints and users whose work can be observed directly.

It is a meaningful step beyond the earlier indication that Content Production might be a better fit. That first conversation created optimism; Tuesday’s welcome supplied the substance. There are systems to learn, technical histories to untangle and decisions about how design should operate inside a newly formed team.

Sam came across as friendly, thoughtful and quietly confident. He was positive without overselling himself, curious about the work and diplomatic about the Experimentation period he is leaving behind. The strongest signal was purposeful enthusiasm: interest in what the systems do, who depends on them and where UX can make the work clearer.

That matters because the assignment will reward someone able to ask strategic questions without floating away from the interface. The immediate preparation is therefore practical: map the products and their users, understand the relationship between Graphics & Automation, Silver and Jupiter, identify the most painful workflows, and establish what a useful first month should produce.

blocks.alt: A ‘naughty problem’ opens the BBC Backstage chapter

runs.text: The transition is provisionally set for Monday 19 October. Before then, the remaining Experimentation work can be closed down cleanly while access, documentation and introductory conversations are lined up for Backstage.

There is still ambiguity, but it is now productive ambiguity attached to actual products rather than an indefinite promise that UX work may appear later. A candid lead, a fresh squad and a supply of “naughty problems” is a considerably stronger place to begin.

The Experimentation era has ended. The moment, as the Fourth Doctor put it, has been prepared for; Backstage now looks like the place where the next version of Sam’s BBC design practice can properly start.

articles.title: Rotterdam emerges as the model for a January solo retreat
articles.standfirst: A four- or five-day winter trip would combine Dutch urbanism, public transport and quiet creative time, with Amsterdam kept as an optional day trip.

blocks.alt: Rotterdam emerges as the model for a January solo retreat

runs.text: Rotterdam has emerged as the leading idea for a first winter solo retreat, with January proposed for a four- or five-day trip built around urbanism, public transport, coffeeshops and uninterrupted time to read and make things.

The plan is deliberately different from a conventional city break. Rather than racing through a checklist of attractions, the trip would use Rotterdam as a temporary base: a private but affordable hotel room, a laptop, long stretches in cafés and enough unstructured time to explore the city at street level. The aim is not simply to see somewhere new. It is to experience what everyday life might feel like in a place designed around different assumptions.

That makes Rotterdam a particularly good fit. Its post-war centre, bold contemporary architecture and unusually visible transport infrastructure offer the sort of urban environment Sam naturally studies. Trams, metro stations, cycle routes, bridges and pedestrian spaces are not background scenery here; they are a large part of the attraction.

blocks.alt: Rotterdam emerges as the model for a January solo retreat

runs.text: The trip would also create space for a more relaxed relationship with solo travel. Taking a laptop makes the days feel purposeful without turning them into remote work. Reading, writing, organising creative projects or developing poster ideas could sit alongside walks and transport journeys, allowing the city to act as both subject and workspace.

Coffeeshops, meaning the Netherlands’ cannabis venues rather than jazz cafés or ordinary coffee shops, are another part of the curiosity. The interest is as much in how the venues operate and fit into city life as in the products themselves. Any visit would need to follow the individual venue’s rules, bring valid identification and remain a contained part of the trip rather than its entire organising principle.

Amsterdam can remain optional rather than becoming the default destination. Dutch rail links make a day trip from Rotterdam entirely realistic, while keeping the hotel base in Rotterdam should preserve the calmer, cheaper shape of the break. Exact January services and fares would still need checked closer to booking, but there is no need to choose between the two cities completely.

blocks.alt: Rotterdam emerges as the model for a January solo retreat

runs.text: January is part of the appeal. The weather will likely make this a colder and darker trip, but that suits the proposed rhythm: architecture and transit during the day, then warm indoor stretches with a book or laptop. Travelling outside the obvious spring and summer period may also make a private room more achievable within a restrained budget.

The proposal now needs to move from an attractive concept to a costed option. The next useful step is a single working budget covering transport from Glasgow, four or five nights in a non-hostel room, local travel, food, coffeeshops and a contingency. That will show whether January is genuinely affordable or whether the same model should move later into 2027.

Within Government for SwS, the idea joins several priorities neatly. It advances the commitment to travel internationally more, tests a genuinely solo trip, supports Mind through time away from routine and feeds Identity through design, cities and independent creative work.

The strength of Rotterdam is therefore not that it offers the loudest possible holiday. It offers something more tailored: a temporary life in another well-designed city, with enough structure to feel safe and enough empty space to think.

articles.title: Railcard expiry puts the next year of travel under review
articles.standfirst: The 26–30 Railcard expires on 16 October, creating a simple £35 test against another year of Glasgow, London and wider rail travel.

blocks.alt: Railcard expiry puts the next year of travel under review

runs.text: A small but useful Money deadline arrives this week: Sam’s digital 26–30 Railcard expires on Friday 16 October, putting the cost of another year’s discounted travel against the journeys likely to follow.

The decision is unusually clean. The official Railcard price is now £35 for one year, the card remains digital-only, and it offers one-third off most qualifying rail fares across Great Britain. It can be renewed during the 30 days before expiry. At 28, Sam remains within the 26–30 eligibility window, so this is not the end of the scheme, merely the point at which continued cover needs an active decision.

blocks.alt: Railcard expiry puts the next year of travel under review

runs.text: The rough break-even calculation is £105 of undiscounted qualifying fares. One-third of £105 is £35, meaning every eligible journey after that point represents a genuine saving. Restrictions still matter, including the fares and times on which the discount applies, but the basic threshold is low enough that a modest year of intercity travel can justify renewal.

Recent travel makes that prospect realistic. The October journey from Edinburgh Waverley to London King’s Cross showed the value and appeal of long-distance rail, while the wider plan to spend more time in London gives the next twelve months a likely southbound pull. Glasgow remains home, but the intention is to travel more, including solo, rather than treating major trips as rare exceptions.

The railcard also supports a broader transport preference. Trains are not simply a fallback between flights and coaches. They are part of the experience: the route, rolling stock, stations and history all carry their own interest. A discount that makes choosing rail easier therefore serves both Money policy and a genuine enthusiasm.

blocks.alt: Railcard expiry puts the next year of travel under review

runs.text: There is still no case for renewing on autopilot merely because the old card exists. The better test is whether £105 of eligible fares is plausible before October 2027. A return trip to London can account for a large part of that total, while journeys to Edinburgh and other UK cities add further weight. If the travel plan becomes quieter, the card may take longer to repay itself; if London visits become regular, it could recover its cost quickly.

Timing matters as well. Letting the card lapse would not prevent a later purchase while Sam remains eligible, but it would create a gap in which discounted tickets could not be used without a valid Railcard at the time of travel. Renewing before Friday keeps the system continuous and avoids having to reconsider it when booking under pressure.

The practical recommendation is therefore to renew, then record the first £35 of savings as repayment rather than invisible money. Once that threshold is crossed, the card can be treated as productive travel infrastructure for the rest of the year.

This is not a dramatic policy shift. It is the kind of small administrative choice that makes larger ambitions easier: a low-cost tool aligned with more movement, more London access and a transport mode Sam already values.

articles.title: Meal prep review makes weekday protein less messy
articles.standfirst: A five-day breakfast plan and a cleaner tofu workflow turn recurring kitchen friction into a practical Body-policy system.

blocks.alt: Meal prep review makes weekday protein less messy

runs.text: Meal preparation in SwS has moved from a loose weekly intention towards a more deliberate system, after a review of two recurring bits of kitchen friction: keeping breakfast ready for workdays and making tofu without turning the process into a sticky production line.

The immediate aim is not an ambitious Sunday batch-cooking regime. It is to remove the repetitive faff from meals that already work. Overnight oats made with skyr and almond milk remain the obvious breakfast base, while tofu, Aromat, olive oil, lemon juice and polenta already form a reliable high-protein main meal. The problem has been less about nutrition than the number of small, messy actions needed each time.

blocks.alt: Meal prep review makes weekday protein less messy

runs.text: For breakfast, the new approach is to prepare several sealed jars at once, keep them properly chilled and treat five days as an upper limit rather than a guarantee. Fresh ingredients, clean containers and the dates on the skyr and almond milk still take priority. Texture is also part of the decision: oats may remain safe while becoming thicker or softer than is actually enjoyable.

That makes the sensible first trial smaller than the theoretical maximum. Three jars can establish whether the mixture holds up well before a full Monday-to-Friday batch is attempted. Fruit, nuts or anything expected to lose texture can be added on the day. The result is a repeatable breakfast with protein already built in and no early-morning measuring.

The tofu workflow needs a different answer. Keeping an opened block submerged in clean water is useful before it is seasoned, but a wet lemon-and-oil marinade is not a week-long storage solution. Once the tofu is cut and coated, the clock is running and the texture can deteriorate. A shorter refrigerated batch, or freezing portions for later, is the more robust option.

blocks.alt: Meal prep review makes weekday protein less messy

runs.text: The cleaner process separates dry preparation from wet preparation. Tofu can be portioned in advance, while a jar of pre-mixed Aromat and polenta becomes the ready-to-use coating. For each meal, one portion goes into a lidded tub or reusable bag with the oil and lemon, then into the dry mix, keeping hands and bowls out of most of the job. Tongs or a fork can take care of the final transfer to the air fryer.

This is small domestic infrastructure rather than a diet overhaul. It preserves a familiar vegetarian routine, protects the protein target and reduces the sensory annoyance of wet coating on the hands. It also fits the wider Government for SwS approach: improve the system around a proven behaviour instead of demanding constant motivation.

The next step is a one-week trial. Success will be measured in fairly ordinary terms: breakfast ready when work begins, tofu cooked without covering the kitchen in polenta, and fewer moments when the inconvenience of preparation makes an easier but less useful option feel tempting.

articles.title: INSTAPLAN turns creative archive into a publishing programme
articles.standfirst: A new Notion headquarters brings 21 planned Instagram posts into a sustainable rhythm built around music posters, IPP archive work and creative collaborations.

blocks.alt: INSTAPLAN turns creative archive into a publishing programme

runs.text: SwS has established INSTAPLAN, a new creative headquarters in Notion that turns an existing archive of music posters, IPP work and collaboration ideas into a practical Instagram publishing programme.

The system brings together a dashboard and publishing pipeline, with 21 planned posts dated from 13 October to 29 November 2026. Its purpose is to make creative work more visible while reducing the pressure to invent something new every time a post is due.

The proposed rhythm is straightforward: two music posters each week, on Tuesday and Thursday, followed by an IPP, collaboration or other creative post on Sunday. A behind-the-scenes Reel can take the Sunday slot when the process offers a stronger story than a finished image.
An archive with more to say

The starting point is work that already exists. Five initial IPP angles have been identified: the project's visual world, its computer-world aesthetic, the funeral and resurrection campaign, printed collateral, and deBasement graphics. Each offers a different route into the archive, allowing a body of work to be presented as a sequence rather than a single retrospective dump.

Those angles are briefs, rather than confirmation that every source file or photograph has been gathered. The next stage is to select the strongest finished assets, organise them into carousels or individual posts, and check any permissions or collaborator approvals.

Music posters form the other regular strand. Beatles and McCartney work sits alongside possibilities involving Talking Heads, Oasis and further visual experiments. The intention is to build a recognisable authored series, with enough variation to show a point of view across different subjects.
Batch first, relax later

INSTAPLAN's central operational idea is to prepare several weeks of material in concentrated sessions. The headquarters proposes gathering candidate work, curating the opening image and carousel order, writing captions, exporting the assets, and then scheduling them through Instagram or Meta Business Suite where available.

blocks.alt: INSTAPLAN turns creative archive into a publishing programme

runs.text: A buffer of at least six finished, captioned posts is recommended before committing to the full rhythm. This makes the calendar a manageable production tool, with room to keep making work between publication dates.

The Notion pipeline tracks the stages from idea and asset gathering through production, readiness, scheduling and publication. It also provides space for captions, asset links, credit checks and results such as reach, saves and shares. A dated entry remains an editorial plan: it does not automatically publish to Instagram.
Presence built on the work

The wider ambition is a more recognisable creative presence rooted in music, culture and genuine collaborations. The HQ includes a stretch target of 1,000 followers by Christmas, alongside a goal of securing a direct music or culture collaboration. These are ambitions, not guaranteed outcomes.

The guardrails are equally concrete. Planned posts should credit collaborators appropriately, avoid implying commissions or artist relationships that did not happen, and preserve time for the work itself. Potential EWTV material remains dependent on the relevant approval.

For the Identity pillar of Government for SwS, INSTAPLAN gives creative development a visible structure. The immediate task is to turn the first batch of briefs into finished posts, creating a sustainable route from work already made to work people can actually discover.

articles.title: I need to talk about cannabis again
articles.standfirst: A personal account of a return to cannabis and what comes next.

blocks.alt: I need to talk about cannabis again

runs.text: I've been putting off writing this, partly because I don't really know how to approach it, and partly because writing it means properly acknowledging something I've been trying not to think too much about.
After a sustained period away from cannabis, I've relapsed.

I don't particularly like writing that. I'm disappointed in myself, and I'm frustrated that I'm back here again, having spent so much time and effort trying to move away from something which, for a long time, had such a significant hold over my life.

But I also want to be honest about what's happened, why it happened, and perhaps most importantly, how I actually feel about it. Because the truth is a little more complicated than simply saying I've made a mistake and won't do it again.
How it happened
It started during a trip to London with my friend Aidan. He's a regular cannabis user, and at the time he didn't know I'd stopped.
We were going to the theatre to see
Cats
, and I agreed to take an edible with him beforehand.

At the time, I think I saw it as a fairly harmless, one-off thing. I was away with a friend, we were doing something fun, and I didn't necessarily see it as the beginning of anything more significant.
The following week, Aidan was coming to Glasgow to see Jane McDonald with me, and we'd discussed smoking together. I obtained some cannabis for the occasion.
This is where things started to unravel.
I decided to test some of it myself beforehand. Then I bought more because I was worried there wouldn't be enough. Then, after Aidan had gone home, I smoked what was left.
Almost immediately afterwards, I went to my parents' house to look after their cat for a week. During that time, I smoked continuously.
What had started as a fairly innocent social experience had turned into something much more familiar.

When I returned home, I managed to stop for a week. But then I went back to it. Throughout September and into October, I've been on and off cannabis, sometimes managing to leave it alone and other times falling back into the same pattern.
And that's where things stand today.
The uncomfortable truth
I think one of the reasons I've found this difficult to confront is that I still really, really enjoy cannabis.

I wish I didn't, in some ways. It would make things considerably easier if I could honestly say I hated it, or that every experience had been miserable, or that I couldn't understand what I'd ever seen in it.
But that's simply not true.

I love the feeling of smoking. I love the ritual of it. I love sitting down in the evening, knowing I've got absolutely nothing else I need to do, putting something on the television or listening to music, and just switching off.
I've missed it enormously.

There have even been moments where I've wished I could take up cigarettes, simply because I enjoy the act of smoking so much. I know that's a terrible idea, and I have no intention of doing it, but it gives some indication of how much I miss that particular experience.
For a little while, I convinced myself that perhaps I'd got to a point where I could have both. That I could enjoy cannabis regularly while still doing everything else I wanted to do with my life.
I don't think that's true anymore.
The problem isn't that I don't enjoy it
The problem is what happens to everything else.

When I'm smoking regularly, I become incredibly insular. I want to be in my flat, in my room, smoking all evening. I don't particularly want to go anywhere or do anything. I don't want to see people. I don't feel especially motivated to work on projects or make progress towards things I've previously been excited about.
My ambitions don't necessarily disappear. They just stop feeling important.
And that's quite a frightening thing to recognise, because I am an ambitious person. I have so many things I want to do, places I want to go, things I want to learn and experiences I want to have.

I want to be physically healthy. I want to get stronger, become a better runner, eat properly and look after myself. I want to make things, develop my career, become more financially secure, spend time with people I care about and generally make something of my life.
But when cannabis becomes a regular part of my routine, all of those things start taking a back seat.

I stop exercising as consistently. My eating habits deteriorate. I become less interested in going out and doing things. The evenings disappear, and eventually the days start to feel a bit interchangeable.
And the worst part is that, while it's happening, I don't always particularly mind.
I'm comfortable. I'm enjoying myself. I'm perfectly content to spend another evening doing exactly the same thing I did the night before.
It's only when I come out of that pattern that I properly appreciate how much I've been missing.
I don't want to spend my late twenties like that.
Where things stand
As I write this, I don't have any cannabis, and I have no plans to obtain any more.
I don't particularly want to, either. I'm ready to stop again, at least for now.

But I'm not going to make some grand declaration that I'll never smoke cannabis again. I've done enough of that sort of thing, and I don't think making an absolute promise about the rest of my life would be particularly honest.
Could I find myself in a situation a month from now where I decide to smoke again? Possibly. I can't say for certain.
I also don't necessarily think that an occasional experience with cannabis is inherently incompatible with the kind of life I want to lead.
But there's a very significant difference between occasionally doing something with a friend and having cannabis readily available in the house, where I can smoke whenever I feel like it.
The latter, I've come to realise, simply doesn't work for me.
It's far too easy for an occasional experience to become an everyday habit. And once it does, it becomes increasingly difficult to justify doing anything else.
So while I'm not ruling out ever using cannabis again, I am recognising that regular access to it is incompatible with my priorities.
That's not a particularly exciting conclusion. It's not even a new one. But it's where I've arrived.
What happens next
I don't want this to become another cycle of stopping, feeling better, making ambitious plans, and then quietly slipping back into old habits.
I also don't want to spend the next few months obsessing over cannabis, counting the days since I last smoked, or treating every passing thought about it as some sort of personal crisis.
I want to get on with my life.
And I think that's where the wider Autumn/Winter 2026–27 programme comes in.
Over the past few months, I've been thinking increasingly about the kind of life I want to build for myself in Glasgow, and particularly here in the Southside.
I love living here. I love having my own place. I love the independence it gives me, the opportunities around me, and the fact that I have so much of my life still ahead of me.
But I don't think I've always made the most of it.
There's a version of my life where I spend my evenings alone in my flat, smoking, watching television and feeling perfectly content with doing very little.

And then there's another version where I'm getting out, exercising, exploring the city, seeing people, making things, reading, learning, travelling and actually following through on the ambitions I have for myself.
I know which one I want.

That doesn't mean I need to be productive every minute of every day. I love spending time at home. I love doing absolutely nothing sometimes. I don't want to turn my life into some exhausting exercise in self-improvement where every spare moment has to be accounted for.
I just want to feel like I'm living properly, rather than letting life happen around me.
That's ultimately what Southsideism needs to be about.

Not some grand reinvention of everything, and not a punishment for having fallen back into an old habit. Just a more deliberate attempt to build a life that feels healthy, interesting, fulfilling and worth getting out of bed for.
There's a lot to work through, and I don't have all the answers yet.
I'm disappointed that I've found myself back in this position. I'm also glad that I can recognise what's happening, and that I haven't entirely lost sight of the things that matter to me.
I still miss cannabis. I'll probably continue to miss it for a while.
But I think I miss the version of myself that's actually doing things with his life considerably more.
And I'd quite like to get back to him.

articles.title: Two books challenge the meaning of technological progress
articles.standfirst: New reading choices bring AI optimism and Silicon Valley transport criticism into conversation.

blocks.alt: Two books challenge the meaning of technological progress

runs.text: The Government for SwS has added two books to its reading list, bringing together competing perspectives on technological progress, artificial intelligence and public transport.
Ethan Mollick's
Co-Intelligence: Living and Working with AI
and Paris Marx's
Road to Nowhere: What Silicon Valley Gets Wrong about the Future of Transportation
have both been purchased, creating an opportunity to examine not simply what technology makes possible, but whether its applications solve the right problems.
Two perspectives on technological progress
Published in 2024,
Co-Intelligence

is Mollick's practical examination of generative AI as a collaborator in working, learning and creative thinking. The Wharton professor encourages readers to experiment with AI, while retaining human oversight and judgement. The book's specific examples inevitably reflect the capabilities of its publication period, but its wider questions about collaboration and responsibility remain pertinent in 2026.
Marx's
Road to Nowhere

, first published in 2022, approaches innovation from a more sceptical direction. Its central concern is the technology industry's tendency to present private vehicles, ride-hailing and automation as answers to transport problems whose roots are often political, spatial and economic.
Where Mollick asks how people might work productively with a new technology, Marx asks who benefits when a particular technological solution is chosen in the first place.
A question of problem definition
Together, the books offer a useful challenge to the assumption that more sophisticated technology automatically produces better outcomes.

For transport, an autonomous car may be an extraordinary engineering achievement without addressing the inefficiency of moving large numbers of people through crowded streets in individual vehicles. Investment in reliable buses, rail and walkable neighbourhoods may address the underlying problem more directly.
In digital design, the equivalent danger is building a compelling interface or AI-powered workflow before establishing whether the service, institution or user actually needs it.

That tension is especially relevant to the Government's Mind and Identity priorities, which encompass learning, critical thinking and the deliberate development of design judgement. The purchases are not a declaration of allegiance to either author's worldview. They are an invitation to examine the assumptions behind both.
Reading critically in 2026

The publication dates matter. AI has developed rapidly since Mollick's book appeared, so individual demonstrations should be read as historical examples rather than a current capability guide. Likewise, Marx's account predates some subsequent developments in autonomous driving and urban mobility. His critique should be assessed against present evidence rather than accepted wholesale.

Neither book needs to provide a complete account of technological change to be valuable. Their strongest contribution may be the questions they encourage readers to ask: who defines a problem, what counts as progress, and how should success be measured?

The new reading pair therefore represents more than two additions to a bookshelf. It provides a framework for examining technological optimism alongside public-interest design, with the human consequences of innovation kept firmly in view.
Further reading:
Co-Intelligence, Penguin

articles.title: The biggest surprise at SNL UK was off camera
articles.standfirst: A London dress rehearsal revealed the human side of live television, from Danny Dyer's quiet audience interaction to close-up warm-up comedy.

blocks.alt: The biggest surprise at SNL UK was off camera

runs.text: A trip to the dress rehearsal of
Saturday Night Live UK
has delivered an unexpected highlight: not a sketch or a celebrity cameo, but the ordinary, human atmosphere inside a major television production.

The 10 October rehearsal in London offered a close-up view of the cast, host Danny Dyer and the audience-facing work that happens around the programme. For SwS, who attended during a weekend visit from Glasgow, the lasting impression was how unremarkably approachable the performers seemed.

Dyer, hosting the episode, appeared relaxed with the cast between moments on stage. At one point, while moving to or from a sketch, he stopped beside an audience member at the end of the row where SwS was seated. The exchange was not heard directly. Afterwards, other audience members asked what he had said, and the person involved described it as a simple enquiry about whether she was enjoying the show.

It was a tiny interaction, but a revealing one. A performer familiar from television was suddenly a person checking in with somebody in the room. There was no grand gesture and no sense of a staged encounter.
The warm-up felt close

The experience also brought the audience unusually near to performers Paddy Young and Ania Magliano, who took part in the warm-up. Their proximity made the event feel less like watching a distant broadcast and more like sharing a room with working comedians preparing an evening's entertainment.

blocks.alt: The biggest surprise at SNL UK was off camera

runs.text: That closeness changed the texture of the experience. On television, a production of this scale is defined by camera angles, edits, sets and carefully controlled transitions. From a studio seat, the small moments between those elements become part of the story. Performers talk, move around, prepare and react in ways that seldom register in the finished programme.

SwS's response was strikingly simple: everyone seemed normal. Nobody appeared especially outrageous or untouchable. Even Dyer, a recognisable and sometimes larger-than-life public figure, seemed more human when observed at close quarters.
A different view of television

The rehearsal was part of a short London visit running from 9 to 11 October. Earlier arrangements had centred on the journey, accommodation and the prospect of seeing a British adaptation of the American sketch-comedy institution. The actual experience offered something less predictable.

A dress rehearsal gives an audience access to a version of the show before its final broadcast. Material and pacing can change, and the room is doing practical work as well as enjoying a performance. It is therefore a different experience from watching a polished episode at home.
The strongest memory may not be a particular joke at all. It is the sense that television's apparent distance can disappear very quickly when the camera is no longer mediating every interaction.

For someone interested in broadcasting, production and the mechanics of live entertainment, that is a worthwhile discovery. The glamour remains, but it sits alongside people simply getting on with their jobs.
The trip has now concluded. Its unexpected lesson was that the people on the other side of the screen can feel considerably less remote when seen from a few feet away.

articles.title: The London move has a Glasgow endgame
articles.standfirst: A London renting plan keeps first-home savings for Glasgow.

blocks.alt: The London move has a Glasgow endgame

runs.text: London is still the ambition. But buying a flat there is not the plan.
The new strategy is to rent alone in London for a period, continue saving through the Lifetime ISA, then return to Glasgow to buy a first home.

It is a significant change in the order of events. Earlier thinking centred on buying a modest Glasgow flat first, partly to get onto the property ladder while local prices remained comparatively accessible. The latest approach puts the experience of London ahead of ownership without giving up the longer-term goal of having a home in Glasgow.
London without giving up Glasgow

The attraction is straightforward. SwS wants the independence, pace and opportunities of London while keeping the interests and routines already established in Scotland. Living alone is a central condition, rather than an optional extra to be dropped when the figures get difficult.
The next stage is financial rather than geographical. The London plan remains conditional on finding work that supports the cost of living alone.
There is no confirmed move date, London job offer or tenancy. The plan remains an ambition rather than a completed relocation.
The price of living alone
The proposed move remains conditional on finding a salary and rental budget that make living alone in London sustainable.

London rent, council tax, bills and moving costs would all have to be covered by one income. Sharing a flat would change the sums, but it would also change the ambition. The aim is to preserve the independence of the present home in Battlefield, not simply to acquire a London postcode.

blocks.alt: The London move has a Glasgow endgame

runs.text: The Barbican is a particular favourite, but it is a reference point for the kind of London life being considered, not a flat search with a fixed address. The location, layout and monthly cost of any eventual home would all need to work in practice. The priority is independence without sacrificing the longer-term plan.
The savings stay in Scotland

The new sequence leaves room for a period in London without making a permanent break with Glasgow. The return is an intention, not a booking or a deadline. It depends on work, the cost of renting and what life in the capital actually feels like after the novelty has worn off.

blocks.alt: The London move has a Glasgow endgame

runs.text: There is still no confirmed timetable. The immediate work is to assess what living alone would cost, what kind of role would support it, and whether the day-to-day experience matches the ambition. Glasgow remains home for now, with London a serious future possibility rather than a decision already carried out. The plan can develop without pretending that a move, a job change or a home purchase has been agreed.

The Lifetime ISA is intended for that eventual first home, rather than the London move itself. Any relocation costs would therefore need to be met separately. That is the practical dividing line between the two ambitions.

articles.title: Three daily editions return to SWS.GOV News
articles.standfirst: The automated News schedule is restored with Notion-only publishing, image-rich articles and safeguards against incomplete drafts.

blocks.alt: A web-fed offset press printing newspapers
blocks.caption: A web-fed offset press printing newspapers

runs.text: An offset printing press in operation, used here to illustrate the editorial publishing process rather than
SWS.GOV
's digital infrastructure. Photograph: Tom T /
Wikimedia Commons
CC BY 2.0
[SWS alt: Close-up of a working offset newspaper printing press with paper running through its rollers.]
SWS.GOV
News is returning to its three-times-daily publishing schedule after a mismatch between an older automated task and the site's newer Notion publishing system was identified and corrected.
The scheduled task had continued to instruct ChatGPT to create articles in Craft, even though
SWS.GOV

had already moved its editorial operation to Notion. That difference was more than a naming problem. Craft is now retained as a legacy source, while new articles are expected to live in the Articles database under
SWS.GOV
Publisher in Notion.

The problem became clear after an attempted Craft publication left an incomplete draft and the recurring News task was paused. The latest change restores that schedule and rewrites its instructions around the actual publishing destination.

The task is again enabled for three daily runs, scheduled for 8am, 2pm and 8pm in Europe/London. Each run is intended to find one genuinely distinct development across SwS activity, from work and travel to technology, culture and Government for SwS decisions.
One home for new articles

Under the revised procedure, the system must check the current Notion database schema, review recent articles for duplication, and create a new page as Draft. Its headline, standfirst, date, tags and Superfeed settings belong in structured database properties. The complete story belongs in the page body.
The status changes to Published only after the article has been read back and checked. A separate website sync must then complete before
SWS.GOV
can be described as carrying the story live. Saving a page in Notion is not, by itself, proof that the public website has updated.

blocks.alt: Newspapers displayed at a newsstand
blocks.caption: Newspapers displayed at a newsstand

runs.text: A newspaper display, illustrating the aim of presenting each
SWS.GOV
story as a complete editorial item. Photograph from
Wikimedia Commons
[SWS alt: Black-and-white photograph of newspapers arranged for sale in a shop.]
More pictures, fewer interruptions

The publication instructions have also been expanded to support more imagery. A relevant lead image is required at the very start of each article, followed by its caption and descriptive alternative text. The workflow aims to add two or three further images throughout a typical story where the subject justifies them.

Images sourced online must have verifiable provenance and reuse rights. A shortage of suitable additional pictures should not hold up an otherwise complete article, although a missing required lead image can leave that individual story in Draft.

Most importantly, a failed article must no longer suspend the entire News operation. Subsequent scheduled runs can continue, while a retry should finish the existing draft rather than creating a duplicate.

The restored task is therefore a practical change to publishing reliability, not a claim that every part of the pipeline has been proven. This test publication is intended to check whether the updated instructions can produce a complete illustrated Notion article and move it through verification without returning to Craft.

articles.title: From Flying Scotsman to Azuma: celebrating the East Coast journey
articles.standfirst: A journey aboard Azuma 801230 opens a window onto more than 160 years of rail travel between Edinburgh and London, with an interactive historical timeline.

blocks.alt: LNER Class 801 Azuma 801220 at London King’s Cross
blocks.caption: LNER Class 801 Azuma 801220 at London King’s Cross

runs.text: LNER Azuma 801220 at King’s Cross before a service to Edinburgh, 20 February 2020. Photograph:
SavageKieran, Wikimedia Commons
CC BY-SA 4.0
. Version straightened and shadows adjusted by DavidArthur. This archive photograph shows a sister unit, not tonight’s 801230.
[SWS alt: A white and red LNER Azuma with a yellow cab front stands beneath the roof of London King’s Cross station.]

A comfortable evening journey aboard LNER Azuma 801230 has prompted a celebration of the railway connecting Edinburgh Waverley with London King’s Cross, and the generations of engineering that made it possible.

Sam boarded the 18:00 departure on 9 October, with a booked arrival at 22:10. His enthusiasm for the train turned a routine trip into an opportunity to look more closely at one of Britain’s great intercity routes.

The nine-car electric Azuma represents a modern chapter in a story stretching back more than 160 years. Its quiet passenger environment and practical comforts make that history tangible: progress experienced from a seat, rather than read from a specification.
A service older than its famous locomotive
The London–Edinburgh express that became the Flying Scotsman began in 1862. The renowned steam locomotive took its name from the service, not the other way round.
That distinction matters. The route’s identity was already established before its most famous engine arrived, built around the promise of connecting two capitals with speed, comfort and reliability.

In 1928, the Flying Scotsman completed its first non-stop London–Edinburgh run in around eight hours. A corridor through the locomotive’s tender enabled a relief crew to reach the cab while the train continued moving. It was an ingenious answer to the human demands of a long-distance service.
From diesel speed to electric intercity
British Rail’s High Speed Train reached the East Coast Main Line in May 1978. The InterCity 125 brought a new generation of diesel-powered travel, with a power car at either end.

The InterCity 225 followed from 1989. Its Class 91 electric locomotive and separate coaches became closely associated with the route. Full public services over the newly electrified East Coast Main Line commenced on 8 July 1991, establishing the infrastructure that allows today’s electric Azuma to travel between Edinburgh and London.

These developments were successive investments in a working national connection. The railway’s appeal depended on the whole journey: stations, infrastructure, staff, rolling stock and the experience of spending several hours aboard.
The Azuma chapter

Azumas entered LNER service in May 2019 and reached Edinburgh services on 1 August. Built by Hitachi using Japanese engineering expertise, the fleet brought faster acceleration and a refreshed passenger environment.

Tonight’s 801230 is a Class 801/2 electric unit. Unlike the bi-mode Class 800, which can undertake regular journeys on diesel beyond the wires, its normal operation relies on overhead electricity. A small diesel engine is reserved for emergency use.
