runs.text: The Government of SwS has today confirmed the restoration of regular use of our private bicycle following the relocation of storage infrastructure to a location directly adjacent to the primary travel routes of SwS.

The Absurdist administration notes that the bicycle storage previously allocated on Gryffe Street was situated approximately five minutes on foot from 37 Holmlea Road. While operationally adequate, the distance between residence and storage introduced a persistent access barrier that materially reduced utilisation of the bicycle.

Under revised storage arrangements, the bicycle is now housed within a Bikehangar facility at the top of Battlefield Avenue. The location sits within the same block as Tenement Barbershop and lies directly on the principal travel corridor used for onward movement across the surrounding area.

The Government for SwS assesses that this relocation substantially reduces the friction associated with bicycle access and is therefore expected to materially increase cycling activity across SwS travel patterns.
As part of the policy shift, the Absurdist administration has confirmed that cycling will be progressively integrated into routine mobility across the city.
The Government of SwS has outlined the following immediate measures:
restoration of the bicycle as a primary transport option for short and medium-distance travel
development of a series of recommended cycling route maps covering key destinations
prioritisation of segregated cycle infrastructure and shared-use paths within those routes
identification of progressive route options incorporating roads that may become viable as cycling confidence increases or under low-traffic conditions
These
route maps
initially cover a set of frequently visited destinations within the travel network of SwS, including the library, cinema, cafés, office locations, and gym facilities.
The Government for SwS has stated that the maps serve both as operational guidance and as a structured framework for gradually expanding the cycling range of SwS across the urban environment.
In parallel with the storage relocation, the Absurdist administration has also confirmed the acquisition of additional cycling equipment.

A pannier bag and helmet have been purchased to support safer and more practical bicycle use. The purchase was partially subsidised through reward points accumulated from the acquisition of the bicycle in the previous year. Following application of these credits, the total financial outlay for the equipment amounted to approximately £8 including delivery to the residence of SwS.

The Government of SwS notes that bicycle usage over the past year has remained steady, though a proportion of cycling activity has occurred through the use of hire bicycles within Glasgow, operated under the Voi system.

While these services have provided useful mobility support, the Absurdist administration has determined that greater utilisation of the personally owned bicycle will strengthen autonomy, reduce travel friction, and expand the operational mobility capacity of SwS.
Future cycling activity is expected to include both functional travel and recreational journeys, including routes along canal infrastructure and across Glasgow’s network of green spaces.
The Government for SwS considers the relocation of bicycle storage, the acquisition of additional equipment, and the introduction of route mapping to constitute a practical transport reform under the
Body
piloti of Governance Under Four Pilotis.
The Absurdist administration will monitor utilisation rates and route development as part of the ongoing implementation of the Spring/Summer 2026 governance programme.

articles.title: “I get FOMO about death”: Sam Smith on love, politics and learning to live with uncertainty
articles.standfirst: The 27-year-old BBC designer reflects on love in Glasgow’s Necropolis, political disillusionment, celebrity crushes from the 90s and why money, empathy and a sunny afternoon in the park still beat everything else.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Sam Smith answers quickly, but not carelessly. The 27-year-old UX designer, who works on the BBC’s account and sign-in systems, has the air of someone who spends a lot of time thinking about how people interact with the world. His answers circle around empathy, freedom and the quiet details of everyday life.

Ask him when he was happiest and he doesn’t hesitate. “In the sun, in the summer, in Glasgow, in a park, with Adam.” The answer is simple and specific, the kind of scene that feels like it could repeat itself every year if you’re lucky.

Smith grew up in Glasgow and still speaks about the city with a mix of affection and political frustration. His biggest disappointment, he says bluntly, is “the Labour government of 2024 failing to do anything with its gigantic majority.” Politics matters to him, though he doesn’t treat it like a football team you support unconditionally. His views on Scottish independence have changed over time. In 2014 he worried that leaving the UK might mean leaving the EU and losing a sense of stability. Brexit and the chaos that followed, he says, changed that calculation entirely. “Now I think it’s time for us to get the hell out.”

For someone whose job involves designing systems used by millions of people, Smith is surprisingly candid about his own habits and flaws. The trait he most dislikes in himself is “waffling when I’m speaking”, though he admits that it sometimes comes from thinking through ideas in real time. What he struggles to tolerate in others is more fundamental: a lack of empathy, or people confidently presenting opinions about things they don’t understand.

His self-description is disarmingly direct: “Gay, twink, white.” Asked what he’d change about his appearance, he shrugs. “Maybe three extra inches in height.” Otherwise, he seems comfortable with who he is.

Love, for Smith, is about ease rather than intensity. It’s the feeling of being able to drop the filters we normally carry around with us. “Just being yourself around someone without fear of judgement,” he says. His most memorable kiss took place in Glasgow’s Necropolis cemetery with his boyfriend Adam, a moment he describes with a kind of quiet reverence. “It’s a very special place,” he says. “And it set me up for a lifetime of many more to come.”

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Like many people in their twenties, Smith thinks about the future with a mix of ambition and mild existential dread. Growing older doesn’t scare him in the abstract; death does. “Eventually there comes a point where you die, and you don’t really have control over that,” he says. “I get FOMO.”
Money, he adds with a laugh, would be the most useful thing to have more of. “Money can be exchanged for goods and services,” he says, invoking a line from The Simpsons. “Including sex and fame.”

If life has taught him one principle worth holding onto, it’s the limits of perspective. “You can’t truly understand something from another person’s point of view,” he says. “The best thing you can do is assume good faith, try to embody empathy, and make the world a bit better with whatever you’re doing.”
As for what happens when we die, he pauses. The hopeful answer would be that something continues. The honest one, he says, is simpler. “Deep down, I think it probably just ends.”

articles.title: Government of SwS Signals Income Push as BBC Midweight Bid Enters Critical Phase
articles.standfirst: The Government for SwS has entered a critical phase in its income strategy, formally applying for a midweight role at the BBC while preparing a bid for its first paid, formalised teaching position in interaction design. With competition fierce and pressure mounting, the administration is betting that a strong narrative, proven delivery, and hard-won experience will be enough to secure advancement.

runs.text: The Government for SwS has confirmed it is entering a decisive phase in its plan to increase income, with two parallel moves now formally in train: a bid for promotion within the BBC and the formalisation of paid teaching work in higher education.

At the centre of the government’s strategy is a long-anticipated application for a Midweight UX Designer role at the BBC. After an extended period of internal stasis, five midweight positions have now been opened across the organisation, prompting what sources describe as a “full mobilisation” inside SwS.
The application has been submitted.

Officials say the campaign is being run as a tightly structured operation, explicitly modelled on the government’s successful trainee scheme application, which ultimately secured entry into the BBC. That earlier effort is widely regarded within SwS as proof that narrative discipline, clear evidence, and relentless preparation can overcome long odds.
This time, the stakes are higher.

The government is understood to be working long hours to assemble a coherent and compelling case that it is already operating at midweight level, if not beyond. The strategy hinges on demonstrating ownership, leadership, and product impact across multiple workstreams, rather than relying on tenure alone.

Internally, there is a sense of cautious confidence. It's believed that there's a strong story to tell, rooted in real delivery rather than aspiration, and that we possess the communication skills required to sell that story effectively in interview.

However, there is no complacency. Competition for the roles is expected to be intense, with strong internal candidates from across the BBC applying for a limited number of posts. One senior source described the field as “crowded, credible, and unforgiving”.

The government has acknowledged privately that failure to secure promotion would mark a turning point. For the first time since entering the BBC, SwS would actively explore career opportunities outside the corporation. While no such move is currently being pursued, contingency planning is said to be under way.
For now, however, the emphasis remains firmly on winning the internal fight.

Alongside the BBC bid, the government has also identified what it describes as its first fully formalised teaching opportunity: a part-time, asynchronous role in Interaction Design at the University of London.
An application is expected shortly.

If successful, the role would represent a significant shift in the government’s approach to education work. For several years, SwS has contributed substantial time and expertise to teaching at Glasgow Caledonian University on an unpaid basis. While officials continue to describe that experience as “formative and worthwhile”, there is now a clear policy direction that educational labour should be recognised and remunerated.
“This is about valuing the work,” one source said. “We’ve already proven we can do it. The next step is being paid for it.”

The teaching role is seen as part of a longer-term ambition to build a parallel income stream that reflects SwS’s experience in design education, mentoring, and curriculum delivery. The asynchronous nature of the post is understood to be particularly attractive, allowing it to sit alongside a full-time role without compromising performance.

Taken together, the BBC promotion bid and the University of London application form the core of the government’s current income-growth agenda. Both are high-pressure, high-stakes moves, and both will test SwS’s capacity to operate under sustained scrutiny.
There is confidence, but also realism. Success is far from guaranteed, and the coming months are expected to be demanding.
The outcome will shape not just earnings, but the future direction of the government itself.

articles.title: Government–commissioned report into Miniature Model Making
articles.standfirst: A government–commissioned report into the art of physical miniature model making

runs.text: 1. Purpose & Scope

Physical architectural models are three-dimensional representations of building designs, used by architects and designers to explore ideas, communicate concepts, and evaluate spatial relationships . Unlike digital models on a screen, physical models allow tactile interaction and true spatial understanding, letting both designers and laypeople grasp form and scale in a visceral way . Models are used throughout the design process – from rough concept massing studies to detailed presentation models – to test designs, inform decision-making, and present proposals . In professional practice and education alike, model making remains a valuable skill, complementing digital methods by providing a tangible perspective on the project .

Why modernist/brutalist buildings for beginners: Post-war modernist and brutalist architecture (such as Scottish new-town projects like Cumbernauld) features simple, massive forms and minimal ornamentation, making them ideal subjects for a first model. These designs emphasize massing, repetition, and structural clarity over intricate details. For example, brutalist structures often consist of bold geometric volumes in raw concrete, eliminating decorative details in favor of honest, straightforward forms . This means a beginner can capture the essence – the blocks, slabs and voids – without needing to reproduce fine ornament. The repetitive modular nature of housing blocks or civic buildings in this style provides practice in cutting and assembling multiple similar components, reinforcing skills through repetition. Moreover, modernist/brutalist models, even when simplified, have a strong visual presence that clearly conveys the architectural concept, which is encouraging for a newcomer.

Scope of this briefing: This document provides foundational guidance on starting from zero in physical model making. It covers the full process: from planning and design, choosing an appropriate scale, acquiring essential tools and materials, basic construction techniques, through to finishing and selecting a suitable first project. The focus is deliberately on beginner-level, hands-on advice – assuming no prior craft experience or equipment. What is not covered: advanced model-making techniques (e.g. laser cutting, 3D printing, complex detailing), professional presentation models, or broader architectural design theory beyond what’s needed to begin model building. The briefing also does not cover structural engineering or large-scale workshop fabrication – it is confined to table-top scale architectural models appropriate for a beginner. By adhering to the guidance here, a novice with strong design interest (especially in modernist/brutalist architecture) will be equipped to build their first simple building model and establish a foundation for more advanced projects.
2. Design & Planning (Digital → Physical)
Before cutting a single piece of card or foam, it’s wise to plan the model digitally or on paper. This section explains how to go from an initial architectural idea to a buildable model plan.

Using Shapr3D on iPad: A recommended approach for tech-savvy beginners is to use a 3D modeling app like Shapr3D on an iPad (with Apple Pencil) to sketch out the building form. Shapr3D provides an intuitive CAD interface where you can quickly create and adjust simple masses – perfect for modernist blocks and brutalist forms. Start by drawing the basic volumes of your building in the app: for example, a rectangular prism for a housing block, additional extruded forms for stair cores or balconies, etc. This digital massing model lets you explore proportions and geometry interactively. You can rotate and view it from all angles, ensuring the model will capture the key silhouettes and relationships. Use the app to establish an appropriate scale as well: model the building at real-world size (or import known dimensions), then decide on a scale (e.g. 1:100) and use the measurement tools to derive the model dimensions for each part. Shapr3D allows you to annotate or measure lengths, so you can note that, for instance, a 30m long facade will be 30 cm long in a 1:100 model. Some designers even export unrolled surfaces or drawings from Shapr3D as cutting templates – for example, one case study used a 1:10 scaled Shapr3D file to create an unrolled surface contour as a guide for cutting pieces out of card . You may similarly generate simple elevation outlines, print them to scale, and use them to trace shapes onto your material.

Level of precision vs. progress: At the beginning, perfect precision is not the goal – an approximation of form is usually sufficient for a concept model. A common pitfall is over-designing the model digitally. Remember that an architectural model is an abstraction; you do not need to model every window frame or door in CAD before building. Determine the overall size, proportions and key divisions (e.g. floor heights, major blocks) to a reasonable accuracy (within a few millimeters at model scale). That level of planning ensures pieces will fit, without getting bogged down in minor details. Know when to stop designing and start building: once the primary dimensions and volumes are decided and you’ve figured out how the pieces can be constructed, it’s time to move on. It’s often in the physical making that additional ideas or solutions will emerge, especially for beginners. Overly detailed digital plans can lead to frustration if they prove too difficult to realize in actual materials. So use digital tools to outline the form and test feasibility, but switch to physical building once you have a workable scheme. In short, design enough to be confident in scale and proportions, then let the real materials and process inform the rest.

Alternatives to digital planning: Digital modeling is helpful but not mandatory. Many beginners successfully plan with hand sketches and simple paper templates. You can draw scaled plans/elevations on graph paper or carton, then use those drawings as cutting guides. For instance, sketch the front view of your building at the target scale on paper; this becomes a template to cut out the facade in card. Similarly, drawing a floor plan outline on paper can guide your base and wall placements. Some modelers make “sketch models” from scrap materials early on – quick, rough constructions that aren’t glued permanently . Such sketch models (e.g. foam offcuts pinned together, or paper folded to shape) let you test the composition and massing in real 3D before committing to the final build. They are extremely useful to check if your design is too complex or if any part might be troublesome to construct. Because they’re temporary, you can adjust or discard them freely without feeling the pressure of perfection . In summary, whether using Shapr3D’s digital canvas or pencil-and-paper, aim to produce a clear but simple plan for the model’s form and measurements. Plan out how pieces will come together, then proceed to building – maintaining flexibility to adapt as you gain hands-on insight.
3. Scale Selection for Beginners

Choosing the right scale for your model is a crucial early decision. Scale affects not only the model’s size but also the level of detail you can (or should) include and the effort required . Scale in this context is the ratio of the model’s measurements to the real building. For example, at 1:100 scale, 1 centimeter on the model represents 1 meter on the real building. As a beginner, it’s important to select a scale that is manageable and suits your subject.

Recommended beginner scales: For a simple building such as a modest housing block, scales in the range of 1:100 to 1:200 are often ideal. At 1:100 (1cm = 1m), you can handle parts easily and represent major elements (walls, windows as openings, etc.) without the model becoming too large. A building of 30m length would be 30cm in the model – a convenient size for desk construction. 1:200 (0.5cm = 1m) is useful for larger structures or sites; it compresses space more, requiring less area, but also means small features like doorways might be only a few millimeters tall (often too fine for a beginner to cut accurately). Many architectural education projects use 1:100 or 1:200 for building models because they balance detail and simplicity. If your focus is a small house or a single room interior, 1:50 could be chosen (allowing more detail, like furniture blocks, since 1cm = 0.5m). Conversely, very large complexes or city massing might use 1:500 or 1:1000, but those scales significantly abstract away detail and can be challenging in a different way (tiny pieces, or very large context base). As a starting point, 1:100 is a good default for many modernist building models – it’s commonly used for building design models and offers a tangible level of detail without overwhelming size .

Trade-offs and scale discipline: Each scale comes with trade-offs between fidelity, size, and complexity. Larger scales (e.g. 1:50) produce bigger models where you can incorporate finer details (windows, texture, etc.), but the model will occupy more space and consume more material. Bigger models also take longer to build. Smaller scales (e.g. 1:200 or 1:500) yield compact models focusing on overall massing; they are faster in terms of fewer parts, but paradoxically can be harder for a beginner if too small, because tiny parts are fiddly to cut and assemble. In fact, “contrary to popular belief, smaller isn’t always faster” – choosing an overly small scale can lead to painstaking hours cutting miniature pieces that would have been unnecessary at a slightly larger scale . You should consider the amount of time and patience you have: it may be better to pick a larger scale and simplify the model’s scope, rather than a tiny scale that becomes frustrating . Once a scale is selected, discipline in its use is key. This means consistently converting real dimensions to model dimensions and maintaining those proportions throughout. Use a scale ruler (an architect’s triangular scale) set to your chosen ratio for quick measurements . For example, if using 1:100, a 10m wall should measure 10 cm on your model; check such conversions for all major parts. Plan for the thickness of materials at scale as well (e.g. a 5mm foamboard wall is 0.5m thick at 1:100 – appropriate for a concrete shear wall perhaps). Maintaining scale discipline ensures the model parts fit together correctly and that the finished piece accurately conveys the size relationships intended. Summary tip: Select the largest scale that still keeps your model within a convenient size, to maximize clarity and ease of building. And remember, the goal is to communicate the design’s essence – you can always indicate only the most important elements and omit the rest (more on that later) . By thoughtfully choosing and sticking to a scale, you set yourself up for a smoother build process and a legible result.
4. Tools: Acquisition & Setup

Building architectural models by hand requires a set of basic tools. This section outlines the absolute minimum toolkit needed, suggests useful upgrades, and covers safe use, maintenance, and budgeting – with a UK context for sourcing items.
Essential minimum tool list: Starting from nothing, you should acquire the following basic tools first:

Cutting implement: A sharp craft knife is the single most important tool. Common options are a utility knife with snap-off blades (e.g. Olfa 9mm), or a precision scalpel (such as a Swann-Morton handle with replaceable 10A blades) . Ensure you have a supply of spare blades. A sharp blade is crucial for clean cuts – and safer (dull blades slip and cause accidents) . A small pair of sharp scissors is also handy for thin card or paper details .

Cutting mat: A self-healing cutting mat (e.g. A3 or A2 size) provides a safe, durable surface for cutting . It protects your table and helps prolong blade life by offering a bit of “give”. Markings on the mat (grid or measurements) are useful for alignment.

Metal ruler (straightedge): A metal (steel or aluminum) ruler, 30 cm length to start (plus a shorter 15 cm for small pieces), is essential for guiding cuts and measuring . Plastic rulers will get sliced by your knife; a metal ruler with a non-slip backing or a cork strip is ideal. Ensure the edge is straight and true. Use the ruler for both measuring and as a straightedge to cut along.

Square / right-angle tool: A small try square or engineers’ square is very helpful for drawing and checking 90° angles . This ensures your model’s corners are straight and pieces align properly. Even a plastic drafting triangle can serve initially, though a solid metal square is more accurate.

Pencil and marker: A mechanical pencil, 0.5mm or thinner (0.3mm HB or H leads), is recommended for marking cut lines precisely without tearing the material . Also have a softer pencil or fine-tip marker to label pieces lightly on non-visible sides if needed. An eraser for removing guidelines is useful.

Adhesives: At minimum, get PVA white glue (wood glue or school glue) for general assembly of card, wood, foam – it’s strong and dries clear (albeit slowly) . Also consider a pack of cyanoacrylate (super glue) for instant bonding of small pieces or dissimilar materials . Masking tape (low-tack painter’s tape) is very useful to hold pieces together temporarily while glue sets, and for marking guidelines.

Support tools: A few pins or clips to hold parts (you can use common push pins, or binder clips for clamping edges) help during gluing . Gather some sandpaper (medium ~120 grit and fine ~300 grit) to smooth rough edges and gently bevel or clean cuts . Also have a rag or paper towels for wiping excess glue, and a small sanding block (could just be a flat wood offcut wrapped in sandpaper) for keeping edges straight while sanding.

With the above, you can accomplish the basic tasks of cutting, measuring, and gluing accurately. This toolkit is generally affordable. For example, in the UK a beginner could acquire a decent knife, mat, ruler, glue, and some sundries for on the order of £30–£50 total (available from art and stationery shops or online).
Recommended beginner upgrades (nice-to-have):

Additional cutting tools: Extra knife types (e.g. a heavier-duty Stanley knife for thick foam, a smaller hobby knife for fine cuts) can be useful. A circle cutter or compass cutter helps in cutting neat circles or arcs in card.
Set of files or micro-sanders: For fine tuning edges, small needle files or an emery board can refine windows or door openings after cutting.

Clamps and weights: A set of small clamps or even reusable heavy objects (metal blocks, small hand vise, or bulldog clips) will secure pieces while glue dries and ensure right angles . Having a couple of metal 90° angle blocks or Lego® bricks can serve as jigs to keep walls perpendicular during assembly.

Tweezers or pliers: Fine-tipped tweezers help in placing small components or pulling glue strings. Small pliers or wire cutters are needed if you work with any wire or pins (for instance, clipping pins used as alignment dowels).

Expanded measuring tools: A triangular scale ruler with multiple scales (1:50, 1:100, 1:200, etc.) simplifies measuring in scale . Also, digital calipers are an optional precision tool if you want to directly measure small lengths accurately (useful but not essential early on).

Cutting aids: A metal safety ruler with a finger guard can protect your hand during cutting. A straightedge with cork back helps keep it from slipping. Also, consider a matte cutter or miniature mitre box if you plan to cut a lot of 90° miters (e.g. in wood strips for frames).

Specialty tools (later on): As you progress, you might invest in tools like a hot wire cutter (for shaping foam with smooth curves), a small tabletop saw (for wood strips), or even time-saving devices like laser-cutting services (some universities or makerspaces offer laser cutting for model parts). These are not needed for initial projects, but you should know they exist for future. For example, laser cutting can precisely cut acrylic, wood, or card for complex models – but it requires learning CAD drafting for cutting and isn’t typically a beginner’s first step .
Tool safety and maintenance: Safety is paramount when using cutting tools and adhesives:

Cutting safety: Always use a sharp blade and proper technique. Never force a dull blade; replace or sharpen it frequently – “accidents often happen with blunt blades because unnecessary pressure is put on the blade, making it easier to slip” . Cut away from your body and hands. Use a ruler as a guide and keep fingers clear of the blade path (some model-makers even wear a cut-resistant glove on the hand holding the ruler for protection). Make multiple light passes with the knife rather than one heavy cut ; this gives better control and avoids snapping blades. Always retract or cover blades when not in use.

Glue and fumes: Work in a well-ventilated area, especially if using solvent-based glues or spray adhesives. Solvent cements (for plastic) and aerosol sprays should be used with windows open or under an extractor, and keep them away from open flames. Super glue can bond skin instantly – wear nitrile gloves or use tweezers for tiny parts, and have acetone handy to debond if needed. Hot glue guns can cause burns; be cautious and use the low-temperature setting if available.

Workspace setup: Ensure you have good lighting over your work area – proper lighting prevents eye strain and cutting errors . Clear a sufficient, stable workspace so you can lay out parts without clutter. Keep a bin for offcuts nearby to immediately dispose of scraps and maintain order . An organized area will prevent accidents (like knocking over a knife or losing sharp blades in a mess).

Maintenance: Store tools dry and clean. Wipe excess glue off applicators and blades before it hardens. For knives, change blades often and dispose of used blades in a sharps container (an old screw-top jar works). Cutting mats last a long time but avoid excessive force that could gouge them; you can rotate the mat periodically so you’re not always cutting in the same groove. If using any power tools (drills, etc.), follow the manufacturer’s safety instructions and wear safety glasses.

Budgeting and sourcing (UK): Getting started need not be expensive. Basic toolkits are available from general craft retailers like Hobbycraft or online marketplaces (Amazon, eBay). Look also at art supply stores such as Cass Art (which carries model-making materials and tools) . For specialty items, the UK has dedicated model-making suppliers – for example, 4D Modelshop in London offers a vast range of raw materials and tools for models (styrene plastic sheets, foam, card, blades, etc.), available via mail order. Even general hardware stores (B&Q, Screwfix) can supply items like knives, blades, and insulation foam. When budgeting, prioritize the essentials mentioned; you can always add tools as needed per project. For instance, buy a quality knife and mat now, and postpone purchasing a hot wire cutter or fancy foam cutter until you actually require it. UK-specific tips: Surgical scalpels (Swann-Morton) and spare blades are inexpensive and high-quality, widely available online. PVA glue (often called wood glue or white glue) comes from brands like Evo-Stik, Gorilla or UniBond, all fine for paper/wood. For foam-safe adhesive, look for solvent-free formulas (standard PVA is safe on foam; solvent glues are not). Many art shops stock A1 or A2 foamboard sheets and mount board, and balsa wood strips, often in their technical drawing or architecture section. In summary, start with a core set of tools that fit your budget and add to your toolbox as your projects grow in complexity. Proper tools are an investment – “invest in high-quality tools because they last longer and give better results” – but even on a tight budget, you can obtain the necessary items to begin model making safely and effectively.
5. Materials: Selection & Use

Choosing the right materials is as important as having the right tools. Different materials have different properties that affect ease of use, appearance, and durability of your model . As a beginner focusing on modernist/brutalist buildings, you will work mostly with a few core, versatile materials. Below we introduce the main materials recommended for starter architectural models – foam board, XPS foam, mountboard (card), plasticard, and balsa wood – explaining when and why to use each, their behavior and handling, and tips on storage and longevity.

Foam Board (Foamcore): Description: Foam board consists of a sheet of polystyrene (foam) sandwiched between two thin paper/card faces. It usually comes in white (also black or other colors) and in various thicknesses (commonly 3mm, 5mm) . Why use: Foam board is lightweight, strong for its weight, and easy to cut, making it ideal for quick massing of building forms . It produces a clean, neutral look – all surfaces smooth and flat – great for modernist forms (often used for all-white concept models) . Corners and junctions can be very neat because the foam core allows precise slicing and joins at 90° . Behavior & handling: Use a sharp knife and multiple light cuts to slice foam board without tearing the paper face . A metal straightedge guide is essential for straight cuts. You can also score one face (cut partially through) and then bend the board to form sharp-edged folds for certain shapes . When gluing, PVA white glue works well – apply thinly to avoid saturating the paper. Hot glue can also be used for instant bonds (the foam core accepts hot glue, but work quickly as it sets fast) . Solvent-based glues or paints should be avoided on foam board because they can melt the foam interior . Limitations: Foam board’s paper surfaces can warp if overly wetted by glue or paint – use glue sparingly and let it dry flat. The foam core is somewhat fragile: edges can dent, and exposed foam at cut edges is soft (corner joints might need reinforcement if load-bearing pieces). It’s not ideal for fine detail or very thin slivers (they will crush). Storage & longevity: Store foam boards flat to prevent bending, and in a dry environment (moisture can cause the paper to bow or delaminate). If kept indoors away from UV light and moisture, foam board models last many years, but note that the foam can yellow slightly over time and the paper may attract dust or discolor. For a durable presentation model, some prefer more robust materials, but for concept and practice models foam board is excellent .

XPS Foam (Insulation Foam): Description: Extruded polystyrene (XPS) foam is a dense foam often sold in insulation boards (commonly blue, pink, gray, or green sheets). Unlike foamcore, it is solid foam without paper facings. It’s sometimes called “styrofoam” in the US (though technically different) or informally “blue foam” after a popular type . Why use: XPS foam is extremely useful for massing studies and topography because it’s very quick to cut and shape . It comes in various thicknesses (5mm up to several centimeters), allowing easy creation of blocks for buildings or layered contours for landscapes . Architects BIG and OMA are known to use foam extensively in conceptual models . It’s lightweight and can be stacked or carved to produce complex forms rapidly. For brutalist subjects, foam can represent solid concrete volumes nicely (painted or unpainted). Behavior & handling: XPS foam cuts with a sharp blade (utility knife) – cut in shallow passes to avoid ragged edges. It also sands well: you can use sandpaper to refine shapes or even create slopes. A hot wire cutter is an optional tool that slices foam smoothly with a heated wire; if you have access to one, it allows very clean cuts and curved slicing, but always use it in ventilated space (melting foam releases fumes) . Glues: Use PVA or wood glue for most XPS foam joins; it adheres well (though drying takes a bit of time). Hot glue can also bond foam quickly, but be cautious – too hot and it can melt a bit of foam, and once stuck it’s hard to reposition. Avoid solvent-based adhesives (like model airplane glue or spray mount with solvents), as they will melt the foam . If you need to attach foam to foam strongly, toothpicks or cocktail sticks can serve as internal pins along with glue. Limitations: XPS foam is fragile under impact – edges and corners dent easily if pressed. Its surface is slightly rough (especially some types that are “bubbly” inside), so it may not give a refined finish for close-up viewing. It’s best for underlayers or rough massing rather than small detail parts. Also, painting requires care: spray paint will dissolve foam unless you first prime it (e.g. with an acrylic gesso or a coat of PVA). Acrylic model paints can be applied by brush as they are water-based. For a “concrete” finish, you might coat foam with a thin layer of filler or plaster, or use a texture paint (more on finishes later). Storage: Keep XPS foam sheets flat, not leaning (to avoid warping). Store in a bag or covered, as the static can attract dirt to the surface. It doesn’t mind humidity in terms of shape, but avoid high heat which could deform it. Longevity: Foam massing models are usually for early design phases – the material can last, but pieces might chip if handled frequently. For a final model, foam might be used internally and clad or painted for protection. In general, insulation foam is a forgiving, inexpensive material that invites quick experimentation – perfect for beginners to cut their teeth (sometimes literally – with a blade!) on basic forms .

Mountboard / Cardboard: Description: Mount board (mounting board) is a thick cardboard typically used for mounting photographs or art. It often has a smooth colored face (white/black/grey) and a cardboard core, around 1.5mm thick (there are also thinner presentation boards and thicker chipboards). More generally, cardstock and cardboard of various types fall in this category of paper-based sheet materials. Why use: Card is cheap, readily available, and versatile . It’s great for planar elements: walls, bases, or simple facade panels. Mountboard in particular is stiff and can hold its shape well for medium-sized models . It can represent neutral surfaces or be painted. Because it’s paper-based, it’s easy to cut (though thicker boards need more effort) and is a classic material for architectural models for both conceptual and semi-detailed models . For a brutalist motif, a grey card can directly suggest concrete color, or layers of card can simulate stratified ground or building levels . Behavior & handling: Use a sharp scalpel or utility knife; cut in multiple passes to avoid crushing the edges . When cutting thick mountboard, try to keep the blade perpendicular to avoid angled edges. Blades will dull quickly on dense card – replace or sharpen frequently . Card edges can be sanded lightly with fine sandpaper to smooth or bevel them. Gluing: PVA works well (especially PVA wood glue which grabs a bit faster and stronger on paper) . Apply glue sparingly and spread thinly – card absorbs moisture and too much glue can warp it. A thicker “tacky glue” (a common craft glue) is often preferred for card because it has less water content and sets faster . Another method is using double-sided tape or spray adhesive for large flat pieces – these give instant bonds and no warping, though placement must be precise (they’re hard to reposition) . Limitations: Cardboard is not as dimensionally stable as plastic or wood; long thin strips may bend. It’s best for relatively short spans or where both edges will be glued to something. Exposed edges of multi-ply card show the layers – sometimes that’s acceptable, sometimes not (you can cover edges with paper or filler if needed). Also, cutting small openings (like tiny windows) in thick card can be tricky to do cleanly. For very fine work, thinner card (or switch to plastic) might be easier. Handling tips: When marking on dark card, use a white pencil or chalk pencil; for light card, a hard pencil or even scoring lightly can mark cut lines. Scoring and bending: You can score halfway through and fold card to make corners (similar to foam board technique), useful for making a crisp corner without a separate joint. Storage: Keep card sheets flat and dry. If they do warp, you can sometimes flatten them under heavy books or press gently opposite to the bend. Avoid humidity and direct sunlight (sun can cause fading of colored card). Longevity: Good quality mountboard is often acid-free and can last decades if kept dry. However, if exposed to moisture or fluctuating humidity, card models can distort. Also, card is a paper product – it can attract insects or mold in poor conditions. For a lasting model, you might seal or paint the card surfaces to protect them. In summary, cardboard is a fundamental material for model-making due to its affordability and versatility – from baseplates to building shells, it will likely feature in your first project .

Plasticard (Styrene Plastic Sheets): Description: “Plasticard” usually refers to sheets of polystyrene or ABS plastic sold for hobby modeling. These are smooth, white (or colored) plastic sheets in thicknesses from ~0.25mm up to a few millimeters. Polystyrene sheet (also called styrene sheet) is common for scratch-building models, as it’s easy to cut and glue with solvent. Why use: Plastic sheet can produce very crisp, clean models with precise detail. It is dimensionally stable (doesn’t warp with normal glue or paint if used properly) and allows finer detail than card – e.g. scoring panel lines to represent facade joints, cutting very thin strips for railings, etc. For a brutalist model, plastic sheet could be useful if you want to achieve sharp-edged facades or repeatable modules (since plastic can be laser-cut or scored with high precision). It also takes paint well, so you can get a uniform concrete-like finish. Behavior & handling: Thin styrene sheets can be cut by scoring with a knife and snapping. For example, use a knife to draw a deep line (without cutting through entirely), then bend the sheet which will snap cleanly along the score . For thicker plastic (>1mm), you may need to saw gently with a fine-tooth model saw or make many passes with a knife. Filing and sanding plastic is very effective – edges can be smoothed and shaped with sandpaper (plastics file easily to refine shapes). One can also heat-bend plastic for curves, but that’s advanced. Gluing: The preferred glue is solvent cement (plastic weld glue) which actually melts and fuses the plastic at the joint, creating a very strong bond and seamless look . Applied with a brush, the solvent glue (like Plastic Weld, MEK, or Tamiya Extra Thin cement) will join styrene pieces in seconds to minutes. This is excellent for assembling plastic parts but use sparingly and in ventilated conditions (the fumes are strong). Alternatively, cyanoacrylate (super glue) works on styrene and ABS as well, giving instant bonds without melting – good for attaching plastic to other materials (like plastic to wood, or to foam, though be careful as super glue can melt some foams). Hot glue is not recommended for plastic sheet – it doesn’t adhere well and the thickness of hot glue can misalign parts. Limitations: Cutting plastic cleanly requires practice; if you only have a knife, very intricate cuts can be tedious (plastics aren’t as forgiving as card for cutting tight corners). Also, polystyrene sheet is relatively expensive compared to card or foam. As a beginner, you might use plasticard sparingly (for instance, one or two key components that need rigidity or fine detail, such as a facade panel with scored window openings, or a base plate that you want to be waterproof and sturdy). Another limitation: standard plasticard is opaque; if you want transparent “windows,” you’d use clear acrylic sheet instead. Working with clear acrylic (Perspex) is a bit different – often scored and snapped, or laser-cut, and bonded with solvent – possibly beyond first model scope. Handling: Keep plastic sheets protected from scratches; the surface can scratch easily (especially clear acrylic or styrene). It helps to leave the protective film on until just before use if it has one. Storage: Store flat, away from heat sources (don’t leave in a hot loft or next to a radiator – it can warp). Also avoid stacking heavy objects on thin plastic as it can permanently deform. Longevity: Plastic models are quite long-lasting – polystyrene won’t degrade quickly. Joints made with solvent weld are essentially as solid as a single piece. Painted plastic holds finish well if primed. So if you build a model with plastic, it could survive many years with minimal change (just protect from UV light which might cause slight yellowing over a very long time). In summary, plasticard is a more advanced material to incorporate once you are comfortable with basics – but even as a beginner, using a bit of it (say, a 0.5mm styrene sheet to mimic a concrete facade panel) can elevate the precision of your model’s appearance. Just be prepared for a different feel in cutting and a need for solvent glue for best results .

Balsa Wood: Description: Balsa is a very light, soft wood sold in sticks, sheets, and blocks (common in model aircraft and architecture models). Typical balsa sheets might be 1mm, 2mm, or 5mm thick; sticks come in square or rectangular cross-sections (e.g. 5×5mm, etc.). Why use: Balsa is popular for architectural models because it’s easy to cut and carve yet can represent wood or concrete textures, and it’s structurally useful for certain elements . It’s perfect for creating small structural members (like columns or beams at model scale), framing systems, or textured surfaces (balsa’s grain can resemble board-formed concrete when stained). Balsa also takes paint and stain well . If your brutalist subject has a prominent grid or brise-soleil, for example, you could use balsa strips to quickly build that grid. Or for a modernist pilotis (columns) under a building, small dowels or balsa sticks work nicely. Behavior & handling: Balsa cuts easily with a sharp hobby knife – it’s so soft that a single pass can go through thin sections. Thicker pieces may be cut with a small saw or by scoring and snapping. The key caution is that balsa grain is fragile; cutting across grain is fine, but cutting along the grain can split the wood if not careful . Always use a very sharp blade and a steady, light touch to avoid crushing it. Sanding: Balsa sands very well (it is so soft that coarse sandpaper will remove material fast). You can shape curves or smooth edges easily. However, its softness means it dents with a fingernail – handle pieces gently to avoid unintended marks. Gluing: PVA (wood glue) works great on balsa, giving a strong bond – it essentially behaves like full-size wood . Super glue also works for instant bonds, but because balsa is porous, CA glue tends to soak in – a thicker gap-filling CA or multiple drops may be needed. Balsa can also be pinned – inserting a tiny pin to hold joints while glue dries (the pins push in easily and can be left as reinforcement or removed later). Limitations: Balsa is not for ultra-thin, highly loaded parts – anything thinner than a couple of millimeters becomes very delicate. It’s best used where a little thickness or depth is acceptable. Also, because it’s wood, grain direction matters for strength: strips are much stronger along the grain than across. Very fine details (like an intricate screen) might be better done in card or plastic, as balsa could break. Handling tips: To avoid splitting, cut perpendicular to grain or support the wood with a backing material when cutting. A common technique: if cutting a narrow strip, cut it slightly oversized and then sand down to final dimension – this puts less stress on it. You can firm up balsa’s surface by applying a coat of clear dope or even PVA diluted with water; this fills the grain and hardens it for easier painting. Storage: Balsa should be kept flat to avoid warping. It’s sensitive to humidity changes – store in a dry place, possibly in a sealed bag. If it does warp, sometimes you can straighten it by slightly dampening and pressing flat until dry. Longevity: Balsa models can be surprisingly durable if kept dry and not handled roughly. But over years, unsealed balsa might absorb humidity and deform. Painted or sealed balsa lasts much better (paint essentially locks out moisture). Given its fragility, balsa components on a model should be protected from handling – e.g. use a base or case if you want the model to last. Many classic architecture models incorporate balsa for its aesthetic and ease of working – as one guide notes, “it has a good finish, is available in many dimensions, easy to cut and creates an accurate model” . It’s an excellent material to learn model-building techniques, especially for creating those repetitive structural elements common in modernist designs.

Each of these materials – foam board, XPS foam, card, plastic, and balsa – has its strengths. Often, they are used in combination. For instance, a beginner’s model might use foam board for main building masses, card for a base and some walls, and bits of balsa for detail (like columns). There is no rigid rule; part of model-making is choosing the right material for each job. As you experiment, you’ll develop an intuition: “take the time to understand the materials you choose… explore the opportunities and limitations of each” . For example, you’ll learn that sharp blades are needed for clean cuts in foam board and that acrylic (plastic) requires solvent glue to bond seamlessly .

Storage and care of materials: Keep all materials dry and flat. Paper-based materials (card, foam board) are highly sensitive to moisture – store them in a dry environment to avoid warping or mildew. Foam and plastics should be kept out of direct sunlight (UV can make them brittle or discolored over a long period). It’s useful to have a dedicated box or portfolio to keep sheet materials from getting bent. Off-cuts of foam and card can be saved for quick study models or test cuts, but organize them so they don’t clutter your workspace. Some materials (like cork or certain foams) might degrade or discolor if exposed to sunlight for long durations, so for any pieces you plan to keep, a coat of paint or primer can help protect them (and also visually unify the model if different materials are used).

In summary, by selecting a material appropriate to each element of your model – considering ease of cutting, appearance, and structural need – you will make the building process smoother and the outcome more successful. Early concept models usually use cheaper, easy materials (foam, card) , whereas if you move toward a final presentation, you might incorporate more durable materials (wood, acrylic) for longevity . This beginner briefing emphasizes foam, card, and wood as they align with modernist forms and beginner-friendly handling. As you gain experience, feel free to venture into other materials (acrylic sheets for windows, MDF or plywood for bases , metal rods or wires for fine details , etc.). The key is to learn the “feel” of each material and leverage its strengths – this will greatly enhance both the process and quality of your architectural models.
6. Construction Techniques (Beginner Level)

With design planned, scale set, tools and materials in hand, it’s time to start construction. This section covers fundamental techniques for cutting and assembling your model, as well as common mistakes beginners face and how to correct them. The aim is to achieve clean, accurate results while building safe work habits and skills.
Cutting Techniques for Clean Edges

Using knives properly: As emphasized, always use a sharp blade. Begin each project with a fresh blade and replace it frequently – this cannot be overstated. A sharp knife will glide and produce smooth edges; a dull one will drag, crush material, and is prone to slipping (leading to accidents or messy cuts) . When cutting, hold the knife vertically (90° to the material) unless intentionally beveling an edge. This ensures the cut edge is square and pieces will fit flush. Apply moderate, even pressure and make multiple light passes rather than a single forceful cut . For example, to cut through 5mm foam board, you might do 3–4 passes: the first scoring the top paper, the next cutting through foam, the last through the bottom paper. This method results in a cleaner cut and preserves your blade longer.

Straight cuts: Use a metal ruler or straightedge as a guide for straight cuts. Press it firmly (you can tape it down if needed for a long cut). Keep the blade snug against the ruler edge as you draw it along. Ensure the ruler doesn’t slip – some modelmakers put a strip of masking tape or sandpaper under the ruler to increase friction . When cutting thick materials like mountboard, also consider flipping the piece over and finishing the cut from the back side along the same line, to avoid tear-out on the bottom face.

Curves and shapes: For gentle curves in card or thin plastic, you can cut freehand slowly, or use flexible curves or French curves as guides. For circles, a compass cutter (adjustable blade on a pivot) cuts neat circles in card. If you lack that, you can trace a circle and cut by rotating the material under a fixed knife tip. Small holes or rounded corners can be made by drilling with a pin vise or using hole punch pliers (for paper/card). Remember you can always sand to refine a shape after cutting: if a curve is a bit rough, use sandpaper or a small file to smooth it to the line.

Cutting foam: When cutting XPS foam, in addition to the above knife technique, a serrated blade (like a bread knife or hacksaw blade) can be used for rough cuts on thick blocks, then sanded to final shape. If using a hot wire cutter, go slowly to avoid ridges and use outdoors or with ventilation (fumes are harmful). And never use a hot wire near flammable materials or without proper guidance.

Safety note: Develop the habit of anchoring your material – either by using your non-cutting hand well away from the blade or by taping the material down – so that if the blade slips it doesn’t hit your hand. Always cut away from yourself and any body parts.
Gluing and Assembly Methods

Choosing adhesives: The two primary glues you’ll use are PVA white glue and cyanoacrylate (super glue), with occasional help from hot glue or double-sided tape. As a beginner, it’s worth understanding which to use when:

PVA (white glue): Best for porous materials (paper, card, wood, foam). It gives a strong, clean bond but requires clamp or support while drying (it usually sets enough in 5–15 minutes, full cure in a few hours). It dries clear but can leave a slight sheen. Use: Apply a thin, even layer on one surface; press the pieces together and hold or tape until it grabs . Wipe any excess that squeezes out immediately with a damp cotton bud to avoid shiny glue marks. Because PVA has water, too much can warp card – apply sparingly. If you need faster setting, tacky glue is a variant that is thicker and grabs quicker .

Super Glue (CA): Good for small parts or mixed materials, and when you need an instant bond . For example, gluing a tiny styrene detail onto card, or fixing a broken corner quickly. Use: A drop of CA is often enough; use the gel type for filling gaps or where you need a moment to position (gel CA gives a few more seconds before setting). Be very careful of your fingers – use tweezers to hold small parts because CA will bond skin (and it’s painful to remove). Also, CA can cause “frosting” (white residue) on plastics if used in a closed space – ensure some airflow.

Hot Glue: Useful in certain cases: attaching structural blocks, or when you need a very quick hold and precision is less critical. E.g., to glue a foam building onto a base, a couple of hot glue dabs will hold it instantly. Caution: Hot glue is thick and can introduce small gaps; it’s also stringy – avoid stretching those glue strings onto visible areas (you can trim them later). Because it hardens fast, only apply a small amount (it cools within seconds). Also, don’t use hot glue for delicate parts – it’s easy to make a mess, and you can’t reposition without tearing things. It’s best for coarse joins or temporary fixes.

Double-sided tape & spray adhesive: These are very clean but offer no adjustment time. Double-sided tape can mount facade layers or paper prints without wrinkles . Spray adhesive (artist’s mount spray) gives an even coat for large surfaces (like laminating a printed facade to foam board). If using spray, mask off areas you don’t want glue on and use in ventilated area. These adhesives are usually permanent, so align carefully when joining pieces.
Assembly strategies:

Dry fit first: Before gluing, always do a dry fit of the pieces. Check that edges meet properly and that you understand how they will be held together. It’s much easier to trim or adjust a piece before glue is applied.

Order of assembly: Plan a logical sequence. For a simple building, one common method is: attach walls together first, then attach the assembly to the base or roof. Often it’s easier to build a “box” (walls around) around a floor plate. In other cases, you might glue walls to a baseplate flat on the work surface to ensure alignment, then add a roof. Consider gravity: build from the bottom up, using horizontal surfaces to keep things level.

Ensuring right angles: Achieving true 90° corners is critical for a neat model (especially modernist architecture with orthogonal forms). Use your try square or a drafting triangle inside corners while assembling to check squareness. A great trick is to use small blocks or Lego pieces as temporary braces: “use solid blocks (metal or wood) as supports to ensure right angles while the glue dries” . For example, when gluing a wall to a base, press a block against the wall to hold it perfectly vertical as the glue sets. Masking tape can act as a “clamp” too – tape the wall in position relative to another until the glue holds.

Apply glue correctly: For PVA, it’s often better to apply glue to both surfaces (if they are porous like card) sparingly, or to one surface if one is non-porous. For instance, gluing card to foam: apply a thin bead to the foam, spread it with a scrap piece or brush, then join. Too much glue leads to squeeze-out and mess. One tip: “apply glue to the piece being added, not the main structure, to avoid excess glue on visible areas” . For CA, use a fine applicator (many bottles come with a nozzle, or use a toothpick to transfer a tiny drop).

Alignment: Mark lightly where pieces should go, so when gluing you can place them quickly and accurately. On a base, pencil in wall lines; on a wall, mark where a facade panel goes, etc. These guides prevent misplacement when the glue is on and time is critical.

Typical joint techniques: In simple models, butt joints (gluing the edge of one piece to the face of another) are most common. For example, wall panels meeting at corners – you glue the edge of one against the inside face of the other. This is easy but remember to account for material thickness (one wall might need to be shorter by the thickness of the other if fitting inside). For a stronger corner, some use a strip of card or wood inside as a cleat to reinforce – e.g., gluing a thin strip along the interior corner like a bracket. Floor or roof pieces often sit on top of walls; ensure walls are flush/even height so the roof lies flat – any discrepancy, trim or sand the wall tops before gluing the roof. If needed, use small pins or toothpicks to peg pieces together (especially in foam or balsa) while glue dries – you can push a pin at an angle through a wall into a base temporarily.

Clamping and drying: Patience during drying is vital. Resist the urge to poke or move pieces too soon. PVA will hold in a few minutes if the fit is good and not under stress, but leaving assemblies for 15-30 minutes largely undisturbed yields much stronger joins. Use masking tape, pins, or small clamps to secure parts so you can work on something else in the meantime . For example, tape a wall to the floor and let it sit while you cut the next wall. If a joint must carry load (like a horizontal floor plate), let the glue fully cure (several hours) before putting weight on it.
Techniques to Avoid Common Mistakes

Beginner model makers often encounter issues like crooked assemblies, messy glue marks, rough edges, or pieces that don’t fit. Being aware of these common errors and having strategies to address them will improve your results:

Inaccurate measurements or fit: Sometimes a wall comes out too long or a roof doesn’t fit because of cumulative small errors. Prevention: Measure twice, cut once. Use the scale ruler and double-check each dimension in your plan. Also account for material thickness in your design (e.g., if two walls overlap at a corner, subtract one thickness from one of them). Correction: If a piece is slightly too large, you can sand or trim it down carefully to fit. If too small (gap), you can fill small gaps with slivers of card or a bit of filler and paint over, or hide it as a “design joint”. In early models, perfection is less critical – focus on the model sitting level and generally matching proportions.

Ragged or slanted cut edges: This can result from dull blades or too much force. Prevention: Always use sharp blades and straightedge for straight cuts. Correction: Small bumps or frays on edges can be sanded smooth (for card/foam, use fine sandpaper gently; for plastic, a file). If an edge will be visible and is rough, one trick is to cap it with a strip of thin card or paper to cover the irregularity. In foamcore, paper “fuzz” can be trimmed with a very sharp blade held almost parallel to the surface, shaving off the fuzz.

Glue smears and excess glue: Dried glue can leave shiny marks or blobs. Prevention: Use less glue and fine applicators (a toothpick or syringe for applying glue in tight spots) . Also wash your hands often; glue on fingers can transfer and also oil/dirt can stain a clean white model, as one source suggests – keeping hands clean prevents soiling the model . Correction: If you get a glue drip on a visible area, try to wipe it immediately. Dried PVA can sometimes be gently scraped off or hidden by painting over. Super glue marks on plastic can be lightly sanded or, if small, sometimes removed with a debonder (but that risks more damage – often better to cover up). For a critical presentation model, messy glue might necessitate re-cutting a piece; but for initial models, you can often overlook minor glue shines.

Walls not perpendicular / skewed geometry: Your building might lean or corners might not align, often due to not holding right angles during assembly. Prevention: Use the alignment tools (square, blocks) and assemble on a flat surface. Check each corner as you glue it. Correction: If something dried crooked, you may carefully cut it apart (with a thin blade or saw) and re-glue correctly. If a wall is leaning, sometimes you can brace it by adding an internal perpendicular piece (like an L-brace) after the fact to prop it at 90°. Slight misalignments can be disguised by base or roof elements covering the joins.

Warping: This can occur especially with paper materials when painted or glued extensively. Baseboards might warp if glued improperly to a support. Prevention: When laminating large areas, use balanced layers of glue or weight it down flat while drying. Paint or prime both sides of card components to balance tension. Correction: Minor warps in a base can be flattened by gently bending opposite or adding a frame underneath. Warped walls can sometimes be straightened by attaching them firmly to perpendicular elements (like gluing in floors or partitions can pull a warped wall straight).

Pieces breaking or coming unglued: Small delicate parts (like a thin balsa stick or a tiny glued joint) may break if stressed. Prevention: Handle the model gingerly, especially until all parts are assembled and the structure stabilizes. Consider reinforcing fragile areas (a dot of glue in a corner, an extra layer of card to thicken a thin wall). Correction: If something breaks, don’t panic – clean up any splinters, and reattach it with a stronger glue (CA for a quick fix, or PVA with a supporting splint if needed). You can even design with this in mind: for instance, make two copies of a tiny detail so if one pings off or gets lost to the carpet monster, you have a backup.

General tip: “There’s no such thing as a stupid question” – if you are unsure how to achieve a certain result, seek advice . This could mean asking a more experienced model maker, consulting online forums, or using AI (as we’ll discuss) to get suggestions for a tricky assembly. Often, a small trick or tool (like using a jig for repetitive parts, or a particular order of operations) can solve a problem that seems daunting.

Learning from mistakes: Even with these precautions, you will make mistakes – that is expected. The best model makers still err, they just know how to fix or hide them! If a mistake happens, assess if it truly harms the model’s purpose. For a concept model, a slightly rough edge likely doesn’t matter for communicating the design. If it does matter, take the time to correct it properly (better to recut a wall now than to regret it later every time you see the model). Keep notes of difficulties you encounter and how you solved them – this builds your personal knowledge base for future models . As one source advises, make mistakes and learn from them; practice is the only way to improve .

By applying these fundamental techniques – precise cutting, appropriate gluing, careful alignment, and iterative correction – you will develop good craftsmanship habits. A beginner can absolutely produce a clean, sturdy model by adhering to these basics. Remember that much of model making is patience and attention to detail: working a bit slower, measuring one extra time, dabbing away that extra glue – these small disciplines separate a “good model from a great one” . Over time, your hand skills will improve, and tasks that initially took great care (like making a razor-straight cut) will become almost second nature. For now, focus on consistency and correctness, and the quality will follow.
7. Surface Treatment & Finish

Once the model’s basic structure is assembled, you have the option to treat its surfaces for a more polished presentation. In architectural modeling, especially at conceptual levels, sometimes less is more – many study models are left in the natural color of the material (all-white, all-brown cardboard, etc.) to emphasize form over detail. However, a bit of finishing can enhance realism or give a model a particular character (for example, a concrete-like texture to suit a brutalist building). This section discusses the spectrum from raw material finish to painted models, basic techniques for priming and painting, how to achieve a “concrete” look, and the principle of restraint and abstraction in model finishes.

Raw vs. painted models: There is a fundamental choice whether to leave the model unpainted (“raw”) or to apply paint/texture to represent materials. Raw models use the inherent colors and textures of the build materials – e.g., white foam board, grey card, natural wood. This approach is common for initial concept models and even many modernist presentation models, because it presents a neutral, unified appearance that draws attention to massing and form. For a beginner, a raw finish is often simpler (no risk of ruining the model with a bad paint job) and can look quite professional if materials are chosen well. For instance, a combination of white foamboard for the building and a black mountboard base can be very crisp. On the other hand, painted models can be more realistic or expressive – you can indicate that a building is concrete by painting it concrete-gray, or differentiate elements (a rooftop plant room in a darker tone, say). Painting also helps to hide the heterogeneity of materials (making foam, card, wood all look uniform). Many final display models are painted or finished to some degree.

As a beginner, you might consider doing a mostly raw model with selective finishing. For example, leave walls the color of white card (simulating white precast concrete perhaps) and just add a light wash or speckle to suggest texture, rather than fully painting. Raw models often have a minimalist aesthetic aligned with modernism (think of a pure white model with sharp shadows highlighting its geometry).
Priming and painting workflow: If you decide to paint, it’s crucial to use the right products and sequence:

Priming: A primer is a preparatory coating that ensures paint adheres well and surfaces are unified in texture. For porous materials (card, wood, foam), a primer will seal the surface so that paint doesn’t soak in unevenly. Spray primer (matte acrylic primer from hobby or art stores, often grey or white) is convenient for models. However, caution: standard spray primers have solvents that melt polystyrene foam – do not spray them directly on foam. You can safely spray on card, wood, plastic. If your model has foam, either avoid spraying those parts or first give them a protective coat (brush on a layer of PVA glue or acrylic gesso to seal the foam). Alternatively, use a foam-safe primer (some brands make water-based spray primers or you can use a craft acrylic paint as a primer by brush). For plastic parts, a light coat of plastic primer or any all-surface primer helps paint stick.

Paint types: Acrylic paints are recommended for beginners – they are water-based, quick-drying, and easy to clean. These come in bottles for brushing or in spray cans. For large uniform areas, spray paint gives a smooth finish (again, ensure compatibility with the substrate). For detail or small models, brush painting with artist acrylics is fine; use soft, wide brushes for large surfaces to minimize brush marks. Enamel paints (oil-based, like model kit paints) provide smooth finishes too but dry slower and have fumes – usually not necessary unless you need a special effect. Colors: For brutalist subjects, shades of grey, white, or concrete-tan are typical. It’s often effective to use a slightly off-white or very light grey for a concrete look rather than pure white, which can be stark.

Application: If using spray paint, do it in light coats. It’s better to do 2–3 thin passes than one heavy coat which might pool or drip. Keep the can moving to avoid oversaturating one spot. For brush painting, slightly dilute acrylic paint with a bit of water or acrylic medium so it flows without leaving strong brush strokes, and apply evenly. Multiple thin coats yield the best result. Make sure parts are dust-free before painting (wipe gently with a soft brush or cloth).

Masking: If you want different areas in different colors, use painter’s masking tape to mask off sections before spraying or painting. Press the tape edges down firmly to prevent bleed. Remove tape carefully after paint dries to avoid peeling the paint or surface below.
Achieving concrete-like finishes: Brutalist architecture is synonymous with raw concrete. There are a few approaches to simulate this on a model:

Texture paint: There are spray paints that contain fine aggregate to mimic stone or concrete texture. Some DIY stores sell “stone effect” spray. Used lightly, these can give a subtle grit that reads like concrete. Test on scrap first to gauge the roughness; you might need to mist it from farther away to avoid too coarse a texture for the scale.

Paint and sand: A homemade technique is to mix a tiny bit of fine sand or tile grout into grey acrylic paint and stipple it on surfaces. This gives a controlled texture. Alternatively, apply paint, then while wet dust on a pinch of very fine sand, and after it sets, seal with another light paint layer.

Pastel and speckling: Real concrete isn’t a flat grey – it has speckles and slight color variations. You can simulate this by speckling the surface: flicking tiny droplets of a slightly darker or lighter grey onto the base coat. One way is to dip a toothbrush in diluted paint and flick it with your thumb to spray tiny dots. Do this sparingly; multiple tones (some lighter, some darker than base) can add realism at scale.

Printed texture: For a small model, one can print a high-resolution photo of concrete texture scaled down, and then laminate it onto surfaces (spraymount or glue). However, this can look artificial if not done perfectly, and is usually more detail than a beginner model needs. Still, it’s an option (some professional models use printed textures for things like brick patterns or concrete panels).

David Neat’s method (advanced): An experienced model-maker described using recycled grey paper sanded with a sponge to create a mottled polished concrete effect . Essentially, a suitable colored paper was abraded to lighten patches, giving very realistic subtle variation. This paper could then be glued as a “veneer” on the model’s floor or wall to represent concrete. Such craftsmanship might be beyond a first attempt, but it illustrates creative approaches. You can experiment with cardstock: take a grey card and sand or dab it with lighter paint to break the uniformity, then use that card to clad your foam or wood blocks.

Formwork lines: If you want to represent board-formed concrete (with those horizontal lines/imprints of wooden formwork), you can scribe lines into the surface (for instance, lightly score foam or card at regular intervals) before painting, so the paint washes into the grooves and accentuates them. Or glue very thin strips of paper to simulate the slight recess lines, then paint over. For a panelized look (precast panels), score a grid on plastic or card before painting, which will remain as fine lines.
Remember scale: any texture should be fine enough not to overwhelm the model. At 1:100, real concrete’s gravel bits would be almost invisible – so keep textures subtle.

After painting or texturing, a matte sealant can be sprayed to even out sheen (architectural models usually look better matte, as concrete is matte; shiny surfaces can make it toy-like unless representing glass). There are clear matte topcoat sprays for this purpose.

Restraint and abstraction: A critical principle in finishing architectural models is restraint. Your goal is not a hyper-realistic miniature (like a hobbyists’ diorama) but an abstracted representation of a building. This means you should deliberately omit excessive detail and focus on conveying the design’s key elements . For example, instead of trying to paint tiny window mullions and curtains, you might simply render all windows as uniform dark recesses or reflective surfaces – just enough to read as “windows” at scale. If the building has texture, you don’t need to replicate every blemish; a consistent treatment that suggests material is enough. A UK government-style briefing might phrase it as: ensure the model “illustrates the essence of the project or concept, including only what’s essential” . By being selective, you save time and avoid cluttering the model with features that may not scale well or may distract from the overall form.

Indeed, many brutalist building models are painted a single solid color or kept monochrome, turning them almost into sculptural objects. This abstraction allows viewers to appreciate the interplay of forms and shadows without literal interpretation. For a first model, you might choose to keep everything one color (e.g. a concrete grey all over). This forgives a lot – if everything is uniform, minor imperfections are less visible and the model looks coherent.

Case in point (stylization): An experienced model maker described a project where, to maintain a clean result, they “took the freedom to stylize aspects of the building and avoid fussy detail”, making the model somewhat of a playfully abstract version of reality . The result had an aesthetic presence of its own while still clearly representing the design. Emulating this, you shouldn’t hesitate to simplify: for instance, representing people as plain silhouettes, trees as simple green cones, or cars as wooden blocks, if you include any context elements at all. Keep finishes minimalistic unless the detail serves a specific communicative purpose.

In summary, for surface treatment: If in doubt, err on the side of under-doing rather than overdoing. A cleanly built model with no paint often looks better than one with a sloppy paint job. If you do finish it, use the techniques above in moderation and test on scraps first. A common beginner approach is to build the model in white, then give it a light spray of grey primer to unify it – that alone can yield a convincing concrete effect without further fuss. And always preserve the integrity of form: ensure paint or finish doesn’t obscure the sharp edges and shapes you’ve crafted. When done, the model’s surface should complement the design, not compete with it. A restrained, well-executed finish will elevate your model, giving it that professional touch while maintaining the conceptual clarity of modernist design.
8. Starter Projects

Getting started is often the hardest step – so having a concrete (pun intended) first project to tackle will focus your efforts. This section suggests a clear starter project tailored to a beginner interested in modernist/brutalist architecture, and offers guidance on scope, what to include or omit, and how to measure success.

Recommended first project: Begin with a simple modernist housing block, ideally inspired by a real post-war design but greatly simplified. For example, consider a low-rise block from the Cumbernauld New Town developments of the 1960s. Cumbernauld’s housing included straightforward geometric blocks of flats with repetitive façades. You might model a single rectangular building volume – say, a three-story apartment block – at a scale like 1:100. This building could be roughly a box shape (for instance, 15 cm long, 5 cm wide, 9 cm tall in model dimensions to represent a small block). The style is plain: flat roof, uniform grid windows. Such a subject lets you practice basic massing and repetition without complex curves or irregular forms.

Why this project: Modernist housing blocks embody the core aspects that are manageable for a novice: clean lines, repeating elements, and modular structure. There is no ornate decoration to carve, no complex roof geometry – just orthogonal forms. At the same time, it’s recognizable and interesting because of its rhythm and proportions (the repetition of windows, perhaps pilotis or a balcony). By choosing a Scottish example, you also tie into your interest region – for instance, a simplified abstraction of a Cumbernauld housing unit would pay homage to that context. It’s a building type that can be represented mostly as extruded rectangles, which is exactly what foamboard and card excel at.

Defining the scope: Keep the project limited to the building exterior form. Do not attempt interior details or removable sections on your first go. Decide if you will include a base representing ground and perhaps one or two adjacent landscape elements for context (like a bit of pavement or a stub of a retaining wall). Including a simple base is helpful for handling the model and “anchoring” it (models look better when they aren’t just floating – a base can be like a picture frame for it ). A piece of mountboard or plywood slightly larger than the building outline can serve as ground.
