What to include (essentials): Aim to capture the overall shape and key architectural features that define the building’s character:
The mass: the rectangular volume of the block, maybe with a slight offset or wing if characteristic.
Rhythm of facade: for instance, the grid of windows or balcony openings. You don’t need to model glass or frames, but you could recess the window areas or use darker card inserts to imply them.

Key structural elements: if the building is on pilotis (columns) or has a prominent staircase tower, include simplified versions of those (e.g., columns as plain cylinders or prisms, a stair core as a smaller attached box).

Levels: Indicate floor divisions perhaps by a subtle line or a step in the facade (some brutalist blocks have strong horizontal lines separating floors). This can be done by layering thin card or scoring a line.
If there’s a distinctive roof form (even a simple parapet), include that outline.

Keep each of these features abstracted: for example, represent windows as blank openings or shallow recesses. You might cut small rectangular holes in the facade pieces before assembly to denote windows (backed with black paper or left open). Or simply paint or draw the window grid onto the facade if cutting them is too fiddly – at 1:200 scale, windows might be so small that a drawn suggestion is enough. The idea is to incorporate the repetitive pattern, not to actually glaze windows with acetate or put curtains.
What to deliberately omit or simplify:

Fine details like window frames, mullions, door handles, railings, etc., should be omitted. They add complexity and are not necessary to convey the design at this stage . For instance, if your block has balconies with railings, you could just model the balcony slabs and skip the thin railings, or indicate them with a single strip of card.

Textures (brick lines, etc.) can be omitted; treat surfaces as planar. Brutalist concrete often is modeled as smooth or uniformly textured – you don’t need to simulate the exact board marks or material joints on a first model.

Context beyond the immediate base: Avoid trying to model multiple buildings or a whole street. That increases scope significantly. One building is plenty. If you’re enthusiastic, you could place one or two simplified context masses (like a plain block next to it to hint at another building, or simple shapes to show landscape forms), but these should be extremely abstract (just foam blocks).
Interior: do not cut the model open or attempt interior furnishings. Keep the building solid; it’s about external form.
By consciously limiting complexity, you ensure the project remains achievable and educational rather than overwhelming.
Example setup: A simplified Cumbernauld housing block model:
Base: 20cm x 15cm piece of grey mountboard, maybe scribed with a line or two to suggest pavement.
Building: Foamcore walls clad in a single layer of thin white card. Dimensions such that it looks like a 3-story slab. Maybe 3 cm per story = 9 cm tall, length 15 cm, width 5 cm.

Facade treatment: Each floor has 5 window bays across. Instead of 15 cut holes (which could be tedious but doable), perhaps cut 5 vertical slots per floor (grouping windows) or glue on contrasting rectangles to denote window strips.
A small vertical recess to mark the stairwell at one end, if applicable.
Everything is painted a uniform light grey to mimic concrete, or left white if using white foamboard (with maybe shadows doing the work).
This is just one interpretation – the key is it’s a single, easily interpretable form.
Success criteria for the first model: How do you know if your model is successful? For a beginner, success is measured less by perfection and more by functional achievement and learning gained:

Structural soundness: The model should stand upright, level and intact. All parts should be securely attached – no walls left loose or sagging. It shouldn’t topple or lean. If you can pick it up and set it down without pieces shifting, that’s a good sign.

Scale accuracy: The model’s dimensions should reasonably reflect the intended scale. If at 1:100, does a door look about 2 cm high? Do the proportions of height/width match the building reference? It need not be exact to the millimeter, but generally convincing. If you show it next to a scale figure (say a 1:100 scale person ~1.8 cm tall), the building should feel correctly scaled (the figure fits in a doorway, etc.).

Neatness of construction: Aim for clean joins and edges. Success is if there are no glaringly uneven cuts or excess glue marks at first glance. All corners should be closed (no gaps) and right-angled (unless the design is intentionally angled). The roof sits flat. The finish (if painted) should be even, with no blotches or unintended brush strokes. Essentially, the model looks tidy and professional for its level – something you’d not be embarrassed to show a colleague or tutor. Minor flaws are normal, but there shouldn’t be major distractions like a wall glued visibly crooked or large glue stains.

Design communication: The model should clearly communicate the chosen building’s primary design aspects. Ask yourself: Does someone unfamiliar with the project get a sense of the building’s form and rhythm by looking at the model? If the answer is yes – e.g., they can see it’s a rectangular housing block with repetitive windows and maybe identify it as a modernist style – then the model has done its job as a communication tool. Even a very simple model can convey a lot if well-proportioned.

Skills learned: Finally, a less tangible but important success criterion: you have practiced and improved skills in the process. Perhaps your cutting got progressively better, or you figured out how to make two pieces align perfectly, or you managed to mix a nice concrete color. These gains indicate success because model making is iterative learning. Document what techniques worked well and where you struggled (for example, maybe you found a great way to keep windows evenly spaced, or you had trouble cutting small pieces – noting this informs your next project).

If any aspect falls short (say, some edges are messy), don’t be discouraged – treat it as a learning point. You can even do a second iteration of the same model, applying the lessons to see improvement. The wonderful thing about a modest starter project is that it’s repeatable and tweakable without a huge time investment.

In summary, a first model like a simplified modernist housing block will give you a tangible accomplishment and experience across all steps: planning, cutting, assembling, finishing. It’s complex enough to be interesting (it’s a real building form) but constrained enough to be tackled with basic methods. Hitting the success criteria above means you’re ready to confidently proceed to more complex builds; missing one or two is simply an indicator of what to focus on next. Either way, completing the starter project will validate your efforts – you’ll have a physical model in hand that you built from scratch, which is a significant milestone.
9. Beginner Roadmap

Embarking on architectural model making is a journey. In the beginning, progress may feel slow, but each step builds your capability. This roadmap outlines a sensible progression for a beginner – from initial preparations through milestones that indicate you’re ready to advance. It’s essentially an actionable plan to go from zero to your first completed model and beyond.

Initial Setup – First Purchases & Workspace: Acquire the essential tools and materials (as detailed in Section 4 and 5). Make a checklist and obtain at least the minimum: knife + blades, cutting mat, metal ruler, glue, a few sheets of foam board/card, etc. Set up a small workspace – a desk or table with good light. Ensure you have a clean, flat surface to work on and somewhere to safely store materials. This initial step sets the foundation; treat it like equipping a mini workshop. (In the UK, for example, you might at this stage place orders with an art supplier or visit a store to get these items – it can be done in a modest budget). Outcome: You have everything needed to start building and a safe space to do it.

Practice & First Build (Learning Phase): Before diving into your “real” project, do a mini practice build. This could be as simple as making a small box or abstract form from scrap material. For instance, cut a 5cm cube from foam board and assemble it, or make a tiny massing model of a house using off-cuts. This practice model is not meant to look like a known building – it’s for you to practice measuring, cutting straight, gluing a corner, etc. Through this, you’ll identify any immediate challenges (maybe you find keeping 90° angles difficult – you then incorporate a try square or support in your method next time). After a practice or two, proceed to your first actual project model (such as the recommended housing block from Section 8). Work through the process methodically: design/planning, then cutting pieces, then assembly, then finishing. It’s okay to break this across multiple sessions. Key tips: Don’t rush; treat each part of the build as its own task (all cutting done carefully, then all assembly, etc.). Use checklists – you can ask yourself or even an AI assistant to generate a construction checklist (e.g., “List the steps to build a simple foamboard house model”) to guide you so nothing is forgotten. Outcome: You build your first complete model. It may not be perfect, but it stands, roughly matches the design, and is recognizably what it’s supposed to be.

Basic Finishing – First Finish: Once the model structure is done, attempt a basic finishing step. For the first model, this might mean priming and painting it a single color, or adding one material texture. For example, you could spray it all in grey primer for a uniform concrete look. Or if left raw, maybe just neatly add a base with painted ground or a printed name label – some small step to “present” the model. This stage teaches you about surface treatments in a low-risk way (since the model is already built, you’re just enhancing it). Use what you learned in Section 7: test paint on a scrap first, ensure compatibility with materials, then apply to the model in thin even coats. If painting feels too risky, even finishing could be simply sealing edges with a marker (e.g., coloring exposed foam edges with grey marker to blend them). Outcome: Your model has a finished look rather than appearing as random pieces of material. It’s ready to be shown or handled without falling apart. Completing this also gives a morale boost – your project looks “done.”

Evaluation & Iteration (Self-Assessment): With one model completed, pause to evaluate against the success criteria (Section 8) and reflect. Note what went well – maybe your cutting was very precise – and what could improve – perhaps your gluing was messy. At this point, it’s highly valuable to document the process: take photos of the model, maybe even during construction steps. Jot down in a notebook or digital document any tips you discovered or mistakes you made. Example: You might note “Next time, use less glue on joints – had to clean a lot of excess” or “Window openings came out clean using the new blade and patience.” If you have access to a tutor or experienced builder, get feedback. Or share pictures on an online forum or with friends for constructive critique. The idea is to consolidate your learning from the first project. Based on this, you can decide what the next project should be to push your skills a bit further (perhaps a slightly larger building, or one with a curve or an interesting section).
Progression – Scaling Up or Adding Complexity: When you feel comfortable with the basics, indicators of readiness to progress include:
You find that you can reliably cut straight lines and assemble right angles without major difficulty.
You understand scale conversions well and your last model pieces fit as intended (mostly no refitting needed).
You’ve started thinking “how could I add more detail?” or “I’d like to try a more challenging shape” – i.e., your confidence has grown.

At this juncture, you might try a more complex model: for example, a civic brutalist structure (maybe a piece of the Cumbernauld Town Centre or another iconic building). Alternatively, you could refine the same model by adding one level of detail (e.g., now add simple window frames or a bit of context like adjacent landscape). Each new project should introduce a new challenge or skill: using a different material (maybe incorporate clear acrylic for windows), working at a different scale (try a 1:200 site model or a larger 1:50 detail model of part of the building), or using a new tool (if you got access to a laser cutter or 3D printer, perhaps test it for repetitive parts). Always scale up complexity gradually. Jumping straight from a simple foam core box to, say, a detailed 1:50 interior model with furniture would be overwhelming. Instead, maybe the second project includes a curved form (to learn how to cut curves or use flexible materials) or introduces topography on the base (to learn layered contour modeling).

While progressing, continue to use AI or other resources as support (as introduced in the next section). For example, as you plan a new project, you might ask an AI, “What’s the best way to model the curved facade of Building X at 1:100?” and get suggestions to try out.
Milestones of progress: A few concrete signs that you have moved past the pure beginner stage might be:
You can complete a model without significant re-cuts or material waste (i.e., your planning and execution are efficient now).
Your models hold together well and you’re starting to present them or use them to explain designs (i.e., they serve their purpose for communication).
You have a good grasp of which materials to use when – you might think “I’ll use plasticard for that thin screen wall because card would be too weak,” showing foresight.
You handle tools confidently and safely: cutting with speed and accuracy, changing blades without hesitation, etc.

Importantly, you have developed a critical eye: you can spot errors in your own work (and even others’) and know how to correct or refine them. This self-critique ability is key for improvement in any craft.

Expanding your toolkit as you progress: With each project, consider if an investment in a new tool or material will help achieve the next goal. For instance, after a couple of hand-cut models, you might buy a small architect’s mitre box and saw to cut wood dowels for columns more cleanly, or get a small rotary tool (Dremel) for precision grinding/sanding of edges. If budget allows and you foresee a lot of modeling, you could explore laser cutting services to cut repeated floor plates or intricate patterns (many architecture students use laser-cutters for complex models once they master the basics). Just remember that these are supplements, not replacements, for fundamental skills – a laser cutter won’t solve design problems or sloppy assembly habits, but in the hands of someone with solid foundational skills (which you are building), it’s a powerful aid.
In summary, the roadmap for a beginner is:
Equip and set up (tools/materials, workspace).
Build a simple model (practice, then first real project) focusing on core techniques.
Finish it modestly to experience surface treatment.
Evaluate and learn from that experience.
Advance in small steps, adding complexity or new methods one at a time.

This ensures steady improvement without jumping in over your head. The path might look like: foamboard house → mid-rise apartment block → complex civic building segment → perhaps a detailed cutaway or a context model with multiple buildings. By the time you follow this, you’ll not be a “beginner” anymore but an intermediate model maker capable of tackling ambitious projects.
10. Using AI as a Support Tool

Entering the world of model making, you have a new ally unavailable to earlier generations of architects: Artificial Intelligence (AI) assistants. AI can serve as a knowledgeable guide, helping you brainstorm solutions, troubleshoot problems, and accelerate learning. However, it’s crucial to use these tools wisely – as support, not as a crutch or replacement for hands-on decision-making. In this section, we discuss how AI (such as chat-based assistants like ChatGPT or others) can assist a beginner model maker, provide example prompts for effective use, and delineate the boundaries of what AI should not replace in your process.
How AI can assist at the beginning:

Answering material and technique questions: As a beginner, you’ll have many “how do I…?” questions. AI can quickly provide information on materials (properties, uses) or methods. For example, if you wonder, “What glue is best for attaching acrylic to foam board?” an AI can outline options (e.g., recommending double-sided tape or specific neutral cure adhesives to avoid melting foam). It’s like having an on-demand mentor or reference book. One source emphasized that it’s impossible to know everything about every material/tool and encouraged asking for advice – AI is one convenient way to ask those “no stupid questions” 24/7. Always verify critical info with a quick cross-check, but AI can give a solid starting point.

Troubleshooting construction issues: If you hit a snag – say your card walls keep warping or your blade tears the foam instead of cutting – you can describe the issue to an AI and get potential solutions. The AI might suggest, for instance, “use multiple light knife passes and a fresh blade, and ensure you’re cutting on a stable surface” (which aligns with best practices we’ve covered). Essentially, it can help diagnose what might be going wrong and propose remedies, drawing from general knowledge.

Checking scale logic and calculations: Math errors happen. You can use AI to double-check your scale conversions or dimensions. For instance, ask “I want a 1:150 model of a 60m long building – how long in cm should the model be?” and it will calculate (60m = 6000cm, /150 = 40cm) for you. It can also help with area scaling if you need to estimate material needs (e.g., “approximately how many A4 sheets of card to cover a 1:200 model of a 50m x 30m footprint building?”). This ensures your planning is sound.

Generating checklists and plans: AI can help you stay organized. You might prompt, “Provide a step-by-step checklist for building an architectural model from foam board, including design, cutting, assembly, and finishing.” The structured response can be used as a guide to follow, so you don’t forget a key step (like ‘mark window positions before cutting walls’). This is especially useful when you’re new and uncertain if you’re approaching the task in the right order.

Inspiration and simplification strategies: If you have a particular building in mind, you could ask, “How can I simplify the Brutalist features of Building X for a 1:100 model?” and AI might respond with suggestions like focusing on the massing and omitting minor details, emphasizing the distinctive silhouette, etc. Similarly, you can use AI to get ideas on abstracting a complex form: “What’s a good way to model a hyperbolic paraboloid roof at small scale?” It might propose using layered card or a bent mesh underlay – ideas you can then refine.

Quick research and reference: AI can summarize or point you to references (though always ensure the info is credible). For example, you could ask, “What are common scales used in UK architecture school models?” and get a quick answer (likely 1:50, 1:100, 1:200 etc. with reasoning). While we already have that knowledge, AI can function as a rapid reference librarian to confirm such points.
Example AI prompts: To illustrate, here are a few good prompts a beginner might use (the ones given in the brief plus some context):

“How should I build this form at 1:100 scale?” – e.g., you show or describe a particular building form. The AI might respond with recommended materials (foam for mass, card for thin fins) and construction approach. This is great for form-specific advice.

“What material is best for this structure?” – e.g., “I have a thin, cantilevered canopy in my design, what model material could support itself at small scale?” AI could suggest using acrylic or basswood for strength, etc.

“How do I simplify this building without losing its character?” – e.g., “I want to model the Barbican Centre, but it’s huge – how to simplify?” AI might say: focus on the main volumes, signature Brutalist elements (like the barrel roof or textured facade), and omit small interior courtyards or repetitive apartments beyond a certain depth. Essentially, AI can help identify the essence to keep.
“Give me tips for cutting complex shapes in foam board” – AI might list techniques like templates, sharp blades, supporting the cut piece, etc.

“What are some common mistakes to avoid in architectural model making?” – It could list things like poor scaling, using wrong glue, not planning joints, etc., which reinforces your awareness (similar to what we covered in Section 6, but AI might give a quick digest).
“How can I make my model look like concrete?” – AI can enumerate methods like painting techniques, as we did, perhaps giving you new ideas or confirming the ones you know.
Using such prompts, you can interact with AI almost like an experienced colleague or teacher’s assistant.
Boundaries: what AI should not replace or do:

The tactile, creative process: AI cannot physically build the model for you, nor can it truly see what you’re seeing. Use it for advice, but the making is up to you. Don’t fall into the trap of over-relying on AI to design or solve everything – the best way to learn is by doing and sometimes by making mistakes and discovering solutions firsthand.

Critical judgment and design decisions: AI can suggest, but you as the designer must decide what simplifications or features matter for your model. For instance, AI might not know exactly which aspect of a building you value most. Use AI suggestions as options, not gospel. Also, AI might not fully grasp aesthetic subtleties – your human judgment on what “feels right” on a model is irreplaceable.

Accuracy on specific or novel problems: AI knowledge is broad but not infallible. It might sometimes give an answer that sounds reasonable but isn’t optimal in practice. For example, it might suggest a glue that technically works but isn’t the easiest to use, or misjudge a material property under model conditions. Always double-check advice that you feel unsure about, perhaps by asking in a model making community or consulting a reliable source. AI shouldn’t be your sole source of truth for critical techniques.

Safety and expert oversight: Do not ask AI for safety-critical instructions (like how to operate a power tool safely) and follow them blindly. While AI could have general safety tips (and often does), for anything involving potentially dangerous equipment or substances, refer to official manuals or expert guidance. Similarly, AI might not know local regulations (e.g., safe disposal of X-Acto blades or aerosol usage guidelines). Use common sense and when in doubt, err on the side of caution or ask a human expert.

Original design creativity: While AI can inspire, try not to let it take over your creative process. Half the joy of model making is problem-solving and improvising solutions – if you outsource all creativity to AI, you miss out on that growth. For instance, instead of asking AI to design your whole model approach, use it to refine your own approach. Maintaining authorship of your work is important (especially if this is in an academic or professional context where your original process is valued).

In summary, view AI as a knowledgeable assistant: great for answering questions and providing guidance, available anytime. It can help you avoid common pitfalls by learning from vast collective knowledge (for example, warning you that “a smaller scale isn’t always faster” or to “anchor your model on a base” , as referenced earlier). However, it’s not a replacement for the hands-on practice, critical thinking, and personal experience that truly develop your skills. AI also cannot replicate the tactile intuition you develop – like how a material cuts or how much pressure to apply – that comes only through doing.

Use AI to supplement your learning: for making plans, getting tips, sanity-checking decisions, and even moral support (“This isn’t gluing right, what can I do?” – sometimes just getting a new idea from AI is a relief). But always loop back to reality: test advice in small experiments, and integrate what works for you.

Example prompt usage scenario: Imagine you are about to glue clear acetate windows and worried about frosting or fogging. You ask an AI, it suggests using a very small amount of PVA or a specialized plastic glue rather than superglue to avoid fogging. You then apply that – great, you averted an issue. But if AI suggested something odd (like “use solvent cement on foamboard” – which you know would melt foam), you’d reject that. This partnership between your growing knowledge and AI’s suggestions can be powerful.

Finally, remember AI doesn’t have ego or tire of questions – so ask anything you’re curious about, even if trivial. Many students might hesitate to bug a teacher with “basic” questions, but an AI will cheerfully answer “How do I clean my cutting mat?” at 3am. Just filter the responses with your own reasoning. By leveraging AI as a tool, you effectively have a round-the-clock tutor to reinforce concepts and explore new ones, while you remain very much the master-builder of your physical model.

Conclusion: You now have in hand a comprehensive briefing on beginning physical model making, from initial purpose to final support tools. This structured guidance, written in a calm, institutional tone, should serve as a reliable reference as you embark on crafting miniature modernist and brutalist structures. By starting with the basics – a simple housing block – and gradually building up your skills, tools, and confidence (with the help of modern aids like AI when appropriate), you will develop a strong foundation in model making. Embrace the process with patience and curiosity. As you progress, refer back to these sections: ensure your scale is chosen wisely, your blades are sharp, your materials well-understood, and your approach methodical yet creative. In doing so, you’ll not only create successful first models, but also prepare yourself for more complex projects, where the rich forms of modernist and brutalist architecture can be brought to life at miniature scale. Good luck, and enjoy the journey of making!
Sources:
First In Architecture – Architectural Model Making: The Guide
ArchDaily – 16 Tips To Improve Your Model-Making Skills (Zilliacus, 2016)
Architecturalmodels.net
– Massing Models Guide (2025)
HowToRhino – Architectural Model Making 101 (Cvetković, 2022)
First In Architecture – Materials for architectural models
Architecturalmodels.net
– Traditional Materials (Kraft board, Foam board, Balsa)
David Neat (model-maker) – Simulating polished concrete in a model
Architizer – Beyond Brutalism: Cumbernauld Town Centre (Wang, 2021)
ArchDaily – 16 Tips… – (on asking for advice & practice)
First In Architecture – (importance of understanding materials & tools)

articles.title: Absurdist Administration Misses Key Glasgow Design Meetup Opportunity
articles.standfirst: The Government of SwS failed to attend the 'WIP' Glasgow design meet-up, an event intended to demonstrate social engagement within the community. The reflection on this absence sheds light on the ongoing challenges of social anxiety and personal growth.

runs.text: In a notable absence, SwS did not participate in the 'WIP' design meetup held in Glasgow, an event that was expected to highlight the Absurdist administration's commitment to pushing beyond our social comfort zone. This meeting was designed as a low-pressure gathering for designers, primarily students and recent graduates, providing a space to share ideas, make connections, and foster community engagement.
Context of the Event

The 'WIP' meetup aimed to create an informal atmosphere for networking and collaboration among emerging designers in Glasgow. By cultivating a space free from pressure and hierarchy, the event represented a significant opportunity for attendees to engage with one another and share their creative journeys. This aligns with the philosophy of the Absurdist administration, which emphasizes intention and constructed meaning in social interactions.
Reflection on Attendance

In a personal reflection, SwS characterized the decision not to attend as a confrontation with social anxiety, recognizing this as a barrier to meaningful engagement with the community. SwS expressed a strong desire for community involvement, stating, “I want to be more embedded in my community. I want to make likeminded, Glasgow-based creative friends.” Despite this longing, feelings of anxiety prevented participation, highlighting the complexities of balancing independence with the need for social interaction.

The narrative shared by SwS illustrates the internal struggle faced by many in their social lives. At 27, SwS noted a growing sense of loneliness, exacerbated by the gradual drifting apart from school friends. This sense of isolation stands in stark contrast to aspirations for a vibrant social and creative life. SwS reflects on this duality: “When I’m with people, I quite often hate it. I long to be back by myself, alone in my room, safe within my womb.” This paradox resonates with the challenges of navigating social landscapes in the modern world, particularly for individuals who thrive on independence but feel drawn to community.
Implications for Personal Growth

The missed opportunity at the 'WIP' event serves not just as a setback but also as a potential learning experience for SwS. The reflection suggests a recognition of the need for gradual exposure to social environments, proposing a strategy of “quiet, slow-paced exposure therapy.” By spending more time in familiar spaces and engaging incrementally with the community, SwS aims to build confidence and comfort in social settings.

Moreover, the analogy drawn between personal growth and achieving a reputation in the creative field highlights a broader narrative about self-worth and validation. SwS speculates that gaining visibility through online platforms may ease the transition into in-person interactions. This reasoning underscores a significant theme in contemporary society, where online presence often informs offline dynamics.
Conclusion

The absence of SwS from the 'WIP' Glasgow design meetup not only reflects individual challenges surrounding social anxiety but also underscores an essential aspect of the Absurdist administration's objective—fostering community ties. As the government looks toward future engagement opportunities, the experience serves as a reminder of the importance of addressing personal barriers to participation in social initiatives.

This situation is poised to be a pivotal moment for SwS, offering valuable lessons in the ongoing pursuit of personal and communal growth within the framework of governance under the Absurdist administration.

articles.title: Introducing the SwSgov Digital Service
articles.standfirst: The Government of SwS has launched the SwSgov Digital Service, a new body modernising and decentralising all government technology. Its first major project, SWS.GOV, brings every update, service, and micro-post into one unified platform built on the GOV.UK Design System.

runs.text: The Government of SwS today announced the launch of the
SwSgov Digital Service (SwSgDS)

, a new design and technology body that will oversee every aspect of SwS government infrastructure. Its remit is ambitious: decentralise how government information is created and delivered, and modernise the entire digital estate.
At the centre of this transformation is
SWS.GOV
, the new online home of the Government of SwS. Modelled on
GOV.UK
and built directly using the official
GOV.UK
Design System

from the UK Government Digital Service, GOV.SWS brings familiar clarity and reliability into the SwS digital environment. It will act as a single, accessible hub for all government services, policy information, updates, and archives. Hosted natively as part of the
smixs.am
infrastructure, the platform provides a consistent, modern foundation for the future.
Crucially,
SWS.GOV
won’t just house long-form content
. Both
press releases and micro-posts

will also be accessible through GOV.SWS, creating a single place to read everything coming out of government, regardless of format. These posts will continue to be authored and managed in Craft and distributed via MCP to the open web, but the site itself will always surface the full, canonical record.
The broader communications ecosystem remains proudly
decentralised

. Long-form statements and policy documents are maintained independently within Craft. Micro-posts, meanwhile, will be published via the official SwS Mastodon instance, ensuring every update exists in an open, federated space rather than a proprietary silo. Thanks to the new infrastructure, these Mastodon updates will also appear automatically on GOV.SWS, but can be accessed anywhere on any platform.
This decentralised data model is mirrored in the evolution of the
iSwS app
, which shifts under the SwSgDS remit. The app is now being reworked as a
native iOS front end

to all these frameworks, ensuring that everything published by the government is identical whether viewed on the web, in the app, or through decentralised protocols. There are no separate codebases, no divergent versions, and no second-class platforms. Every device accesses the same data, in the same structure, from the same source of truth.
Alongside this decentralisation, SwSgDS will continue adopting
centralised tools where they enhance interoperability and real-world usefulness

. This includes systems that integrate directly with Apple Shortcuts, third-party apps, the open web, automation pipelines, and AI-driven workflows. The goal is not decentralisation for its own sake, but a balanced, resilient, user-centred digital estate.

The creation of the SwSgov Digital Service marks a major shift in how the Government of SwS designs, builds, and communicates. It introduces standards where inconsistency once lived, coherence where tools once drifted apart, and a long-term digital vision grounded in clarity, independence, and interoperability.
SwSgDS will roll out this new infrastructure in the coming weeks, with further updates as
SWS.GOV
, the Mastodon backend, MCP distribution system, and redesigned iSwS app move toward full public launch.
The digital future of SwS is open, modern, decentralised, and beautifully structured. With SwSgDS, that future officially enters service today.

articles.title: SwS 2026 Election Results: Absurdists Secure Majority Amidst Shifting Political Landscape
articles.standfirst: The results of the SwS 2026 election reveal a significant shift in the political framework, with the Absurdists gaining seats and the Modernists facing a sharp decline.

runs.text: The SwS 2026 election results have been officially released, indicating a tumultuous yet notable shift in the political landscape of the Government of SwS. The results show a consolidation of power for the Absurdist administration, which has secured a total of 68 seats, a gain of 12 from the previous cycle.
Absurdists Strengthen Their Position

The Absurdist party, currently leading the government, has successfully strengthened its hold. With a focus on promoting governance through intentional living, the Absurdists have emphasized structural reforms across the four pilotis: Body, Mind, Identity, and Money. Their electoral manifesto highlighted various achievements since taking office, including enhancements in physical health, personal productivity, and financial planning. The Absurdist emphasis on intentional direction in governance has resonated with the electorate, resulting in a significant increase in support. Their achievements include the elimination of cannabis use, an increase in VO₂ Max, and the midweight promotion.
Other Parties’ Performance

In contrast, the Stoics showed a substantial increase, claiming 24 seats—an impressive gain of 24 compared to their previous position. This could indicate a growing appeal for their philosophy, which promotes resilience and practical ethics in governance. The Absurdist party have already indicated the growing influence of the Stoics could impact their government in the next term. The Modernists, who famously oversaw the collapse of the Common Consensus, faced a stark decline, dropping to just 2 seats—a loss of 34. Similarly, NBNS and the NOW party lost seats, each registering losses of 23 and 7, respectively. The Socialist party also experienced a minor reduction, securing only 1 seat, a decrease of 2.
Implications of the Results

The outcome of the 2026 election not only reflects the changing dynamics within the SwS political scene but also hints at the evolving attitudes of the citizens toward governance and personal philosophies. The Absurdist administration's campaign achievements were articulated through concrete initiatives, with pledges for new policies aimed at enhancing personal lives and societal engagement should they continue in leadership.
Moving forward, the Absurdists have announced ambitious new initiatives, including:
Body
: Improved fitness programs, broader nutritional options, and stricter environmental practices in households.
Mind
: Focused improvements in digital engagement, exploring stoicism alongside absurdism, and learning coding skills for enhanced personal development.
Identity
: Commitment to civic engagement, direct interaction with social media for professional purposes, and publication of personal sentiments within a structured format.
Money
: Diversifying income streams through creative means and transparent reporting of financial activity.
These initiatives, if implemented effectively, could further cement the Absurdists' connection to the electorate and bolster their authority in governance.
Conclusion

The 2026 elections have showcased a decisive moment in the political development of the Government of SwS. With the Absurdists poised to enact their vision for the future of SwS under the principles of intentional living, other parties will need to reevaluate their positions and engage with the electorate to remain relevant in an increasingly complex political environment. As the newly elected administration prepares for its next term, all eyes will be on the execution of their ambitious agenda, set against the backdrop of a changing societal landscape that continues to define SwS.

articles.title: Government launches all new SWS.GOV
articles.standfirst: SWS.GOV is the new unified home for every service, dashboard, and update from the Government of SwS. It brings tools for the body, mind, identity, money, and administration together in one clean, platform built on the GOV.UK design system.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is the new digital home of the Government of SwS, bringing every service, dashboard, record, and tool into one clear, modern platform. Built on the
GOV.UK
Design System and powered by the new SwSgov Digital Service, the site gives citizens a structured way to navigate the full landscape of SwS governance, from personal metrics to national policy.

The platform is organised around the core pillars of life in SwS. Under Tools and Services, you’ll find essentials like the Press Office, Objectives and Progress Tracker, Policies, Health Dashboard, and the full archive of SwS history and outputs. The Body section hosts everything related to fitness, stretching, strength training, running, food planning, safe foods, and substance-use records, all grouped to make day-to-day management easier and more intentional.
"We've seriously built something that's better than the website of any nation in the world."

The Mind pillar brings together daily notes, learning tools, reading, meditation, and dedicated spaces like Pacific Quay for reflection and long-form thinking. Identity covers your personal data dashboards: basic information, plant care, academic results, flat records, digital devices, and the full Style Archive. Financial life sits under Money, with pages for income, expenditure, growth, and home ownership. An Admin section rounds things out with tools for creating entries and refreshing site content.
SWS.GOV

is designed to be the single, authoritative place to access every part of your government and your life within it. Clean, structured, and future-focused, the site represents the new era of SwS governance: connected, intentional, and beautifully organised.

articles.title: Three days until DIBI
articles.standfirst: DIBI returns to Edinburgh in three days for two packed days of product, design and technology talks at Dynamic Earth.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: DIBI conference branding at an earlier event. Image: HeadBox / The Biscuit Room.
Three days until DIBI
DIBI is back in Edinburgh this week, with the two-day digital product and technology conference due to open at Dynamic Earth on Wednesday 30 September.

The event, which runs into Thursday 1 October, bills itself around “actionable insights for product people” and brings design, development and product thinking together rather than treating them as separate disciplines. For a UX practice increasingly concerned with experimentation, evidence and how design operates inside wider product systems, that makes this year’s programme particularly well timed.

DIBI says its speakers are intended to inform, challenge and inspire across commercial, creative and technical domains. Product designer Joel Miller of Figma is among the names currently promoted by organisers, while Herb Kim is returning as host. Alongside the talks, the conference includes practical workshops and networking across the two days.

The timing lands during a busy stretch of design work. The BBC calendar shows Experiment Enablement UX stand-ups continuing this week, alongside a Data UX check-in on Tuesday. A separate session on opportunities for experimentation in product engineering teams has been cancelled pending clearer H2 planning outcomes, a small but telling reminder that the organisational conditions around experimentation remain in motion.

That context matters. Recent experimentation work has repeatedly surfaced questions about ownership, measurement confidence, governance and the point at which specialist input enters the process. DIBI’s broad product-and-tech framing offers a useful chance to look beyond individual UX methods and towards how design decisions survive contact with engineering, commercial constraints and organisational reality.

There is also a strong practical streak to the event. Organisers promise workshops built around tools, techniques and ideas that attendees can apply directly in their roles. That emphasis should help separate the conference from the familiar circuit of inspirational design talks that sound good on stage but struggle to make it into Monday morning’s work.
Dynamic Earth will host the conference again, placing the event beside Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Conference passes are currently advertised at £255 excluding VAT.

With three days to go, the interesting question is less whether DIBI can produce another round of polished product talks and more whether its mix of design, development and business thinking can offer anything genuinely useful for the messier work now happening around experimentation.
For
SWS.GOV
, that is the bit worth watching.

articles.title: SWS.GOV gets a proper backlog
articles.standfirst: A new Notion board brings SWS.GOV work into one backlog, with dedicated views across the site and a simple to-do, doing and done workflow.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Project board logo. Source: Wikimedia Commons.
SWS.GOV
gets a proper backlog
SWS.GOV
has moved its redesign work into a single project board, giving Project Indigo a clearer route from idea to done.

The new setup uses a straightforward Kanban workflow: to do, doing and done. It is deliberately simple, but the board is split into dedicated views for the main parts of the site, including the homepage, recipes, goals, planner, archive, iFit, bookshelf, news, reader and search, alongside an all-projects view.
That matters because
SWS.GOV

is no longer one redesign job. Project Indigo has grown into a rolling rebuild touching the site’s visual language, navigation and a string of individual services. The homepage is becoming a personalised dashboard, search is expanding beyond the archive, News has become an active publishing stream, and older areas such as Recipes and Archive are being reworked rather than simply reskinned.

Until now, much of that work has lived across conversations, prototypes, code and individual decisions. The new project board gives those moving parts a common operational layer. Each ticket can carry basic information and its own tasks, while filtered views mean a homepage job can sit in the same underlying system as a Planner or Bookshelf job without turning the board into a wall of noise.

The change is modest compared with the visible parts of Indigo, but it tackles a familiar product-design problem: once a project becomes broad enough, the work around the work starts to matter. A redesign can look coherent in Figma while the delivery backlog quietly fragments across notes and memory.
For
SWS.GOV

, the immediate consequence is less glamorous but more useful. There is now one place to see what is waiting, what is active and what has actually shipped, without losing the ability to focus on one service at a time.

The board also arrives at a useful point in Indigo’s rollout. The redesign is intended to continue progressively through the end of 2026, which means old and new parts of the site will coexist for a while. That makes prioritisation more important: unfinished work is no longer just a list of design ideas, but a live queue against a site already changing underneath it.

The test now is whether the board stays current. A Kanban system only earns its keep when tickets move with the work. If that happens, Project Indigo has gained something it badly needed: not another feature, but a proper backlog.

articles.title: A small offer becomes a poster
articles.standfirst: A fleeting offer of help on Battlefield Road has become the latest raw material for an increasingly everyday strand of poster-making.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Battlefield Road in Glasgow’s Southside. Image: Scotland’s Property Guide.
A small offer becomes a poster
A two-second exchange on Battlefield Road has ended up doing something rather bigger than expected: becoming the subject of a new poster experiment.

The moment itself was almost aggressively ordinary. Walking along the Glasgow Southside street, Sam Smith spotted a man trying to get through a doorway while pushing a pram. With the door proving awkward, Smith offered a hand and moved to hold it open.
“Do you need a hand, mate?” was the offer. The man replied that he was all right, and the pair carried on with their day.

That could easily have been the end of it. Instead, the tiny encounter was later turned into a visual study, using the real streetscape as the setting and stripping the incident back to its basic ingredients: a pavement, a doorway, two strangers and an offer that was not actually needed.

The first version treated the scene fairly literally before the direction shifted towards something more avant-garde. Excess text was removed and the real location became more important, leaving the image to carry most of the story rather than explaining the event in words.

It is a small development, but it fits a wider pattern in recent creative work. Posters have increasingly become less about waiting for a suitably grand subject and more about treating everyday material as something worth designing around. That can mean a piece of music, a personal joke, a local place or, in this case, a social interaction lasting only seconds.

The result also captures something recognisable about city life. Offers of help are made, declined and forgotten constantly. There was no rescue, no dramatic intervention and no reason to inflate the exchange into one. The man with the pram said he was fine. Smith accepted that. Everyone moved on.

That lack of drama is precisely what made the incident useful as visual material. Rather than presenting the moment as an act of heroism, the poster can focus on the awkward choreography of two people briefly negotiating the same doorway and then separating again.

The setting matters too. Battlefield Road is not an abstract backdrop but part of the everyday geography of home: sandstone tenements, shopfronts, traffic and the repeated routes of ordinary Southside life. Using it directly pushes the work closer to a kind of personal visual record rather than a generic design exercise.
The poster remains an experiment rather than a major project. But the underlying idea is potentially more durable: make things from what is already happening, instead of waiting for a perfect brief.
On Wednesday, that meant a man, a pram and a door. By Thursday, it had become another entry in a growing visual archive of everyday life.

articles.title: Comedy night at the King’s
articles.standfirst: A planned Glasgow comedy night put Vittorio Angelone on the King’s Theatre stage as his latest UK tour reached the city.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Vittorio Angelone on his 2026 tour. Image: Vittorio Angelone official website / Just the Tonic Comedy Club.
Comedy night at the King’s
Vittorio Angelone brought his latest stand-up show to Glasgow on Thursday, taking over the King’s Theatre for a 7.30pm date on his 2026 UK tour.

The Northern Irish comic arrived in the city on 24 September as part of a run that continues to Leeds on 28 September. The Glasgow performance was listed by both the venue and British Comedy Guide, making the King’s one of the larger traditional theatres on a tour built around Angelone’s fast-growing live audience.

Angelone’s route into comedy was not especially conventional. His official biography says he grew up in Belfast before moving to London to train as a classical musician, later switching to stand-up. He has since completed sell-out tours and appeared at the Edinburgh Fringe in 2022, 2023, 2024 and 2025.

His first Edinburgh run also brought a nomination for Best Newcomer at the Edinburgh Comedy Awards in 2022. Since then, online clips, sketches and podcast appearances have helped turn him into a recognisable name well beyond the club circuit.

The current show, You Can’t Say Nothing Anymore, continues a style that plays with uncomfortable subjects and the tension around what can and cannot be joked about. Angelone has previously said that he works to keep the jokes from becoming nasty or mean, while still taking an audience towards ideas they may find uncomfortable.

That combination has made the live show a more interesting prospect than a straightforward night of safe observational comedy. It also fits a wider strand of contemporary stand-up in which podcasts and short online clips sit alongside the traditional touring circuit, allowing performers to build a sizeable audience before television becomes the main route to recognition.

The King’s Theatre date placed that newer comedy career inside one of Glasgow’s most traditional entertainment venues. The theatre has long hosted touring drama, musicals, comedy and pantomime, giving the night a deliberately old-school setting for a performer whose audience has been built in a very modern way.
For
SWS.GOV

, the Glasgow stop lands as a cultural break in a busy late-September stretch dominated by design work, experimentation and personal projects. It also comes just days before the DIBI design conference begins in Edinburgh, shifting the diary from live comedy back towards product, technology and design.
One night, one microphone and a packed theatre is a fairly simple proposition. In a week full of systems, prototypes and planning, that simplicity is part of the point.

articles.title: The casino floor looks familiar
articles.standfirst: A casino-floor thought experiment has turned into a sharper look at the design mechanics shared by slot machines and attention-hungry digital products.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Slot machines at the Model T Casino in Winnemucca, Nevada. Image: Mx. Granger / Wikimedia Commons, CC0.
The casino floor looks familiar
A grim casino-floor thought experiment has opened up a much bigger design question: how different is a slot machine, really, from the digital products fighting to keep people tapping and scrolling?

The comparison came after a discussion about the extreme pull of slot machines, from people sitting at machines for hours to the strange tunnel vision that can make everything else in the room feel irrelevant. The uncomfortable follow-up was closer to home. Endless social feeds can produce a milder version of the same basic feeling: one more pull, one more refresh, one more clip.

That does not make Instagram a casino, and scrolling is not financially equivalent to gambling. But the overlap in interaction design is hard to miss. Both can use rapid feedback, uncertain rewards and frictionless repetition to turn a tiny action into a loop.

The evidence around gambling machines is particularly stark. Research has linked the rapid, continuous nature of electronic gaming machines with sustained play, while studies of near-misses have found that apparently almost-winning can increase arousal and distort a player's sense of control. The UK's Gambling Commission has explicitly treated product design as a safety issue rather than a cosmetic one.

Its rules for online slots now ban autoplay, features that speed up play, spins faster than 2.5 seconds and celebratory sounds or imagery when a player has actually lost money overall on the spin. The regulator says the aim is to reduce intensity and stop products exploiting or encouraging problem gambling behaviour. A later assessment found evidence that the 2021 changes reduced play intensity without producing harmful unintended consequences.
For
SWS.GOV
, the interesting bit is the UX lesson.

Designers usually talk about reducing friction as though it is automatically good. Make the next action obvious. Remove unnecessary steps. Keep momentum. Reward engagement. In most services that can be sensible. But a casino floor is a fairly brutal demonstration of what happens when an experience becomes exceptionally good at keeping somebody inside a loop whose interests are not necessarily aligned with theirs.
The same question applies, with very different stakes, to feeds, short-form video, notifications and other attention products. A successful interaction metric can still describe a poor human outcome.

That makes the casino comparison less a claim that all persuasive design is addictive and more a useful stress test. If an interface is optimised to make stopping harder, what exactly is being improved?
The answer matters well beyond gambling. The strongest design may sometimes be the design that gives people a clean way out.

articles.title: A free hour lands on Friday
articles.standfirst: BBC Product Group staff have been given a free hour next Friday to switch off and spend time on something for themselves.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: BBC Scotland at Pacific Quay in Glasgow. Image: Batchelor/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0.
A free hour lands on Friday
BBC staff in the Product Group are being handed an extra hour next Friday with one instruction: use it for yourself.

A Free Hour has appeared in the BBC calendar for 14:00 to 15:00 on Friday 2 October, extending an initiative already being used by some teams across the wider Product Group. The calendar note says colleagues should switch off and spend the time doing something just for them.

The suggestions are deliberately ordinary. A walk, meeting a friend or doing some gardening are all offered as examples. There is no workshop, no output and no request to turn the hour into another piece of professional development.
For a working week built around stand-ups, reviews, catch-ups and delivery, that absence of an agenda is the point.

The hour arrives at the end of a busy stretch in the work diary. The coming week includes regular team check-ins, UX stand-ups, a sprint review and a session on end-to-end work, alongside the DIBI Conference in Edinburgh on 30 September and 1 October.
That makes the timing notable. Instead of filling another available slot, the invitation deliberately protects one.

The free hour lands on Friday, which is separately marked as a non-working day in the BBC calendar. The practical effect may therefore vary depending on individual working patterns, but the Product Group invitation itself is explicit: the time is intended for switching off rather than squeezing in another task.

The move fits a broader BBC approach that has long linked working practices with wellbeing. Public BBC flexible-working policy describes work-life balance as relevant to motivation, performance, productivity and stress. The organisation's health and attendance policy also says managers have a role in supporting the health and wellbeing of their teams.

This particular initiative is much smaller and more immediate than a formal policy change. It is an hour in the diary, not a new employment entitlement, and the calendar wording makes no wider promise about how often it will happen.

But its simplicity is arguably what makes it noticeable. Modern knowledge work has a habit of colonising spare gaps with messages, admin and quick meetings. Blocking an hour and explicitly telling people not to optimise it into more work cuts against that instinct.

There is also something refreshingly specific about the examples. Nobody is being asked to meditate, complete a wellbeing module or demonstrate that the hour was productive. Walking, seeing a friend or gardening are enough.
For teams working largely through digital calendars and collaboration tools, the intervention is almost comically low-tech: put an hour in the diary and give it back.
No grand programme. No deliverable. Just 60 minutes back.

articles.title: Paris palace faces the value test
articles.standfirst: A Paris luxury stay is under consideration as the Four Seasons George V is weighed against the premium attached to one of the city’s grandest hotels.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Four Seasons Hotel George V, Paris. Photo: Alan Light/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
Paris palace faces the value test
One of Paris’s grandest hotels has landed on the travel shortlist, but the question is not whether it is luxurious. It is whether that luxury is actually worth paying for.

The Four Seasons Hotel George V, just off the Champs-Élysées in the capital’s Golden Triangle, is being weighed as a possible stay. It is an Art Deco landmark dating from 1928, with 243 rooms and suites, a spa and pool, and three restaurants carrying six Michelin stars between them in the 2026 guide.

That makes the George V an unusually complete luxury proposition. Le Cinq has now held three Michelin stars for ten consecutive years under chef Christian Le Squer, while L’Orangerie retains two and Le George one. The hotel’s accommodation ranges from 37–40 sq m Superior Rooms to vast signature suites, with some rooms and suites offering terraces, balconies or Eiffel Tower views.
But
SWS.GOV

’s interest is less about ticking off luxury credentials than testing the value equation. A spectacular lobby, elaborate flowers and attentive service can make a hotel feel like part of the trip rather than somewhere to sleep. The catch is that this only works if enough time is actually spent there to enjoy it.

For a Paris visit built around long days in the city, restaurants, museums and wandering neighbourhoods, a palace hotel can become an extremely expensive base for showering and sleeping. The George V makes a stronger case when the hotel itself is deliberately treated as an experience: breakfast in, time at the pool or spa, a drink in La Galerie, and enough breathing room to appreciate the service and surroundings.

There is also a design argument. The hotel sits firmly in the traditional grand-Paris category rather than the stripped-back Scandinavian look often favoured elsewhere. Its interiors combine historic Art Deco character, classical French furniture and contemporary pieces. That makes it a fairly maximalist choice, but also a chance to experience a kind of hospitality design that would be difficult to reproduce at a normal city hotel.
No booking decision has been made. For now, the George V remains in the category of tempting extravagance rather than obvious value.

The verdict is therefore awkwardly simple: the hotel appears capable of justifying its reputation, but not automatically its price. If the stay becomes part of the holiday, the maths gets easier. If Paris itself is the whole point, the money may be better kept for Paris.

articles.title: Artwork gets the green light
articles.standfirst: A finished album-art experiment has cleared its final design pass and is ready to carry Sam Smith’s name in public.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: A coloured vinyl record on an Audio-Technica turntable. Picture: M. Johnson/Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0
Artwork gets the green light

A new piece of album artwork is ready to leave the drafts folder after a final design pass on Wednesday, turning a quick visual experiment into something Sam Smith is prepared to put his name on and publish.

The work was developed and refined during a wider burst of poster-making and graphic experimentation. The finished version was reviewed again on 23 September, with attention shifting from whether the concept worked at all to the smaller details that separate a promising draft from a piece that feels finished: hierarchy, spacing, balance and the treatment of individual elements.

That matters because the project sits inside a broader push to make personal design work more visible rather than leaving it as private practice. Recent plans include keeping poster-making running in the background while building a simple place to sell selected work through a dropship model. The album artwork is not itself a confirmed commercial release, but it is another piece of evidence that the creative pipeline is becoming more regular and more public-facing.

The timing is useful. A separate planning exercise this week pulled five active strands into one Notion-based system, including the poster shop, personal finances, Blender experiments, England Weekend Television and outreach connected to that project. The aim is less about adding another productivity layer and more about stopping good ideas from competing for the same bit of mental space.

Wednesday’s artwork review also showed a shift in the standard being applied. The question was no longer simply whether the image looked good enough. It became whether individual components could still be improved before the name went on it. That is a more demanding test, and a healthier one for work intended to sit alongside professional design output.

There is no announced release date, client or record attached to the artwork, and it should not be mistaken for a commissioned sleeve. For now it remains a self-directed design piece. But it has crossed a small threshold: from experiment to finished work worth sharing. With a poster storefront also on the agenda, that distinction could become increasingly important as more of the personal archive moves into public view.

articles.title: A wee exhibition became something bigger
articles.standfirst: A trip to Get Glasgow Moving’s tenth-anniversary exhibition turned into a small but useful test of what happens when anxiety stops getting the final say.

runs.text: A wee exhibition became something bigger

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: An illustrated view of a transport exhibition, created for
SWS.GOV
I nearly didn’t go.

Get Glasgow Moving’s tenth-anniversary exhibition at the New Glasgow Society was exactly the sort of thing I’d normally be interested in: Glasgow, public transport, civic campaigning and people trying to make the city work better. The campaign itself was founded in 2016, and the exhibition looks back over its first decade.
The problem was the bit between being interested in it and actually walking through the door.

I was going on my own. I didn’t know exactly what the room would be like, who would be there or whether I’d end up awkwardly having to speak to people. None of that was especially dramatic, but it was enough for my brain to start producing reasons not to bother.
I went anyway.
Once I was inside, the whole thing became considerably less intimidating. I looked around the exhibition, spoke briefly to the people there and bought an orange Get Glasgow Moving T-shirt.
That should probably be the end of the story. Person goes to exhibition. Person enjoys exhibition. Person buys T-shirt.
But the interesting bit was how badly the anxiety beforehand predicted the actual experience.
Getting through the door

The New Glasgow Society describes itself as a civic society focused on Glasgow’s beauty, history and character, using campaigning, discussion, projects, talks and exhibitions. Get Glasgow Moving, meanwhile, is a grassroots campaign for a more integrated, accessible and publicly accountable public transport network across the region.
In other words, this was not a random social obligation. It sat almost absurdly neatly at the intersection of things I care about.
That makes the instinct to avoid it more interesting.

I’ve started thinking about the difference between discomfort that is genuinely telling you something useful and discomfort that is simply the price of doing something unfamiliar. I’m very good at building systems that make life comfortable. Usually that is sensible. But comfort can quietly become a decision-making framework of its own.
The exhibition was a tiny example of what happens when it isn’t.
I didn’t suddenly become an extrovert. I didn’t spend the afternoon networking with everyone in the room. Nothing transformative happened in the conventional sense.
I just went in.
From watching to joining in
The more important thought came while I was there.

I’ve followed organisations like Get Glasgow Moving for years. I’m interested in how Glasgow works, how it moves and how it could be better. But there is an easy habit of treating the people who actually organise things, campaign, speak publicly and participate in civic life as a separate category of person.
Standing in the exhibition, that distinction felt a bit daft.
There is no fundamental reason I couldn’t eventually be one of the people contributing to something like this rather than simply following it from the outside.
The difficult part is making sure this does not become another isolated moment of confidence that feels meaningful for a week and then disappears. I’ve had those before.
So the useful lesson isn’t that anxiety has been defeated. It hasn’t. It is that being anxious and doing something anyway are perfectly capable of happening at the same time.
If something matters, discomfort alone probably shouldn’t get a veto.
And, at minimum, I now have a very good orange T-shirt.

articles.title: H2 pause for experimentation talks
articles.standfirst: A recurring discussion on experimentation opportunities has been paused until the BBC’s second-half planning position becomes clearer.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: BBC Scotland’s Pacific Quay headquarters in Glasgow. Image: OCS.
H2 pause for experimentation talks

A recurring BBC discussion on opportunities for product engineering teams to use experimentation has been cancelled for now, with the calendar note saying it can return once the outcome of second-half planning is clearer.

The change appeared on the BBC calendar for Wednesday 23 September, where a 40-minute session titled “Experimentaion for product engineering teams - opportunities” was marked cancelled. The accompanying note was unusually direct: the series is being stopped until there is greater clarity on H2 planning outcomes, with an expectation that there will be a need for it again.

It is a small diary change, but one that lands at a significant point for experimentation work. Recent months have involved a push to make experimentation easier to run across product teams, alongside work on the operating model, measurement confidence, dependencies and governance. Those themes were also central to the experimentation challenges session held on 17 September.

The pause does not amount to a cancellation of experimentation work itself. The Experiment Enablement UX stand-up remains in the BBC calendar for Friday 25 September, followed by another stand-up and a sprint review on Tuesday 29 September. That distinction matters: the regular delivery rhythm is still visible, while the wider conversation with product engineering teams is being held back pending planning decisions.

That makes the timing more interesting than the meeting title might suggest. Experimentation work has already exposed a familiar set of organisational problems: unclear ownership, handover friction, inconsistent practice, delays caused by approvals and specialist input, and difficulty establishing confidence in metrics when tools or tracking disagree. A broader opportunity discussion is most useful when teams know what they are actually trying to deliver and who has capacity to support it.

The calendar change therefore reads less like retreat and more like sequencing. Rather than continuing a recurring forum while H2 priorities are unsettled, the discussion can restart against a clearer set of commitments.

There is also a busy end to September ahead. The BBC calendar shows an Experiment Enablement sprint review on 29 September, while the DIBI conference begins at Dynamic Earth in Edinburgh on 30 September. That event has already been flagged as a useful chance to look outward at wider design and technology practice after an unusually experimentation-heavy period at work.

For now, the practical message is simple: delivery continues, but one strand of the wider experimentation conversation is on hold. What replaces it, and how quickly it returns, will depend on where the BBC’s H2 planning lands.

articles.title: Invoice ready on £150 Stereo design job
articles.standfirst: A £150 invoice for Stereo Presents marks the latest paid graphic-design commission moving from finished work to payment.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Stereo on Renfield Lane in Glasgow city centre. Picture: Hidden Scotland.
Invoice ready on £150 Stereo design job
A PAID Glasgow design job has moved into its final, less glamorous phase: getting the invoice out the door.

A £150 bill for graphic-design work on Stereo Presents’ IPP 3 campaign was prepared on Tuesday, 22 September, marking another small but concrete piece of independent work alongside the day job at the BBC.

The invoice, numbered INV-0002, covers one graphic-design commission and is addressed to Stereo Presents CIC. A draft email with the PDF attached is ready to send, with the recipient back after an out-of-office period on 21 September.

It is not a giant agency account or a life-changing cheque. But that is precisely what makes it useful evidence of something more practical: paid creative work continuing to exist outside the main UX role, with a real client, a defined deliverable and an actual number attached to it.

Stereo itself is a long-running independent fixture in Glasgow city centre. The venue says it has operated since 2007 from its Renfield Lane home, combining a café and bar with gigs, club nights and community events. It describes itself as rooted in DIY culture, experimentation and community, and as a supporter of local and home-grown talent.

That makes the commission a neat fit with the wider strand of side work already developing around Glasgow culture and independent projects. Recent planning has also put poster-making, a possible dropship shop, England Weekend Television and exploratory Blender work into a single Notion system, an attempt to stop a growing pile of ideas competing for attention at once.

The Stereo job is different from those speculative projects because the commercial loop is already almost complete. The design work has been delivered, the fee is fixed and the paperwork exists. What remains is administration: send the email, wait for payment and close the job properly.

The £150 fee is modest, particularly against a longer-term freelance day-rate ambition of £400, but it provides a useful benchmark. Small commissions can expose the boring infrastructure that creative side work needs if it is ever to become repeatable: invoicing, contact details, payment references, file storage and a clear record of what was supplied.

There is also a timing advantage. Wednesday’s BBC calendar has a busy start, including a 09:00 Account Epic Review, but the recurring experimentation opportunities session later in the morning has been cancelled while H2 planning becomes clearer. That leaves more space later in the day to close loose ends rather than open another project.
For now, the headline is simple. The work is done. The invoice is ready. The next milestone is money in the bank.

articles.title: Five projects, one place
articles.standfirst: A new Notion hub will bring posters, money, Blender, England Weekend Television and outreach into one manageable plan.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Notion will become the central hub for a new personal project system. Image: Notion Labs/Wikimedia Commons
Five projects, one place
A sprawling list of creative ambitions is being pulled into one system after a push to turn a busy mix of side projects into something that can actually be managed.

The new setup will use Notion as a central hub for five live strands: an ongoing poster practice and possible dropship shop, a personal finances reset, experiments in Blender, further work on England Weekend Television, and a plan to cold-call photographer Ed Campbell.

The move follows a blunt problem: there is plenty to do, but no single place showing what matters now, what can wait and what the next action actually is. Rather than treating every idea as equally urgent, the plan is to give each project a home, a status and a clear next step.

It is a small bit of admin with a bigger purpose. The poster work is intended to continue in the background while a route to selling prints through dropshipping is explored. Money needs its own practical track rather than competing for attention with creative work. Blender, meanwhile, is deliberately being kept playful, with room for experiments to grow into something more substantial without forcing a commercial outcome too early.

England Weekend Television remains a separate active project, with further development planned alongside direct outreach to Ed Campbell. The point is not to cram all of that into one week. It is to stop the projects becoming a single undifferentiated cloud of things that ought to be happening.

Notion is a fairly natural fit for that job. The company describes the product as a connected workspace combining documents, projects and databases, and its project tools support tasks, dependencies and custom properties. That makes it possible to keep a lightweight portfolio view while still giving each strand its own notes and actions.

The wider shift is from remembering projects to running them. A dashboard can show the handful of things currently moving, while ideas that are not active can stay visible without demanding immediate attention.

That matters because the aim is not maximum productivity for its own sake. The mix includes commercial work, personal housekeeping and things being done simply because they are interesting. A useful system has to preserve that distinction rather than turn every hobby into another job.

The immediate result is simple: five projects now have a prospective common home, and the next phase is to turn the list into a working rhythm rather than another beautifully organised graveyard of intentions.

articles.title: Government marks tremendous victory in new approach to discomfort
articles.standfirst: A successful visit to the Get Glasgow Moving exhibition will form the starting point for a wider approach to anxiety, participation and doing things that matter.

runs.text: Government marks tremendous victory in new approach to discomfort

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Government for SwS marks a new approach to discomfort following a visit to the Get Glasgow Moving anniversary exhibition.
The Government for SwS has today celebrated a tremendous victory following a successful solo visit to the Get Glasgow Moving 10-year anniversary exhibition at the New Glasgow Society.

The visit followed considerable anticipatory anxiety about attending the exhibition alone, entering an unfamiliar social environment and potentially encountering people involved with an organisation in which Sam has a longstanding interest.
Despite this, Sam attended the exhibition, viewed the work, briefly interacted with staff and purchased an orange Get Glasgow Moving T-shirt.
The Government considers the apparently routine visit significant because it provides further evidence that anticipatory anxiety is a poor predictor of Sam’s experience once an activity has begun.
A new approach to discomfort
Following the visit, the Government has set out a developing principle for future personal and professional decisions:
Comfort is useful infrastructure, but a bad decision-maker.
The Government will not pursue discomfort for its own sake, nor abandon routines, systems or accommodations that make everyday life easier.
Instead, where an opportunity is important to Sam and anxiety is the principal reason for avoiding it, greater weight will be given to the underlying desire to participate.
This will particularly apply to opportunities involving community participation, public speaking, professional development, creative work and involvement in Glasgow’s civic and cultural life.

The objective is not to eliminate anticipatory anxiety before taking action. Instead, the Government will support a longer-term shift towards becoming comfortable with being uncomfortable and developing greater confidence in Sam’s ability to act while anxious.
From observation to participation
The Get Glasgow Moving exhibition is also significant because of Sam’s longer-term interest in becoming involved with the organisation and contributing more directly to positive change in Glasgow.
During the exhibition, Sam concluded that there was no fundamental reason why he could not eventually become part of spaces such as this.

The Government recognises that previous successful experiences have not always resulted in sustained behavioural change. Periods of increased confidence have sometimes been followed by months without further action.
