The next phase will therefore focus on converting individual successes into continued participation rather than treating them as isolated achievements.
Success will not require Sam to become naturally extroverted, eliminate anxiety or perform confidently in every unfamiliar situation.
If something matters, discomfort alone is not a veto.
Today’s visit represents the first practical demonstration of that approach.
The orange T-shirt will be retained as evidence of the tremendous victory.

articles.title: Sagging has become the default at home
articles.standfirst: Sagging has shifted from an outward styling choice to an everyday default at home, revealing a clearer boundary between private comfort, personal presentation, family and work.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Sagging trousers at Tate Modern, London, 2010. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Gaywash (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Sagging has become the default at home
Something has changed in the relationship between SwS and sagging. What was once mainly a way of dressing outside the home has become the default even when nobody else is around.

At the family home, sagging tended to stop at the front door. Trousers might be worn low while out, but at home they were pulled back up. Living independently has removed that distinction. The waistband is now routinely visible while relaxing around the flat and the habit can continue into bed. It no longer needs an occasion, an outfit or another person to see it.

The remaining boundaries are revealing. Sagging is still generally switched off around family and at work, where a different standard of presentation takes over. Elsewhere, the low waistband has increasingly become the neutral position rather than a deliberate styling decision made each time.

That does not necessarily need a grand psychological explanation. Repetition can turn a chosen look into something familiar and automatic. But the change is still useful to notice: sagging now appears to function as part of personal presentation even in private, rather than only as a signal sent to other people.

There is also a stronger sense of ownership in being able to dress this way at home. The move from a family home, where the style was compartmentalised, to a private space where it does not need to be moderated has allowed it to become more continuous. The distinction is less between public and private than between environments where the style feels available and those where it does not.

Recent conversations have pushed that observation further, including the question of what it means psychologically when a clothing habit persists with no audience at all. The most defensible conclusion is fairly simple: the behaviour has become normalised enough that its private continuation now feels unremarkable. Anything more specific about motive would be speculation.

That interest also produced the deliberately niche sag-score app concept developed on Monday. The idea of using an iPhone camera and depth sensing to measure how low trousers are sitting is less the main story than a consequence of paying unusually close attention to the habit. Quantifying the drop turns something intuitive into something observable.

For now, there is no new rule or policy around sagging. The useful record is the change itself: a style once associated mainly with going out has become part of everyday life at home, while clear boundaries around family and work remain.

articles.title: DIBI countdown begins
articles.standfirst: With DIBI 2026 just eight days away, attention turns to two days of practical product design and technology thinking at Dynamic Earth.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: DIBI conference branding at an earlier event. Image: HeadBox / The Biscuit Room.
DIBI countdown begins
DIBI is heading back to Edinburgh next week, with the two-day digital product and technology conference due to open at Dynamic Earth on Wednesday 30 September.

The event, which runs into Thursday 1 October, bills itself around “actionable insights for product people” and brings design, development and product thinking together rather than treating them as separate disciplines. For a UX practice increasingly concerned with experimentation, evidence and how design operates inside wider product systems, that makes this year’s programme particularly well timed.

DIBI says its speakers are intended to inform, challenge and inspire across commercial, creative and technical domains. Product designer Joel Miller of Figma is among the names currently promoted by organisers, while Herb Kim is returning as host. Alongside the talks, the conference includes practical workshops and networking across the two days.

The timing lands during a busy stretch of design work. The BBC calendar shows Experiment Enablement UX stand-ups continuing this week, alongside a Data UX check-in today and an Account Epic Review on Wednesday. A separate session on opportunities for experimentation in product engineering teams has been cancelled pending clearer H2 planning outcomes, a small but telling reminder that the organisational conditions around experimentation remain in motion.

That context matters. Recent experimentation work has repeatedly surfaced questions about ownership, measurement confidence, governance and the point at which specialist input enters the process. DIBI’s broad product-and-tech framing offers a useful chance to look beyond individual UX methods and towards how design decisions survive contact with engineering, commercial constraints and organisational reality.

There is also a strong practical streak to the event. Organisers promise workshops built around tools, techniques and ideas that attendees can apply directly in their roles. That emphasis should help separate the conference from the familiar circuit of inspirational design talks that sound good on stage but struggle to make it into Monday morning’s work.
Dynamic Earth will host the conference again, placing the event beside Holyrood in central Edinburgh. Conference passes are currently advertised at £255 excluding VAT.

With eight days to go, the interesting question is less whether DIBI can produce another round of polished product talks and more whether its mix of design, development and business thinking can offer anything genuinely useful for the messier work now happening around experimentation.
For
SWS.GOV
, that is the bit worth watching.

articles.title: Two minutes, one button, one tiny Pi
articles.standfirst: A pocket-sized Raspberry Pi device could turn a single button press into a two-minute timer backed by a randomly selected local audio track.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W. Image: Raspberry Pi Ltd
Two minutes, one button, one tiny Pi

A new pocket-sized hardware idea could turn a single physical button into a deliberately simple two-minute ritual: press it, start a timer and hear one randomly chosen two-minute audio track from a local library.

The concept, explored on Monday night, is deliberately narrower than most smart-device projects. Rather than adding a screen full of controls or relying on a phone, the proposed machine would do one thing immediately. A button press would trigger a two-minute countdown while a small speaker plays a randomly selected recording stored on the device itself.

The current plan is for a battery-operated build based around Raspberry Pi hardware, with a physical push button, local audio storage and a compact speaker. That keeps the core interaction self-contained and avoids needing a network connection once the audio library has been loaded.

A Raspberry Pi Zero-class board is a plausible fit for that brief. The current Zero 2 W measures just 65mm by 30mm and combines a 1GHz quad-core processor with a microSD slot and a 40-pin GPIO header footprint, giving a small enclosure enough computing power to handle audio playback, timing and button input without the bulk of a full-size computer.

Raspberry Pi itself describes the Zero 2 W as suitable for embedded projects including Bluetooth speakers and other small connected devices. For this build, though, the attraction is less about connectivity than physicality. The useful bit is the ability to wire a real button into GPIO and make the interaction instant and predictable.

The software could remain equally lean. On startup, the Pi would wait for a button event. Once pressed, it would choose an audio file at random, begin playback and run the two-minute timer in parallel. At the end, playback stops and the machine returns to its waiting state. A simple lockout would prevent repeated presses from starting overlapping sessions.

There are still hardware decisions to make. Battery capacity, amplifier choice, speaker size, charging circuitry and the enclosure will determine whether the finished object feels like a neat handheld product or a desk-bound prototype. A smaller microcontroller could potentially handle an even more stripped-back version, but a Pi offers an easier route for managing a changing local playlist and ordinary audio files.

The idea also marks a shift from recent screen-heavy personal projects towards a deliberately tangible bit of interaction design. The experience is defined by one control, one fixed duration and a small element of surprise. There is no account, feed or menu to navigate.
That constraint is the point. Two minutes in, the device is finished with you until the next press.

articles.title: Ten years of Get Glasgow Moving
articles.standfirst: A ten-year exhibition charts how a grassroots Glasgow transport campaign moved from protest to the brink of bus franchising and Clyde Metro.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Buchanan Bus Station in Glasgow, photographed in July 2026. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Richard Sutcliffe (CC BY-SA 2.0).
Ten years of Get Glasgow Moving

A Glasgow transport campaign that began with a group of local people in 2016 is marking its first decade with an exhibition tracing ten years of pressure for a simpler, more integrated public transport system.

Get Glasgow Moving’s 10th Anniversary Exhibition is running at the New Glasgow Society on Argyle Street from 18 to 23 September, opening daily from noon until 17:00. The show looks back at the campaign’s wins and setbacks since its launch a decade ago and places that history against a much bigger question: how close Glasgow now is to the kind of joined-up network campaigners have spent years demanding.

The timing is sharp. Get Glasgow Moving says the region is now on the cusp of major change through Strathclyde Partnership for Transport’s work on bus franchising and the longer-term Clyde Metro programme. Those projects are not finished deals, and their eventual shape still matters, but they represent a markedly different transport landscape from the one the campaign entered in September 2016.
For
SWS.GOV

, the exhibition lands squarely in familiar territory. Glasgow’s fragmented transport system, the balance between public control and private operation, and the way streets and networks shape everyday life have all become recurring interests. A Sunday trip into town has now put the anniversary exhibition on the agenda as a compact bit of transport history rather than another abstract policy debate.

The campaign’s story is useful precisely because it joins those two levels together. Bus regulation can sound procedural. Integration can sound like a diagram. But the practical argument is much simpler: whether a passenger can move around Greater Glasgow without having to think about competing operators, disconnected tickets or a network whose parts do not always behave like one system.

That is also why the anniversary arrives at an interesting point politically. The exhibition describes bus franchising and Clyde Metro as routes towards a world-class integrated system, while its retrospective format makes clear that the present position took years of campaigning rather than appearing overnight. The launch event on 17 September brought together activists involved in the campaign’s early years to discuss that journey.

The New Glasgow Society exhibition is free to visit and does not require booking. Its Argyle Street location also makes the subject feel appropriately embedded in the city it is arguing about, rather than sealed off in a transport conference or policy document.

Ten years on, the campaign has not reached an end point. But an exhibition built around a decade of pressure offers a useful chance to see how far Glasgow’s transport debate has shifted, and how much of the original case for change is now moving from campaigning language into actual plans.

articles.title: One more year of a third off
articles.standfirst: A £35 renewal will keep a third off most rail fares for another year as the current 26–30 Railcard enters its final month.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: a ScotRail Class 385 at Glasgow Central. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by TriStateGuy.
One more year of a third off
The countdown is on for another year of cheaper train travel, with the current 26–30 Railcard due to expire on 16 October and the renewal window already open.

The simplest route is also the obvious one: renew the existing digital Railcard through the official Railcard account. The 26–30 card costs £35 for one year and cuts a third from most eligible rail fares across Great Britain. There is no three-year version, so there is little scope for clever shopping around here.

Official Railcard guidance says renewals can be made up to 30 days before expiry. That means the 16 October card is now comfortably inside the renewal window. For a digital Railcard bought online, renewal can be completed through the existing account and generally does not require another eligibility check.

The current card already lives in the official Railcard app, making continuity fairly painless. Once the replacement is ready, the digital card can be added to the phone rather than waiting for anything to arrive through the post.

At £35, the maths remains fairly forgiving. Railcard says the 26–30 version saves holders a third on train tickets and estimates average annual savings of £283 after the cost of the card, based on journeys made between April 2025 and March 2026. The precise saving will obviously depend on how much rail travel actually happens over the next year.

There are some restrictions worth remembering. A £12 minimum fare normally applies to journeys made between 04:30 and 09:59 from Monday to Friday, although Advance fares and public holidays are exempt. The card covers Standard Anytime, Off-Peak, Super Off-Peak and Advance tickets, with First Class Advance also included.

The timing also removes any age-related complication. A 26–30 Railcard can be bought while the holder is aged 26 to 30 and then used for its full one-year validity. With the existing card expiring next month, renewal is available now rather than requiring a switch to another product.

There is therefore no benefit in letting the current card lapse and creating a gap in discounted travel. The practical job is small: sign into the existing Railcard account, renew for £35 before 16 October, then make sure the new digital card is active in the app before using a discounted ticket after the old one expires.

It is hardly the most dramatic bit of Government business, but it is exactly the sort of boring admin that becomes expensive when ignored. One payment keeps the familiar one-third discount running for another year, with no new card to carry and no reason to leave it until the final day.

articles.title: Old iPad eyed for SWS.GOV kiosk
articles.standfirst: A search for a cheap full-screen iPad has opened up a simple route to giving SWS.GOV a dedicated always-on kiosk display.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: iPad (10th generation). Source: Wikimedia Commons, image by Riski394.
Old iPad eyed for
SWS.GOV
kiosk
A cheap second-hand iPad is being considered for a new job inside the
SWS.GOV
setup: a dedicated full-screen kiosk for the growing personal dashboard.

The idea emerged from a deliberately narrow hardware search this week. The requirement is not for a powerful tablet, a laptop replacement or another general-purpose device. It needs to run a web browser, lose the old physical Home button and present a modern edge-to-edge screen that can sit permanently on the
SWS.GOV
experience.

That makes older full-screen iPads unusually well suited to the brief. Apple’s tenth-generation iPad, released in October 2022, was the first standard iPad to adopt the flatter modern design without a Home button. It also moved the base model to USB-C, making permanent power and mounting simpler than on older Lightning-based models.

Apple still lists the tenth-generation model among iPads using USB-C. The model has since been replaced by the newer A16 iPad, leaving the older hardware as the more interesting target for a used-device search rather than a new purchase.
The important bit is what the screen would actually do. Project Indigo has been pushing
SWS.GOV

away from being a collection of pages and towards something closer to a personal operating dashboard. The redesigned homepage is intended to surface useful information, services and Government material in one place, while universal search reaches across the SWS archive, Google and the
SWS.GOV
ChatGPT project.
Putting that interface on a dedicated device changes the proposition slightly. Instead of
SWS.GOV
being something opened deliberately in a browser, it could become an ambient display: always available, immediately glanceable and separate from the phone or main computer.

That is why performance is not the priority. A kiosk does not need the latest processor, large storage capacity or premium cameras. Browser support, a clean full-screen display, reliable Wi-Fi and the ability to remain powered are the useful bits. Buying used also makes more sense for hardware expected to spend most of its life attached to a stand or wall rather than carried around.

There are still practical details to settle. A suitable second-hand model has not yet been bought, and the final setup would need a secure mount, sensible charging arrangement and a browser configuration that keeps the interface on screen without unnecessary controls getting in the way.
The hardware search nevertheless gives Project Indigo a possible physical endpoint. The redesign has so far concentrated on making
SWS.GOV
more personal and useful on the web. A cheap retired iPad could turn that same interface into a small piece of infrastructure in the flat.

articles.title: The buzz is back at GCU
articles.standfirst: A two-hour Masters introduction at Glasgow Caledonian University ended on a high as presenting familiar design material delivered an unexpected Friday buzz.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Glasgow Caledonian University campus. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Knwwsss.
The buzz is back at GCU

A Friday afternoon presentation at Glasgow Caledonian University has turned a carefully prepared return to the classroom into something more immediate: a reminder that talking about design can be genuinely good fun.

The Masters week-one introduction ran from 15:00 to 17:00 on Friday 18 September, according to the BBC calendar. It was the surviving half of a two-session plan after the earlier introduction was cancelled, making the afternoon the first proper chance to deliver the material to students.

Preparation had been deliberately light by the time the session arrived. After one run through the presenter notes, the material already felt familiar enough to avoid grinding through repeated rehearsals. The calculation was simple: the subject matter was known, the structure was understood and over-rehearsing risked making the delivery stiffer rather than better.

That approach paid off. Once the presentation was finished, the verdict was emphatic: it had been fun, with a particular buzz coming from presenting something already understood well enough to speak about naturally rather than simply reading a script.

The session drew on practical design thinking rather than treating UX as a procession of screens. One exercise asked students to design a doorbell, a prompt that predictably encourages a rectangle with a button. The brief then shifts to the actual need: design a way of knowing somebody is at the door. The change is small, but it opens the problem up and demonstrates why designers need to separate a user need from the first obvious solution.

The presentation also tackled generative AI, now difficult to avoid in a design course in 2026. The emphasis was on responsible use: AI can help explore ideas, accelerate parts of a design process and support more complex prototyping, but it should complement rather than replace design thinking. Privacy, safe tooling, checking outputs and being transparent about its use remain part of the job.

For SwS, the more interesting outcome came after the slides were done. Presenting is not a routine part of every working day, but the afternoon reinforced a useful distinction between nerves caused by unfamiliarity and the energy that comes from explaining a subject with genuine command of it.

That matters beyond one university session. Recent work has involved research synthesis, experimentation practice and explaining complex design processes to different audiences. Being able to turn that knowledge into a clear story is increasingly part of the design work itself, not an extra task bolted on afterwards.

The GCU appearance therefore closes the week on a different note from the planning that preceded it. What began as another item in the calendar ended as a fairly strong argument for doing more of this sort of thing: know the material, keep the structure clear, then get up and talk about it.

articles.title: Project Indigo redraws SWS.GOV
articles.standfirst: A beta overhaul introduces a personalised dashboard, universal search and a new design language as SWS.GOV begins its biggest rebuild yet.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Glasgow City Chambers, a suitably governmental backdrop for the latest
SWS.GOV
rebuild. Source: Wikimedia Commons.
Project Indigo redraws
SWS.GOV
SWS.GOV
has begun its biggest visual and functional overhaul yet, with the new Project Indigo experience now in beta and a markedly different idea of what the Government’s digital front door should do.

The rebuild centres on a redesigned homepage that behaves less like a conventional government landing page and more like a personal dashboard. Information is intended to be more useful at a glance, with stronger personalisation and quicker routes into the services, records and tools that matter day to day.
It is also a deliberate break from the site’s earlier look.
SWS.GOV

has long borrowed heavily from the visual language established by the UK Government Digital Service. Project Indigo keeps the same underlying commitment to clarity, accessibility and straightforward interaction, but moves towards a more distinctive modernist digital design language of its own.

That means redesigned components across the site, with new typography, colour, depth and animation being introduced as individual areas are rebuilt. The change is being rolled out progressively rather than through a single big-bang replacement, allowing older sections to remain available while their Indigo versions are completed.
Search is one of the more ambitious parts of the beta. A new universal search experience is designed to work across the
SWS.GOV
archive while also opening routes into Google and the dedicated
SWS.GOV
ChatGPT project. The aim is to make search less of a simple list of site results and more of a common starting point for finding, researching or asking for something.
The News experience has also been rebuilt. That work lands alongside a wider shift in how
SWS.GOV

content is produced, with Google Docs now acting as the canonical source for structured articles and publishing metadata. The new front end is therefore arriving at the same time as the machinery behind it is becoming more formal and reliable.
Project Indigo also marks a change in the Government’s approach to AI. Existing AI features built directly into
SWS.GOV

, including the article-writing tool, are being deprecated. Rather than maintaining separate lightweight AI features on the site, the direction now is towards closer integration with ChatGPT itself, where the broader Government for SwS context and archive can be used more effectively.

That distinction matters. The earlier approach treated AI as a feature added to individual pages. Indigo instead treats it as part of the wider information architecture, sitting alongside search, the archive and the dashboard rather than competing with them.
The rest of
SWS.GOV

will now be rebuilt piece by piece around the same principles. Planned and emerging areas include a redesigned Archive, Planner and Recipes experience, alongside the continuing conversion of existing pages to the new component system.
There is no single switch-over date for the whole site. For now, Project Indigo remains a beta running alongside the older experience. But the direction is settled: the previous
SWS.GOV
established the system; Indigo is intended to turn it into a genuinely useful personal operating surface.

articles.title: The farm hiding beside Cumbernauld’s motorway
articles.standfirst: A look at Mainhead Farm and the roads around Westerwood has opened a new line of inquiry into the landscape Cumbernauld’s New Town inherited.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Mainhead Farm, now home to Caulders Cumbernauld. Image: Caulders Garden Centres.
The farm hiding beside Cumbernauld’s motorway
A garden centre beside one of Cumbernauld’s busiest junctions has become the starting point for a deeper look at what survived when the New Town arrived.

Caulders Cumbernauld sits at Mainhead Farm beside Westerwood Roundabout, just off the M80. The business itself is a relatively recent occupant: Caulders says it took over the Cumbernauld centre in 2019 and has since expanded its plant area, restaurant and shop. But the site name points to an older layer of the landscape that is easy to miss among the motorway slips, roundabouts and industrial roads.
The question now being explored is how much of the road pattern around Mainhead predates the New Town, and how much was imposed as Cumbernauld expanded north and west.

That distinction matters because Cumbernauld was not built on empty ground. The town was designated in December 1955, but existing farms, villages and routes were already spread across the area. The original New Town was later enlarged north of the old A80, with Westfield, Balloch, Westerwood and Carrickstone among the areas brought into the planned expansion.

Wardpark adds another clue. The industrial estate became a major employment zone during the New Town era, and its road connections were necessarily important to the developing town. The former Burroughs factory there is recorded as the first factory of the Cumbernauld New Town. That makes the route towards Wardpark an obvious candidate for comparing pre-development roads with the infrastructure created for the planned town.

Carrickstone tells a slightly different story. Modern housing came later, but the name is much older. Historic mapping records Carrickstone Farm, while the area is associated with the Carrick Stone, the Roman altar that remains in the open air. The result is a familiar Cumbernauld pattern: a modern neighbourhood carrying forward a name from the rural landscape it replaced.

Mainhead now looks particularly interesting because the garden centre still presents itself using the farm name. Its address is officially Mainhead Farm, Westerwood Roundabout, Cumbernauld, G68 0EB. The surviving stonework visible around the centre also raises the obvious question of whether parts of the present complex belong to an earlier farm building, although that has not yet been established from a reliable historic source.

The next stage is therefore less about guessing from architecture and more about maps. Comparing Ordnance Survey sheets from before 1955 with New Town plans and later aerial photography should show which alignments were retained, diverted or erased as the A80, Wardpark and the western neighbourhoods developed.

It is a small investigation, but a revealing one. Cumbernauld is usually read through its modernist architecture and post-war planning. Around Westerwood, the older landscape may still be sitting in plain sight, encoded in a farm name, a bend in a road and the routes that the New Town chose not to wipe away.

articles.title: Project Indigo begins a new era for SWS.GOV
articles.standfirst: Project Indigo introduces a more personal, useful and integrated SWS.GOV, with a redesigned homepage, universal search and closer ChatGPT integration.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Project Indigo begins a new era for
SWS.GOV
Government for SwS has today announced Project Indigo, a major redesign of
SWS.GOV
that introduces a more useful, personal and integrated experience across the government’s digital platform.
Project Indigo is now available in beta. It replaces the previous GDS-derived visual approach with a new design language developed specifically for
SWS.GOV

. The principles that shaped the existing site remain: accessibility, clarity and simplicity. Indigo builds on those foundations with redesigned components, richer interaction, greater use of depth and motion, and a more distinctive visual identity.

At the centre of the new experience is a completely redesigned homepage. Rather than acting primarily as a route into different parts of the site, the homepage is becoming a personalised dashboard for SwS, bringing together useful information, government activity, services and content in one place.
News has also been rebuilt around a new experience designed to make Government for SwS communications easier to find and browse.
Project Indigo introduces universal search across
SWS.GOV

SWS.GOV
ChatGPT project. Search therefore becomes more than a way of finding pages: it provides a common route into the government’s records, external information and its growing AI capabilities.
This reflects a wider change in the relationship between
SWS.GOV
and ChatGPT. Rather than maintaining separate AI features within the website, the two systems will become more closely integrated. Existing
SWS.GOV
AI tools, including the article writer, will therefore be deprecated as this work progresses.
The beta does not represent a completed redesign. The rest of
SWS.GOV
will be rebuilt piece by piece around the principles established through Project Indigo, with existing sections moving to the new components and interaction patterns over time.
Project Indigo establishes the direction for the next generation of
SWS.GOV
: a platform that is more personal, more useful and more closely connected to the systems through which Government for SwS increasingly operates.

articles.title: GCU teaching return puts design challenge in focus
articles.standfirst: A return to Glasgow Caledonian University will put professional UX practice in front of Masters students as a new design project gets under way.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Glasgow Caledonian University campus in Glasgow. Source: Study UK, British Council.
GCU teaching return puts design challenge in focus
A return to Glasgow Caledonian University is set to put day-to-day professional UX practice directly in front of Masters students, as a new design project begins on Friday.

The two-hour introduction, scheduled for 15:00 to 17:00 on 18 September, marks another step in SwS’s growing involvement with teaching and industry outreach. The session is intended to introduce the design project to Masters students and follows earlier planning with Kevin around how to turn real design practice into a useful student challenge.

The timing is notable. SwS joined the BBC through its UX trainee route in 2022 after studying at Glasgow Caledonian, and has since moved through junior and midweight design roles into the Data and Experimentation Enablement team. Returning to the university therefore brings the route back round: recent professional experience is now becoming material for students beginning their own advanced design work.

The planned challenge is built around an everyday object rather than a grand speculative brief. A doorbell provides the starting point, giving students something immediately understandable while opening up harder questions about users, context, accessibility, behaviour and the consequences of adding technology to an apparently simple interaction.

That simplicity is useful. A doorbell has a clear basic job, but designing one well means thinking beyond the button itself. Who is arriving? Who is inside? What happens if someone cannot hear it, reach it or respond immediately? What information should be captured, and what should not? Once cameras, recognition systems, notifications or AI enter the picture, the design problem quickly becomes as much about judgement as interface craft.

The teaching plan is expected to use those tensions to push students beyond producing a polished screen. Ethics and AI form part of the wider discussion, with the emphasis on asking whether a capability should be used and what trade-offs it creates, rather than treating new technology as an automatic improvement.

That approach closely matches the work SwS has been doing at the BBC. Recent experimentation research has focused less on isolated interface problems and more on the systems around them: ownership, evidence, dependencies, governance and the points where apparently local decisions create effects elsewhere. The university session applies the same kind of thinking in a different setting.

Friday is already marked as a non-working day on the BBC calendar, with an out-of-office block from midday, clearing the afternoon for the university session. A first version of the introduction had appeared on Thursday’s calendar before being cancelled and replaced by the Friday slot.

The result is a small but meaningful expansion of the work beyond the BBC. Rather than presenting UX as a set of methods or portfolio conventions, the session has the chance to show design as the messier practice it actually is: framing problems, making choices with incomplete information and being able to explain why a decision is responsible.
For SwS, it is also a return to familiar ground with a rather different role. The next visit to GCU is not about being a student. It is about helping set the problem.

articles.title: GCU teaching return moves to Friday
articles.standfirst: A planned first Masters introduction at Glasgow Caledonian University was cancelled on Thursday, leaving Friday’s second session as the new start for the design teaching return.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Glasgow Caledonian University’s Cowcaddens campus. Source: Wikimedia Commons.
GCU teaching return moves to Friday

A planned return to Glasgow Caledonian University has shifted by a day after the first of two Masters introduction sessions was cancelled, leaving Friday afternoon as the new starting point for the design teaching work.

The BBC calendar had originally shown a two-hour session at the Cowcaddens campus from 13:00 on Thursday 17 September, but that entry is now marked cancelled. A second session remains in place for Friday 18 September from 15:00 to 17:00, described as the second of two sessions introducing the design project to Masters students.

The change is a small scheduling move, but a meaningful update to plans set out earlier this week. The teaching return had been prepared around a practical design challenge developed with Kevin, using the everyday problem of a doorbell as a route into broader questions about design decisions, ethics and the growing role of AI.

That work is intended to be more than a conventional guest lecture. The challenge gives students a deliberately ordinary object and asks them to think through the people, systems and consequences around it. The aim is to move quickly from an apparently simple interface problem into the messier territory that sits behind real product design.

Friday’s session will also mark a return to familiar ground. SwS studied at Glasgow Caledonian before leaving during the final year to join the BBC, and has since returned as a guest contributor. The university’s Glasgow operation remains a single-site city campus at Cowcaddens, where undergraduate and postgraduate teaching is concentrated within walking distance of the city centre.

The timing now sits alongside a non-working day on the BBC calendar. An out-of-office block begins at noon on Friday, before the GCU session starts at 15:00. That creates a cleaner break between BBC work and the university commitment than Thursday’s original arrangement would have allowed.

Thursday itself remains busy. A morning web experimentation session focused on self-service, targeting, assignment, tracking and measurement was followed by the wider UX&D Studio Day from 13:00. The cancelled GCU introduction would have overlapped directly with that three-hour cross-location event.

The revised plan therefore leaves the teaching work with a more distinct slot of its own. There is no indication in the calendar that Friday’s session has been cancelled or moved, so it remains the confirmed next step at the time of writing.

The substance of the project has not changed. The task is still to introduce Masters students to a design problem that can open out into questions of responsibility, technology and human judgement, rather than simply teaching a set of interface techniques.
For
SWS.GOV
, the new development is straightforward: Thursday’s planned start did not happen. Friday is now the date that matters.

articles.title: Experimentation Day puts web challenges in focus
articles.standfirst: A BBC-wide Experimentation Day has put evidence-led decision making centre stage as SwS prepares to test months of workflow research against the practical challenges of experimenting on the web.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: BBC Scotland at Pacific Quay in Glasgow. Source: Wikimedia Commons, photograph by Batchelor.
Experimentation Day puts web challenges in focus

A BBC-wide day focused on experimentation has landed at a useful moment for SwS, as months of work mapping how experiments actually happen moves towards a sharper test against the problems teams face on the web.

Experimentation Day 2026 ran from 10:00 to 15:30 on Wednesday 16 September, with a programme built around understanding users and making better decisions. The internal event brought together keynote talks, BBC lightning talks, roundtable discussions and a closing session on decision making.

For SwS, the timing is unusually neat. The current rotation in experimentation has spent recent months examining the end-to-end journey from IDEATE through PLAN, BUILD, TEST, DECIDE and LEARN, with research repeatedly surfacing friction around ownership, measurement confidence, dependencies and governance.

The emerging picture is not simply that experiments are technically difficult. Earlier problems can accumulate across the process. Unclear ownership and inconsistent involvement at the start can lead to gaps later, while uncertainty around measurement can make teams less confident in the evidence they have. By the time an experiment reaches a decision, unresolved issues can increase the need for deeper analysis and specialist input before a conclusion can be reached.

That work now has an immediate next test. The BBC calendar shows a one-hour session on Thursday morning titled “Challenges in Expeirmentation Web”, intended to capture and validate where web experimentation is slow, complex or dependent on specialist support.

Its scope runs across the full workflow, from identifying an opportunity through setup, targeting and activation to measurement and analysis. The session is also due to examine where teams cannot self-serve, limitations around signed-in and signed-out identity, targeting and segmentation, assignment and tracking, and gaps in the metrics available for analysis.

That makes Thursday less of a fresh discovery exercise and more of a chance to pressure-test the wider operating-model findings against a specific platform. The strongest opportunity is to see whether the same structural problems found across experimentation show up in web delivery, and where the web introduces genuinely different constraints.

The distinction matters. Recent synthesis has increasingly moved away from isolated pain points towards a connected account of how the system behaves. Measurement consistency, for example, is not only an analytics concern if weak confidence in data later forces additional review. Governance is not only a final sign-off issue if missing input earlier creates the need for specialist voices at the end.

The calendar also points to a busy day around the session, with an Experiment Enablement UX stand-up beforehand and the wider UX&D Studio Day beginning at 13:00. The web discussion, however, is the clearest continuation of the current experimentation work.

After several months spent turning interviews, process maps and research synthesis into a usable view of the problem, the next step is increasingly concrete: establish which problems are shared, which are web-specific, and where better enablement could remove friction without simply moving it elsewhere.

articles.title: Oasis cinema trip caps music-heavy day
articles.standfirst: A Glasgow cinema trip to see Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger rounds off a day dominated by the band’s return to the spotlight.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger. Image: film poster. Source: The FADER.
Oasis cinema trip caps music-heavy day
A trip into Glasgow for Oasis: Don’t Look Back In Anger is set to round off a day in which the Manchester band has been difficult to escape.

The 2026 documentary, directed by Dylan Southern and Will Lovelace, follows Liam and Noel Gallagher through the Oasis Live ’25 reunion tour. The film combines rehearsal, backstage and onstage footage with the brothers’ first joint interviews in more than 20 years, turning last year’s comeback into a two-hour cinema account of one of the biggest music stories of 2025.

The Glasgow screening is due to finish at 22:59 on Tuesday 15 September. With the film itself running for 123 minutes, the feature is expected to begin at roughly 20:56, after the usual cinema advertising and trailers. Travel planning earlier in the evening centred on getting from Mount Florida into Glasgow Central with enough time to spare rather than cutting the journey fine.

Several trains offered workable options. A 19:35 departure from Mount Florida, arriving at Glasgow Central at 19:45, provided a particularly comfortable margin before the advertised cinema time, while later services remained possible. The exercise was a small but familiar bit of logistics: work backwards from the actual likely film start, then decide how much hanging around in town is preferable to the risk of arriving late.

The film itself arrived in UK cinemas this month after the extraordinary scale of the Oasis reunion. It documents the Live ’25 tour, which brought Liam and Noel back onto the same stage after the band’s 2009 split. Official cinema material describes the documentary as an account not just of the performances but of the emotional impact of the comeback across generations of fans.

That makes the screening more than a straightforward concert film. The reunion was already one of the defining popular-culture events of last year, while Don’t Look Back In Anger packages the rehearsals, performances and renewed Gallagher partnership into a permanent record of it.

The cinema trip also lands amid another burst of Oasis activity. The band remains firmly back in the cultural conversation rather than existing purely as a 1990s concern, with the documentary extending the comeback beyond the stadium shows and into cinemas.

For SwS, the attraction is simpler. Oasis have remained part of the regular music rotation, and a big-screen documentary offers the sort of concentrated music-and-film night that streaming at home does not quite reproduce.

Barring any last-minute change of plan, the evening therefore ends in a cinema rather than on the sofa. After working out train times, running times and the difference between the advertised screening and the probable feature start, there is only one part left: actually watching the thing.

articles.title: Cowgate short film takes shape
articles.standfirst: A woodland visit has developed into Cowgate, a short film project rooted in childhood geography and deliberately small-scale production.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Woodland near Cumbernauld. Source: Geograph Britain and Ireland.
Cowgate short film takes shape

A return to woodland around Cumbernauld has turned into a new creative project, with Cowgate now taking shape as a short film built around memory, place and the strange gap between childhood geography and adult reality.

The project emerged from a visit to a wooded area near the Whitelees estate, where an old railway alignment and steep slopes provided the setting for a compact story. The script follows Sam returning to a spot he remembers from years earlier, initially struggling to identify the right opening through vegetation that has become considerably more overgrown.

That search is the engine of the opening sequence. The character walks, stops, doubles back and eventually recognises the route before pushing through the trees and attempting the descent. At the bottom, a barbed-wire fence provides the first physical reminder that the place has changed since childhood.

The film then pushes the premise into comedy. Gavin, Jack and Johnny enter the story, with Johnny eventually discovered in an absurd state after apparently being missing at Cowgate since 2021. The script deliberately mixes recognisable local geography and conversational Glasgow humour with a ridiculous time-gap payoff.

Development has moved quickly beyond a loose idea. A full scene has been drafted, visual storyboard work has begun and poster concepts have already been explored using character and location references. That makes Cowgate a more concrete production prospect than the quick woodland-film exercise that prompted it.

The location is central rather than incidental. Cumbernauld is unusually rich in wooded corridors, a legacy partly tied to the New Town’s extensive green-space planning. The Wildlife Trusts describes Cumbernauld Glen as ancient woodland used by walkers, cyclists and horse riders, while the Woodland Trust records the nearby Glencryan Woodland at more than 57 hectares. The wider landscape gives a small production access to paths, slopes, dense vegetation and infrastructure without requiring a constructed set.

That also suits the intended scale. Cowgate is not currently being treated as a large production with an elaborate crew or effects pipeline. The appeal is that much of its character can come from the real environment, a small cast and dialogue that sounds deliberately ordinary even as the situation becomes increasingly stupid.

The project also sits alongside a separate recent idea to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roam game. Both use the town less as generic scenery and more as source material, drawing on remembered routes, overlooked infrastructure and places that carry meaning precisely because they are mundane.

No filming date or completed production plan has yet been confirmed. The significant change is that the idea now has a title, a developed script, a defined location language and an emerging visual identity. What started as a question about what could be filmed quickly in the woods has become a short film with a recognisable shape of its own.

articles.title: Cumbernauld game plan takes shape
articles.standfirst: SwS has begun turning a long-held idea to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roam game into a practical Blender and Unity project.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Cumbernauld Town Centre in 1963. Image: MIT DOME.
Cumbernauld game plan takes shape
A long-held plan to recreate Cumbernauld as a free-roaming game world has moved a step closer to becoming a practical project, with Blender and Unity emerging as the likely route for building it.
The idea resurfaced during work this weekend on tools for sculpting landscapes, importing 3D models and creating explorable environments without having to hand-code an entire game from scratch.

The ambition is deliberately bigger than a static architectural model. The concept discussed would allow Cumbernauld to be rebuilt as a functioning virtual town, with roads, buildings, interiors and public transport all potentially added over time. Buses, cars, trains and even underground systems were among the elements considered possible using pre-made assets, custom Blender models and AI-assisted coding.
It revives what was described as a childhood dream of having “The Simpsons: Hit & Run in Cumbernauld”, but with modern tools making the prospect considerably less far-fetched than it once was.

The immediate route would be to create the base geography and key landmarks first, rather than attempting the whole town in one go. Terrain could be sculpted, selected buildings modelled in Blender and the pieces assembled inside Unity into a simple free-roam prototype. Existing asset packs could then cover less distinctive objects such as vehicles, street furniture and vegetation.

Cumbernauld is particularly suited to the idea because so much of its identity comes from the way the New Town was planned as a complete system rather than a conventional town that grew gradually. The original New Town was designated in 1956, with its roads, neighbourhoods, pedestrian routes and town centre shaped around a strongly planned post-war vision.

That physical environment is also entering a period of major real-world change. North Lanarkshire Council says the regeneration of The Centre Cumbernauld will involve its complete replacement over a long-term programme, with demolition expected to take around eight to 10 years. Current estimates put the first demolition stage in 2027-28 and the second in 2031-33.

That gives a digital recreation an extra archival dimension. A sufficiently detailed version could eventually preserve parts of the town as they existed before the next wave of redevelopment, while still functioning as a game rather than a heritage model.

No full development programme has been committed to and there is no finished prototype yet. The significance of the latest work is narrower: the project now has a plausible technical route, with the modelling work able to be done manually while Unity handles the explorable environment and AI can help bridge gaps in programming.

For an idea that once amounted to little more than wanting a hometown version of a favourite game, that is enough to move it from “wouldn’t it be good?” territory into something that could actually be built.

articles.title: Digital reset reaches public release
articles.standfirst: The public release of iOS 27 has caught up with SwS’s recent clean-install reset, moving the rebuilt Apple setup from release-candidate software onto the finished platform.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: Image: Apple’s iOS 27 and wider OS release. Source: Apple.
Digital reset reaches public release

SwS’s recent wholesale digital reset has reached its next stage after Apple released iOS 27 to the public, bringing the rebuilt personal setup onto the finished version of the software it was designed around.

The reset began before the general release, using the iOS 27, macOS 27 and watchOS 27 release candidates as the basis for a clean start across the main Apple devices. The iPhone and Mac were wiped, applications were reinstalled from scratch and the hardware itself was cleaned as part of a wider attempt to remove years of digital clutter.

Apple released iOS 27 on Monday 14 September, alongside its other major operating-system updates. The software brings the new Siri AI experience, further refinements to Liquid Glass and broader performance and search improvements. Apple says Siri AI can use personal context, work across apps and continue conversations through a dedicated Siri app.

For SwS, the timing means the reset is no longer sitting on pre-release software. The operating system around which the new setup was built has now become the standard public release, turning what began as an early clean-install exercise into the normal day-to-day configuration.

The bigger change remains organisational rather than cosmetic. Apple Photos has been reduced primarily to photographs captured on iPhone, while Google Photos is being used as the central home for the wider image archive, including older photographs, screenshots, textures and other visual material.

Google Drive has also been established as the main source of truth for projects and files, with Google Calendar taking over as the primary calendar. ChatGPT Projects are being used more deliberately for ongoing work, while Apollo Reborn has restored the preferred Reddit setup.

The approach is essentially a rejection of the usual upgrade cycle where new software is installed on top of an increasingly messy existing system. Instead, the September release became an excuse to reconsider what belongs on each device and which service should own each category of information.

There are practical benefits to doing that now. iOS 27’s improved system search and the new Siri AI both put greater emphasis on finding and acting on personal information. A cleaner division between photos, files, calendars and ongoing projects should make that information easier to manage even where Apple’s own intelligence features are not doing the work directly.

No further large-scale reset is planned. The focus now shifts from rebuilding the system to seeing whether the new structure survives ordinary use without gradually accumulating the same duplication and clutter it was designed to remove.
The software has changed overnight. The more interesting test is whether the habits change with it.

articles.title: Press Office statement: Google Docs publishing launch
articles.standfirst: The Government confirms a secure Google Docs publishing route for Project Indigo content.

runs.text: Statement
The Government has opened a controlled Google Docs publishing workflow for Project Indigo. Documents are separated by Drive folder, validated before publication and synced to a private site index.
Write access is limited to the connected allowlisted account, while public article rendering uses only the generated site data.
This is a demonstration Press Office entry.

articles.title: Government confirms Project Indigo content integration
articles.standfirst: News and Press Office documents can now feed their own Project Indigo homepage carousels.

runs.text: Separate feeds, one publishing system
Project Indigo now reads published Google articles by section. News documents populate the News row and Press Office documents populate the official updates row.
Each row displays the three newest published entries and keeps the original static cards as fallbacks when a section has fewer articles.
This is demonstration content created for launch testing.

articles.title: One feed for SwS and the wider world
articles.standfirst: Work has begun on a new SWS.GOV Superfeed designed to mix Government for SwS updates with the wider news in one ranked stream.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is moving towards a single news stream combining Government for SwS updates with stories from the wider world.
The plan is still at proposal stage, with implementation details and ranking weights yet to be settled.

The proposal would combine articles published through Craft with posts pulled from external RSS feeds. Instead of keeping personal publishing and outside news in separate lanes, the same ranking system would decide what appears prominently on the homepage and how the News section is ordered.
The idea is more ambitious than a simple chronological list.
SWS.GOV

material would receive a built-in advantage, reflecting the site’s role as the main record of SwS activity, but it would not automatically occupy every top slot. A sufficiently significant external story could rise above routine SwS updates.
That creates an unusual but useful editorial model: a personal website behaving more like a live news product, where a new
SWS.GOV
policy, project update or announcement can sit directly alongside major events in the wider world.
The proposal emerged during work on making better use of Codex with the
SWS.GOV

GitHub project. The immediate development brief is to build the feed as a reusable source rather than hard-wire it to one screen. That means the same ordered stream could power the homepage, become the default sorting method for News, or be called elsewhere in Project Indigo.
Craft is becoming more important to that system too.
SWS.GOV

’s publishing workflow is now moving towards the existing Articles collection in the Publisher space, with structured fields for status, section, tags and Superfeed behaviour. New fields include an importance setting and a pinned state, giving first-party articles explicit signals that can eventually feed into ranking.

For now, the default importance is Automatic. That leaves the system to make the normal ordering decision rather than requiring every article to be manually labelled Breaking, Major, Standard or Minor. Pinning is also off by default.
The key challenge is ranking without turning the feed into noise. Recency alone would be too crude: a minor
SWS.GOV
post published five minutes ago should not necessarily bury a genuinely major story. Equally, an external RSS source should not overwhelm the site simply because it publishes more frequently.

No final ranking formula has been implemented or announced. The current work is a product and engineering brief, and the precise weighting between source, recency, importance and other signals remains to be decided.
The direction is nevertheless clear. Project Indigo is moving away from a collection of separate content rows towards one editorial layer capable of answering a much simpler question: what should
SWS.GOV
show first right now?

articles.title: SWS.GOV plans switch from Craft to Notion
articles.standfirst: A proposed change to article publishing would put Notion at the centre of editing while keeping the website independent of its API.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is planning to move its article publishing system from Craft to Notion, in a proposed overhaul intended to make the site easier to maintain without introducing a paid content-management service.

The change is being considered as part of Project Indigo, the continuing rebuild of the Government for SwS website. Craft currently stores the official Articles collection, including News, Press Office and Daily Note content. It also provides the structured information used to decide which articles appear on the site and how they are presented.

Notion would take over as the place where articles are written, organised and prepared for publication. Its database system could manage titles, summaries, sections, tags, publishing dates and statuses, alongside the importance and pinning controls used by
SWS.GOV
's Superfeed.

The appeal is partly financial. Notion's Free plan offers unlimited pages and blocks for an individual workspace and access to its public API. That makes it a potential long-term home for a growing archive without a recurring subscription for the editorial software itself.

But the proposal is not simply to replace one API with another. Notion has request limits and its hosted media links can expire. Relying on live Notion requests every time someone opens an article would leave the website exposed to slow responses, temporary outages and unnecessary API traffic.
The preferred approach is to treat Notion as the editorial source while keeping a separate, persistent copy of published content for the website to serve. Changes would be synchronised into
SWS.GOV
, where articles could be validated, transformed into the site's existing content format and cached. Images would also need a dependable storage arrangement.
That separation matters as
SWS.GOV

develops its Superfeed. The system is designed to combine first-party Government for SwS news with stories from external RSS sources, applying editorial importance, recency and source signals to choose what appears most prominently. A change of writing software should not alter that ranking model or break established article links.
An inspection of the
SWS.GOV

GitHub repository found that the website already uses a dedicated article repository interface. The Superfeed obtains articles through that abstraction rather than depending directly on Craft. A Notion implementation could therefore reuse much of the existing presentation and ranking infrastructure.

Not everything is ready to switch. Craft-specific editing screens, publishing endpoints, image uploads and existing article conversion logic would still need to be adapted. Existing posts would have to be migrated and checked for formatting, images, dates and metadata, with their public URLs preserved.
The proposal also comes just after the introduction of a dedicated
SWS.GOV

News workflow inside ChatGPT. That workflow currently creates and verifies articles in Craft. If the migration proceeds, its publishing destination and verification steps would need to change as well.

No migration has yet been completed, and there is no confirmed launch date. The next stage would be to build and test a Notion article adapter, establish reliable synchronisation and then move the current archive before retiring Craft as the primary article source.
The wider aim is straightforward: keep editing convenient, publishing inexpensive and the website resilient, without allowing the choice of content editor to dictate the architecture of
SWS.GOV

articles.title: A newsroom inside ChatGPT
articles.standfirst: A new private SWS.GOV News plugin packages the editorial and publishing workflow for ChatGPT, with Craft verification built in.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: SWS.GOV
has acquired its own ChatGPT news-writing workflow after a private plugin was created on Wednesday 7 October, giving the site a reusable route from conversation to publication in Craft.
The plugin, named
SWS.GOV

News, was registered as a private version 0.1.0 release. Its job is to make a routine which previously required a long set of instructions available whenever a news story is needed. Rather than manually specifying the destination and fields each time, the editorial requirements now travel with the plugin.

The new workflow begins before a word is written. It asks ChatGPT to examine recent conversations across work, design, personal projects and everyday developments, then check the BBC calendar for relevant upcoming events. It must also inspect existing
SWS.GOV
articles to avoid recycling a story already published. A genuine follow-up needs a material new development; otherwise, no filler article should be produced.

Once a story is chosen, the brief calls for roughly 500 words of British-English reporting. Headlines must vary, and the writing should be brisk without tipping into parody. The rules prohibit invented quotes, officials, reactions or achievements. Proposals must remain proposals, not be presented as completed launches.

The destination is precise: the Articles collection in the Publisher space on Craft. Every new article starts as a Draft and carries its headline, unique slug, standfirst, publication date, News section, relevant tags and Craft source type. Superfeed importance is Automatic by default, and pinning stays off.

The crucial safeguard is verification. The article body and metadata must be read back before the status can change to Published. A second read confirms the final state. If an interrupted write leaves an incomplete item, the workflow is meant to repair that item instead of creating a duplicate.

The plugin follows an eventful first test of the direct Craft workflow. A Superfeed story was written and published on 7 October, although intermediate edits encountered tool-call restrictions before the full article could be verified. That experience exposed the value of keeping creation, writing and publication as separate checks.

There is an important limit. Creating the plugin establishes its reusable instructions; it does not by itself prove that every future Craft write will succeed. The plugin still depends on access to the relevant connected services, and its own end-to-end publishing behaviour remains to be tested.
For Project Indigo, the significance is practical.
SWS.GOV

already has a structured home for articles and an emerging Superfeed model for displaying them. A dedicated ChatGPT newsroom workflow is another attempt to reduce the work between spotting a worthwhile development and placing a properly checked report in the publishing system.
The newsroom has a new front door. The next test is whether it can use it reliably.

articles.title: GFT screenings set for SWS.GOV homepage
articles.standfirst: Plans for a live cinema carousel and listings page could later expand to Edinburgh Filmhouse.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: SWS.GOV
is planning to bring Glasgow Film Theatre screenings directly onto its homepage, with a new daily film carousel and a dedicated cinema listings page under consideration as part of Project Indigo.

The proposed feature, titled “Today at the GFT”, would display posters for films showing at the Glasgow cinema, with screening times listed beneath each title. Individual times would link to official booking pages, allowing the site to act as a straightforward guide to what is on without replacing the cinema’s own ticketing service.
The design brief calls for a deliberately minimal interface. Posters would sit in a horizontally scrolling row, using the established
SWS.GOV

typography, spacing and layout rather than introducing a separate cinema-themed design. On smaller screens the carousel would support touch gestures and show part of the next poster to indicate that more films are available. Subtle hover states, restrained transitions and keyboard navigation are also planned.

Films with several screenings on the same day would appear only once, with their times grouped together in chronological order. Screenings that have already passed would be subdued or removed so the component remains useful throughout the day. A separate listings page would offer a fuller programme, including date navigation and additional film information where available.
Finding a reliable source

The idea follows an investigation into Simple Cinema Listings, an independent website that presents GFT schedules in a stripped-back format. Its creator has previously described using Selenium browser automation to navigate the cinema website and collect listing links.

A more direct route may be possible. GFT’s website has previously exposed a GraphQL endpoint that could provide structured screening information without the need to automate clicks through the public interface. The endpoint and its current capabilities have not yet been verified, so the technical approach remains subject to investigation.
Under the proposed architecture,
SWS.GOV

would fetch and standardise cinema information on the server, cache it and make it available through an internal API. A refresh roughly every six hours is being considered, with the most recent successful data retained if the source temporarily becomes unavailable. The system would use UK local time and avoid displaying outdated screenings.
That separation would allow cinema data to be reused elsewhere in
SWS.GOV
, potentially including Planner or future recommendations features. Film showings would be handled as events rather than published news articles.
Edinburgh could follow
The plans are unlikely to stop at Glasgow.
Edinburgh Filmhouse is a likely candidate for inclusion in a future phase
, extending the listings beyond GFT and creating the possibility of a two-city independent cinema guide.

Simple Cinema Listings already demonstrates the appeal of presenting programming from both venues in a consistent format. However, Filmhouse would require its own investigation into available data sources, permissions and update reliability before an integration could be confirmed.
The proposal reflects a broader Project Indigo ambition to make
SWS.GOV

useful as a daily destination, combining personal publishing with practical information about life beyond the website. Cinema listings would offer a particularly tangible example: a simple glance at the homepage could reveal whether there is something worth seeing that evening.

No launch date has been confirmed, and neither cinema integration is yet live. The next step is to establish a reliable and appropriate source for GFT data, then implement and test the homepage component and wider listings interface.

articles.title: Pollok walk turns into a 10K
articles.standfirst: An after-work walk from the Southside into Pollok Country Park covered 9.83km, with more than two hours spent on foot.

blocks.alt: Image
blocks.caption: Image

runs.text: What started as a decision to get out after work turned into a substantial Southside walk on Wednesday, with a 9.83km route through Shawlands, Pollokshaws and Pollok Country Park.

The walk began at 16:09 and finished at 18:50, taking 2 hours 40 minutes from start to finish. Apple Watch recorded 2 hours 16 minutes of workout time, an average pace of 13 minutes 50 seconds per kilometre and 105 metres of elevation gain.

The route headed west from the Battlefield and Shawlands area, continued through Pollokshaws and entered Pollok Country Park before looping back east by a different route. Rather than treating the park as a single destination, the walk became a broad circuit through the Southside and the park landscape.

The original plan had been considerably less ambitious: an after-work visit to Pollok Country Park, with the possibility of a relatively short wander before heading home. In practice, the route grew into a little over six miles on foot.

The walk also provided an opportunity to pay closer attention to the changing urban landscape between Shawlands and Pollok. The route passes from dense tenement neighbourhoods and major roads into the older fabric of Pollokshaws, before crossing into the much greener and quieter park.

That contrast was part of the point. Recent Government for SwS thinking has put greater emphasis on spending time outdoors, moving around Glasgow on foot and engaging more deliberately with the Southside rather than defaulting to time at home after work.

The physical effort was significant without being a conventional high-intensity workout. Average heart rate was 125 bpm and the watch recorded 435 active calories, rising to 611 total calories over the session. The workout was rated at effort level 7, or Hard.

Heart rate remained relatively steady through the earlier kilometres before climbing later in the walk. The recorded graph shows a late peak of around 169 bpm. The first four kilometre splits were completed at between 11:46 and 12:41 per kilometre, before the pace slowed as the route continued.

The result is a useful addition to the normal Body routine. Walking does not replace the existing strength programme, but a long, low-intensity session can add meaningful movement and time outdoors without requiring another gym workout.

More importantly, it demonstrated that a weekday evening can accommodate something more substantial than the usual transition from work to home. Pollok Country Park is close enough to become part of normal Southside life rather than something reserved for a planned weekend trip.
The 9.83km circuit may have been more than intended, but that was ultimately the success of it: a spontaneous after-work walk became a proper Glasgow excursion.

articles.title: DIBI warning over culturally thin design
articles.standfirst: A standout Edinburgh conference talk challenges the idea that a single interface can work equally well across cultures.

blocks.alt: DIBI warning over culturally thin design

runs.text: A warning against culturally generic digital products has emerged as one of the strongest lessons from DIBI 2026, following a talk in Edinburgh on Thursday 1 October about what designers lose when they assume one interface can serve the whole world.

French designer Guillaume Valin examined how culture influences the way people interpret symbols, names, language and familiar digital conventions. The argument went beyond translating strings or swapping regional imagery. A product can be technically accessible and globally available while still making assumptions rooted in a narrow cultural context.

For SwS, whose work centres on UX design and experimentation, the session stood out among two days of presentations and workshops at DIBI. Its central lesson was that international design requires more than consistency. It demands attention to the meanings that different people attach to apparently universal interface elements.
The danger of a universal default

Valin drew attention to PlayStation controller symbols, phonetic name fields and changing interpretations of the @ symbol. These examples point to a recurring design problem: an element that seems obvious to one audience may carry a different association, or no useful association at all, for another.

Names are a particularly practical example. An interface built around a single set of assumptions about pronunciation, ordering or characters may work smoothly for its original audience but create unnecessary work elsewhere. Adding a translated label does not resolve a flawed underlying model.

The discussion also questioned whether redundancy in interfaces is always wasteful. Extra cues, labels or explanations can help establish meaning where a supposedly intuitive symbol does not travel well. Removing them in pursuit of visual simplicity may make a product cleaner for one group and less understandable for another.

Valin's suggested direction was a common product core supported by an adaptive layer, rather than either completely separate regional products or a rigid, one-size-fits-all interface. That distinction has direct implications for design systems: consistency should protect coherent behaviour, not freeze every cultural assumption into a universal component.
A question for AI design
The talk extended the issue to AI, raising the possibility that systems trained and deployed at enormous scale could flatten cultural differences rather than reflect them.

The risk is not necessarily an obviously incorrect answer or interface. It is something subtler: outputs that feel broadly acceptable but lack the local voice, context and distinctions that give communication meaning. Valin described the result as culturally thin.

The observation adds nuance to the wider AI debate heard at DIBI. Other sessions focused on the growing influence of AI in products and workplaces, including the relationship between AI systems and established software tools. Valin's contribution asked a different question: what qualities should technological progress preserve?

For Government for SwS, the practical response is to treat cultural assumptions as design decisions that can be identified, tested and reconsidered. That applies to forms, terminology, icons, content and the increasingly common use of generative AI in design workflows.
Beyond the conference

DIBI took place across 30 September and 1 October, with workshops and talks covering storytelling, coding, product development and artificial intelligence. The cultural design session became a personal highlight, offering a particularly useful counterweight to claims that AI and global design systems naturally make digital work more universal.
Its lesson is straightforward but demanding. A product does not become inclusive simply because it can be used everywhere. Designers must understand what changes when it arrives somewhere new.
The challenge is not to abandon shared standards. It is to make sure that shared standards leave room for difference.
